countries.name: Germany
countries.tagline: Slate, sugar and the northern edge of ripeness: the country that taught the world what Riesling can do, now making some of Europe's most exciting Pinot Noir.

stats.note: OIV State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026). Destatis puts the 2025 must/wine output at 7.55 mhl; the 2026 harvest was estimated at about 8 mhl in October 2026.

countries.overview:
Germany sits right on the edge of where wine grapes ripen, and almost everything that makes its wine special flows from that fact. Along the 50th parallel the growing season is long and cool, so grapes hang on the vine into October and November, building flavour slowly while keeping their acidity. Riesling, the grape Germany made famous, thrives on that knife edge: it can give bone-dry wines of lime and slate, featherweight Kabinett with 8 percent alcohol and a lick of sweetness, or Trockenbeerenauslese as thick as honey that will outlive its makers. Germany grows close to half of the world's Riesling, and no other country uses it in so many voices.

The vineyards follow rivers. The Rhine and its tributaries (Mosel, Saar, Ruwer, Nahe, Main, Neckar, Ahr) cut deep valleys into the old rocks of central Europe, and the best sites are the south-facing slopes where the water reflects light and holds warmth. On the Mosel those slopes are made of Devonian slate so steep that vines are tied to single stakes and worked by hand or by winch. In the Pfalz and Rheinhessen the land opens into rolling limestone, loess and sandstone, and in Baden's Kaiserstuhl the vines grow on the terraces of an extinct volcano, in the warmest corner of the country. Thirteen official wine regions (Anbaugebiete) cover about 102,000 hectares, from the Swiss border to Saxony on the Elbe.

History left Germany with a ladder of ripeness. The 1971 wine law ranked quality wine by the sugar in the grapes at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese, plus Eiswein from grapes frozen on the vine. The system rewarded ripeness in a country where ripeness was rare, but it also allowed bland, sweet blends to wear prestigious names. The same law merged some 30,000 vineyard names into about 2,600 Einzellagen and invented roughly 160 Großlagen, collective sites that let wine from a dozen villages borrow the name of the most famous one. Cheap Liebfraumilch and Piesporter Michelsberg flooded export markets in the 1970s and 1980s and dragged the country's reputation down with them.

The comeback was led by growers. The VDP, an association of about 200 leading estates, built its own Burgundy-style pyramid (Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage, Grosse Lage) and branded the dry wines from its top sites Grosses Gewächs. The national law followed: the 2021 reform reorganised German wine around origin instead of sugar, demoted the Großlage to a mere 'Region', and made the new rules binding from the 2026 vintage. Germany now sells itself the way Burgundy does, by place.

The other revolution is in the glass. Most German wine drunk at home is now dry (trocken), and warming summers have changed what is possible. Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) covers more than a tenth of the vineyard, making Germany one of the largest Pinot Noir growers in the world, and the reds of the Ahr, Baden, Franken's red sandstone and the Pfalz now sit comfortably beside good Burgundy. Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder and Chardonnay have spread, Silvaner has been rediscovered in Franken and Rheinhessen, and Sekt made by the traditional method is finally being taken seriously by the growers themselves.

Climate change is a gift with a bill attached. Vintages that would once have failed now ripen every year, but hail, drought, spring frost and torrential rain arrive more often; the July 2021 flood tore through the Ahr valley and destroyed cellars that had stood for centuries. The 2025 harvest came in at about 7.6 million hectolitres, 10 percent under the recent average, and the productive vineyard keeps shrinking slowly as small growers retire. What remains is more ambitious than at any point since the late nineteenth century, when the best Rheingau and Mosel Rieslings cost more than first-growth Bordeaux.

history.title: Romans plant the Mosel
history.text: Roman soldiers and settlers brought the vine to the Rhine and Mosel. Augusta Treverorum (Trier) became an imperial capital in the late empire, and its court and garrisons needed wine. Excavated press houses at Piesport, Brauneberg and Erden show that wine was made on the same slopes that are famous today.

history.title: The Neumagen wine ship
history.text: A stone funerary monument carved around 220 AD shows a galley rowed by oarsmen and loaded with wine casks. Found in 1878 at Neumagen in the walls of a later Roman fort, it is the most famous image of Roman wine trade north of the Alps; the original is in the Rheinisches Landesmuseum in Trier.

history.title: The Speyer bottle
history.text: A glass amphora-bottle found in a Roman grave near Speyer in 1867 still holds liquid: the oldest known bottle of wine, sealed with olive oil and resin. It sits, unopened, in the Historisches Museum der Pfalz.

history.title: Ausonius writes the Mosella
history.text: The Gallo-Roman poet Ausonius described vine-clad slopes reflected in the river in his poem Mosella, the first literary portrait of a German wine landscape.

history.title: Charlemagne's estates
history.text: Charlemagne's gift of the fiscus Hammelburg to the abbey of Fulda in 777 includes the earliest documented vineyards in Franken, and his estate ordinance Capitulare de villis set rules for clean winemaking. Legend credits him with ordering vines on the Johannisberg after seeing the snow melt there first.

history.title: Cistercians found Kloster Eberbach
history.text: Monks from Clairvaux settled in the Rheingau and built one of the largest wine businesses of medieval Europe, with their own ships on the Rhine. They walled the Steinberg, and their cellars still hold historic vintages.

history.title: First written mention of Riesling
history.text: An inventory of the Counts of Katzenelnbogen at Rüsselsheim records money spent on 'riesslingen in die wingarten', the earliest known reference to the grape.

history.title: Schloss Johannisberg goes all Riesling
history.text: After the Prince-Abbot of Fulda acquired the Johannisberg, the estate was replanted around 1720 with Riesling alone, often called the first large single-variety Riesling vineyard.

history.title: The late-harvest courier
history.text: The courier carrying permission to begin the harvest from Fulda to Johannisberg arrived weeks late. The grapes had rotted with botrytis, the wine turned out superb, and the Spätlese (late harvest) was born, at least according to the legend that a statue at the castle commemorates.

history.title: The first Eiswein
history.text: Growers in Dromersheim near Bingen pressed grapes frozen in the hard winter of 1829 to 1830, the first documented German ice wine.

history.title: Maps and crossings
history.text: Prussia's 1868 tax map of the Mosel and Saar ranked vineyards by value, a ranking the VDP later used for its Grosse Lage. In 1872 the Geisenheim research institute opened, and in 1882 Hermann Müller from Thurgau bred the cross that became Müller-Thurgau there.

history.title: The wine law of 1971
history.text: The Prädikat ladder was codified, about 30,000 vineyard names were cut to some 2,600 Einzellagen, and around 160 Großlagen were created. The Nahe became a region in its own right. The law shaped German labels for half a century.

history.title: Origin replaces sugar
history.text: A reform in force from 27 January 2021 reorganised quality wine into an origin pyramid (Anbaugebiet, Region, Ortswein, Lagenwein) and required former Großlagen to carry the word 'Region'. The rules are binding from the 2026 vintage; in 2025 a court refused to let Zell keep 'Zeller Schwarze Katz'.

history.title: The Ahr flood
history.text: A stalled storm turned the little Ahr into a torrent that killed more than 130 people in the valley and wrecked wineries from Altenahr to Bad Neuenahr. Growers rebuilt with help from a nationwide 'Flutwein' campaign.

countries.classification:
Two pyramids now coexist on German labels, and a wine nerd needs both.

The legal pyramid starts with Deutscher Wein (no origin beyond Germany) and Landwein (a PGI, 26 regions). Most wine is Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein, which are PDO wines from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete. Under the 2021 reform, origin is layered inside the PDO: the Anbaugebiet (a wine labelled only 'Pfalz' is meant to be dry), the Region (the old Bereich or Großlage, which must now be printed as 'Region Michelsberg' and the like), the Ortswein from a single village (85 percent of grapes from the village), and the Lagenwein from a single vineyard, which must name both village and site ('Hochheimer Hölle'). A Gewann, a lieu-dit within a vineyard, may appear if it is registered. The rule of thumb written into the law is: the smaller the origin, the stricter the rules.

The Prädikat ladder survives as a measure of grape ripeness at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese (BA), Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) and Eiswein. Prädikatswein may not be chaptalised. In practice Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese increasingly signal fruity sweetness, while dry wines are labelled trocken; 'feinherb' is an unregulated term for off-dry.

The private pyramid belongs to the VDP: Gutswein (estate wine), Ortswein (village), Erste Lage (premier cru) and Grosse Lage (grand cru). Dry wine from a Grosse Lage is a Grosses Gewächs (GG), hand-picked, capped at 50 hl/ha and released no earlier than September of the year after harvest (reds a year later). Since the 2024 vintage the terms Grosses Gewächs and Erstes Gewächs are also defined in the national wine ordinance, and responsibility for classifying vineyards as Erste or Grosse Lage has shifted to the VDP and the national growers' association, so the two pyramids are slowly converging.

Sparkling wine is Sekt; Sekt b.A. comes from a named Anbaugebiet, and Winzersekt is grower-made by the traditional method. Liebfraumilch is a legally defined, mild Qualitätswein from Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Rheingau or Nahe.
countries.climate_soils:
Germany is a cool continental to temperate maritime country where every degree of warmth counts. Rivers moderate frost and reflect sunlight; forests on the hilltops (Hunsrück, Taunus, Haardt, Odenwald, Black Forest) shelter the slopes from wind and rain. Most top vineyards face south to south-west at 100 to 350 metres.

The rocks are unusually varied. Devonian slate and quartzite of the Rhenish Massif dominate the Mosel, Saar, Ruwer, Mittelrhein, Ahr and western Rheingau, giving lean, smoky, mineral wines. The Nahe mixes slate with volcanic porphyry, melaphyre and sandstone. Rheinhessen's Roter Hang is red Permian sandstone and shale, while its southern Wonnegau and Franken's Maindreieck sit on limestone. The Pfalz has sandstone, limestone, loess and a basalt outcrop at Forst. Baden runs from granite in the Ortenau to volcanic rock on the Kaiserstuhl and limestone in the Markgräflerland; Franken shows the full Triassic sequence of red sandstone, shell limestone and Keuper marl; Saxony has granite and gneiss on the Elbe.

Warming since the 1980s has advanced harvests by two to three weeks. Must weights that were once exceptional are now routine, which helps reds and dry wines but threatens the delicate, low-alcohol Kabinett style; growers increasingly pick earlier, choose cooler sites and plant fungus-resistant varieties.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: About a quarter of the vineyard and the national signature; dominant in the Mosel, Rheingau, Nahe, Mittelrhein and much of the Pfalz. Germany holds close to half the world's Riesling.

grapes.name: Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir)
grapes.note: Second most planted variety and Germany's great red, from the Ahr's slate to the Kaiserstuhl's volcanic soils and Franken's red sandstone.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau (Rivaner)
grapes.note: The Geisenheim cross of 1882 that dominated after 1970; still widespread for easy whites, especially in Rheinhessen, Baden and Franken.

grapes.name: Grauburgunder and Weißburgunder
grapes.note: Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc, both expanding fast, especially in Baden and the Pfalz.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.note: Franken's classic and Rheinhessen's heritage grape; earthy, herbal and deeply food-friendly.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.note: A deep-coloured 1955 Weinsberg cross that boomed in the 1990s for soft reds.

grapes.name: Lemberger and Trollinger
grapes.note: Blaufränkisch and Schiava, the red pillars of Württemberg.

grapes.name: Frühburgunder
grapes.note: An early-ripening Pinot mutation, a specialty of the Ahr and Franken.

grapes.name: Scheurebe and Kerner
grapes.note: Aromatic crosses: Scheurebe (1916, Alzey) can be thrilling sweet or dry; Kerner was bred at Weinsberg in 1929.

grapes.name: Elbling and Gutedel
grapes.note: Ancient Elbling survives on the Obermosel limestone; Gutedel (Chasselas) is the house wine of the Markgräflerland.

countries.name: Austria
countries.tagline: Grüner Veltliner on Danube terraces, Blaufränkisch in Pannonian heat, and a wine country reborn from scandal into one of Europe's most rigorous.

stats.note: OIV State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (2.5 mhl, 17th in the OIV table); Statistik Austria counted 2.56 mhl for 2025, the biggest crop since 2018. Vineyard area 44,210 ha per Austrian Wine and Advantage Austria.

countries.overview:
Austria makes wine only in its east, where the Alps drop to the Danube and the Pannonian plain, and almost all of its 44,210 hectares lie in four federal states: Niederösterreich (Lower Austria), Burgenland, Steiermark (Styria) and Wien (Vienna). That small area holds a surprising range of climates. Cool air drains off the forested Waldviertel into the Danube valley at night; hot, dry continental summers bake the plains around Lake Neusiedl; and warm, wet Mediterranean influence reaches the steep green hills of southern Styria on the Slovenian border. So Austria does crisp whites, serious reds and some of the world's great sweet wines with equal conviction.

Grüner Veltliner is the national grape, on about a third of the vineyard (32.3 percent). It can be a light, peppery tavern wine for a summer evening or a dense single-vineyard white from the Wachau, Kamptal or Kremstal that stands beside white Burgundy and ages for twenty years. Riesling covers far fewer hectares but gives some of the country's most profound wines on the stony Danube terraces. Among reds, Zweigelt (13.4 percent, a 1922 Klosterneuburg crossing) is the everyday favourite, while Blaufränkisch (5.8 percent) is Austria's most expressive red, a grape that shows its soil the way Pinot Noir does, at its best in Mittelburgenland, on the Leithaberg and at Eisenberg. Welschriesling, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir, the Thermenregion's Zierfandler and Rotgipfler, Styria's Sauvignon Blanc and Gelber Muskateller, and Vienna's Gemischter Satz field blends complete the picture.

The defining event of modern Austrian wine was a disaster. In 1985 German laboratories found diethylene glycol in Austrian wines on German supermarket shelves; a small group of brokers had been adding it to fake the richness of expensive late-harvest wines. Germany issued a health warning, Japan banned Austrian wine outright, and exports collapsed from about 45 million litres a year to 4.4 million in 1986. Parliament passed what was then Europe's strictest wine law within weeks, a national marketing board was set up, and a generation of growers turned from cheap sweet wine to dry, terroir-driven quality. Export volumes only regained their pre-scandal level around 2001, but the wines that came back were far better than those that left.

Since 2002 Austria has built a French-style appellation system, the DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus), region by region. The Weinviertel was first; with the Thermenregion in 2023, all of the country's specific wine-growing areas were covered by 18 DACs, each with rules about grapes and style that tell the drinker what the place stands for. Most use a Burgundy-like pyramid of regional wine (Gebietswein), village wine (Ortswein) and single-vineyard wine (Riedenwein). Private groups classified the best sites first (Vinea Wachau, the ÖTW in the Danube regions, Styria's STK), and a 2023 ordinance created the legal basis for official Erste Lage and Große Lage vineyards, region by region, from 2025 onward.

Austria is also a leader in green farming: 10,432 hectares, a quarter of the vineyard, are certified organic, one of the highest shares of any wine country, and biodynamics has deep roots from Nikolaihof in the Wachau to the Pannobile growers of Gols. The Heuriger, the tavern where growers sell their own young wine under a bunch of pine twigs, keeps wine part of daily life, above all in Vienna, the only world capital with a serious wine industry inside its city limits. The 2025 harvest was generous (2.56 million hectolitres, 37 percent more than the frost- and hail-hit 2024) and, as in most recent vintages, the quality was high. Exports reached 60.6 million litres worth 218.9 million euros.

history.title: Grape seeds at Zagersdorf
history.text: Seeds of cultivated grapes from a Hallstatt-era burial mound at Zagersdorf in Burgenland are among the oldest evidence of viticulture in central Europe. Celtic bronze wine flagons of the fifth century BC turned up at the Dürrnberg near Hallein.

history.title: Romans on the Danube
history.text: The Romans held the Danube frontier from Carnuntum and Favianis (Mautern). Emperor Probus (276 to 282) is credited with lifting limits on vine planting north of the Alps, and viticulture spread through Noricum and Pannonia.

history.title: Klosterneuburg founded
history.text: Margrave Leopold III founded the Augustinian abbey of Klosterneuburg, still Austria's largest private wine estate after about 900 years. Bavarian and Austrian abbeys (Tegernsee, Niederaltaich, Göttweig, Melk, Zwettl) built the Wachau and Kamptal terraces.

history.title: The first named vineyard
history.text: The Kremser Sandgrube (1208) and the Steiner Pfaffenberg (1230) are the oldest recorded vineyard names in Austria, proof that the single site has been a unit of value here for eight centuries.

history.title: The Ungeld
history.text: Duke Rudolf IV introduced the Ungeld, the first tax on wine sold in taverns, a sign of how central wine was to the medieval economy of Vienna and Lower Austria.

history.title: Rust buys its freedom with wine
history.text: The lakeside town of Rust paid Emperor Leopold I a large sum in gold and a quantity of its prized Ausbruch sweet wine to become a royal free town, a status it still holds as Austria's smallest statutory city.

history.title: Joseph II's Heuriger decree
history.text: Emperor Joseph II allowed all residents to sell wine and juice they had made themselves, founding the Heuriger and Buschenschank tavern tradition.

history.title: Klosterneuburg school and phylloxera
history.text: The wine school at Klosterneuburg (1860), one of the oldest in the world, gave Austria the KMW must-weight scale. Phylloxera was found in Austria in 1872; replanting favoured Grüner Veltliner.

history.title: Zweigelt is crossed
history.text: Friedrich Zweigelt crossed Sankt Laurent with Blaufränkisch at Klosterneuburg. The grape, first called Rotburger, became Austria's most planted red. Zweigelt's Nazi party record has since led some growers to call for the old name again.

history.title: Lenz Moser's high culture
history.text: Lenz Moser III at Rohrendorf promoted wide-spaced, high-trained vines (Hochkultur), which cut labour costs and were adopted across Austria and abroad.

history.title: The glycol scandal
history.text: Diethylene glycol was found in Austrian wines in German supermarkets from late June 1985. A German health warning followed on 9 July and Japan banned Austrian wine. A strict new wine law passed on 29 August 1985. Exports fell to a tenth and took about 15 years to recover.

history.title: Vinea Wachau and Smaragd
history.text: Wachau growers founded Vinea Wachau in 1983 and adopted the Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd categories for unchaptalised dry wines; Smaragd was first used in 1986.

history.title: Two wine landscapes on the UNESCO list
history.text: The Wachau Cultural Landscape was inscribed in 2000 and the Fertő/Neusiedlersee Cultural Landscape in 2001.

history.title: The DAC system
history.text: Weinviertel DAC (from the 2002 vintage) began the system; Thermenregion DAC (2023 vintage) completed it at 18 DACs. A 2023 ordinance created the legal basis for official Erste and Große Lagen.

countries.classification:
Austrian labels mix three layers, and the most useful is origin.

DAC. Each of the 18 DACs fixes the grapes and style that may use the regional name; anything else from the same place is sold under the broader federal-state origin (Niederösterreich, Burgenland, Steiermark, Wien). A Kamptal DAC is therefore always Grüner Veltliner or Riesling, a Mittelburgenland DAC always Blaufränkisch, a Weststeiermark DAC usually Schilcher. Most DACs now use three tiers: Gebietswein (regional), Ortswein (village) and Riedenwein (single vineyard, labelled 'Ried' plus the site name), with stricter yields, later release dates and often hand harvesting higher up. A 2023 collective ordinance lets each region classify Rieden as Erste Lage and, at least five years later, Große Lage, with criteria including history, homogeneity of soil and climate, market value and critical reputation; the terms may appear only on DAC wines.

Quality levels. Qualitätswein (including the light, unchaptalised Kabinett) and Prädikatswein, graded by must weight in degrees KMW (Klosterneuburger Mostwaage): Spätlese (19), Auslese (21), Eiswein, Strohwein or Schilfwein (straw- or reed-dried grapes) and Beerenauslese (25), Ausbruch (27) and Trockenbeerenauslese (30).

Private classifications. In the Wachau, Vinea Wachau's Steinfeder (up to 11.5 percent alcohol), Federspiel (11.5 to 12.5) and Smaragd (above 12.5) describe ripeness for unchaptalised dry wines. The ÖTW (Österreichische Traditionsweingüter, founded 1991, 78 members by 2023) has used 'ÖTW Erste Lage' since the 2009 vintage for top Danube-region sites, and Styria's STK and Burgenland groups such as Pannobile and Renommierte Weingüter Burgenland apply their own rules.
countries.climate_soils:
Austria's vineyards meet three climatic forces. The Pannonian plain to the east pushes hot, dry summers and cold winters into Burgenland, the Weinviertel and the Thermenregion. Along the Danube, cool northern air from the Waldviertel plateau drops into the valleys at night, preserving acidity and aroma in Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal wines. In Styria, Mediterranean influence brings more rain and warmth, so grapes grow on steep, well-drained slopes to avoid rot.

Soils are just as varied. The Danube terraces sit on the crystalline rocks of the Bohemian Massif (gneiss, amphibolite, mica schist, granulite), often covered by loess; the Kamptal's Heiligenstein is Permian desert sandstone. The Weinviertel is mostly loess, with limestone and the Waschberg klippen. Lake Neusiedl's eastern shore is sand, gravel and saline soils; the Leithagebirge is Leitha limestone and schist; Mittelburgenland has heavy, deep clays; Eisenberg has greenschist and iron-rich loam. Southern Styria's opok (calcareous marl and sandstone) and schist contrast with the basalt and tuff of the Vulkanland.

Lake Neusiedl, a steppe lake under two metres deep and 315 square kilometres in area, warms the region and its autumn mists favour noble rot, making Burgenland one of the most reliable botrytis areas in the world.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.note: About 32 percent of the vineyard. Peppery and fresh in the Weinviertel, deep and mineral on the Danube. Its parents are Traminer and an ancient vine found at St. Georgen in the Leithagebirge.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.note: About 13 percent; juicy, cherry-fruited red, the backbone of Neusiedlersee DAC and much Carnuntum and Weinviertel red.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.note: About 6 percent; crisp everyday white in Styria and Burgenland and a great botrytis grape around Lake Neusiedl. Unrelated to Riesling.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.note: About 6 percent; Austria's noblest red, peppery, dark-fruited and site-sensitive, dominant in Mittelburgenland, Eisenberg, Leithaberg and Rosalia.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: A small share of the vineyard but the summit of Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal quality.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc and Gelber Muskateller
grapes.note: The aromatic stars of Styria.

grapes.name: Zierfandler and Rotgipfler
grapes.note: Thermenregion specialities around Gumpoldskirchen, often blended as Spätrot-Rotgipfler.

grapes.name: Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Thermenregion and northern Burgenland reds of growing finesse.

grapes.name: Blauer Wildbacher
grapes.note: The source of Schilcher, West Styria's searingly fresh rosé.

grapes.name: Roter Veltliner, Neuburger, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay (Morillon)
grapes.note: Supporting whites; Roter Veltliner is a Wagram speciality, Morillon is the Styrian name for Chardonnay.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.tagline: Terraced lakeshores and Alpine valleys where Chasselas, Petite Arvine and Cornalin grow almost nowhere else, and the Swiss drink nearly all of it.

stats.note: Federal Office for Agriculture (FOAG) via swissinfo.ch: 82 million litres harvested in 2025 from 14,432 ha. OIV puts Swiss consumption at 2.3 mhl in 2025, so imports dominate.

countries.overview:
Switzerland has about 14,400 hectares of vines, less than the Rheingau and Mosel combined, spread across all 26 cantons but concentrated in the French-speaking west and the Italian-speaking south. Its wine is almost a secret: the Swiss drink nearly all of it, exports are a tiny share, and the country imports about two thirds of what it consumes. Yet within that small output are some of the most spectacular vineyards in Europe and a set of grapes found almost nowhere else.

The landscape does the work. Vines cling to terraces above Lake Geneva in Lavaux (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007), climb the sun-baked slopes of the Rhône valley in the Valais to over 1,100 metres at Visperterminen, line the Jura lakes of Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten, and grow on the pergolas and hills of Ticino. Lakes and mountains create warm pockets: in the Valais the Alps block rain and the föhn wind dries the slopes, making it one of the sunniest and driest places in Switzerland. Many of the finest vineyards are so steep that they are worked by hand, monorail and even helicopter.

Chasselas is the white grape that defines western Switzerland, especially Vaud. It is neutral on its own but takes on the character of place so clearly that Swiss growers treat it the way Burgundians treat Chardonnay: Dézaley tastes different from Yvorne, and a well-kept Chasselas can age for decades. Pinot Noir is the most planted grape overall, from the Bündner Herrschaft in Graubünden to Neuchâtel and the Valais, and Gamay, Merlot (the grape of Ticino since the early twentieth century) and Müller-Thurgau follow. The Valais alone has dozens of varieties, including the native or Alpine Petite Arvine, Amigne, Humagne Blanche, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Heida (Savagnin).

Swiss wine law delegates appellations to the cantons. Geneva introduced the first cantonal AOC rules in the late 1980s, the Valais introduced a quality hierarchy in 1990, and today each canton runs one or more AOCs, some with Grand Cru or Premier Grand Cru levels. The result is local and sometimes confusing (Fendant is Valais Chasselas, Dôle a Pinot-Gamay blend, Johannisberg is Sylvaner), but it maps closely onto the country's patchwork of languages and cantons.

Pressures are real. The area under vine has fallen slowly for decades, and federal support was needed in 2024 and 2025 as cheap imports and falling consumption squeezed prices. The 2025 harvest of 82 million litres was up 9 percent from a small 2024 but about 9 million litres below the ten-year average, and growers in Ticino fought an invasion of Japanese beetle. The quality, on all accounts, was excellent.

history.title: A Celtic wine bottle in the Valais
history.text: A ceramic bottle found in a Celtic tomb at Sembrancher in the Valais, dated to the second century BC, is the oldest evidence of wine in Switzerland.

history.title: Romans bring the vine
history.text: Roman settlements at Aventicum (Avenches), Octodurus (Martigny) and around Lake Geneva spread viticulture. Some Valais grapes, perhaps Amigne and Rèze, may descend from vines of that era.

history.title: Monks terrace Lavaux
history.text: Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries, with the bishops of Lausanne, built the first terraces of Lavaux; the Cistercians of Hautcrêt and Montheron shaped the Dézaley.

history.title: First Fête des Vignerons
history.text: The Confrérie des Vignerons of Vevey staged its first great festival on 9 August 1797. It is held about once a generation; the 2019 edition filled a 20,000-seat arena, and UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2016.

history.title: Phylloxera and mildew
history.text: Phylloxera and powdery mildew reached Switzerland in the late nineteenth century. The vineyard fell from about 33,000 ha at the end of the century to about 12,500 ha around 1960.

history.title: Merlot comes to Ticino
history.text: After phylloxera destroyed Ticino's old vineyards, Merlot from Bordeaux was planted from 1906 and became the canton's signature.

history.title: Cantonal AOCs
history.text: Geneva led the move to French-style cantonal appellations, and the Valais introduced the first cantonal quality hierarchy in 1990.

history.title: Lavaux becomes World Heritage
history.text: Lavaux, Vineyard Terraces, was inscribed by UNESCO in July 2007: about 830 hectares of terraces along 30 km of the north shore of Lake Geneva.

countries.classification:
Appellations are cantonal. Each canton defines its AOC or AOCs, permitted grapes, yields and minimum sugar levels; federal law sets the framework. Most cantons have a single cantonal AOC (Genève, Valais, Neuchâtel, Ticino, Zürich, Schaffhausen, Graubünden and so on); Vaud divides itself into eight regional AOCs (Chablais, Lavaux, Calamin, Dézaley, La Côte, Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars and Vully), with communal names such as Yvorne, Aigle, Epesses, Saint-Saphorin, Féchy and Mont-sur-Rolle used inside them.

Grand Cru levels exist in several cantons. Vaud has two Grand Cru AOCs (Dézaley and Calamin) plus 'Premier Grand Cru' for individual estates, the Valais allows communes to define Grand Cru rules (Salgesch, Vétroz, Fully, Saint-Léonard and others), Geneva has Premier Cru communes, and the Neuchâtel and Three Lakes cantons have their own. Traditional names are protected locally: Fendant (Valais Chasselas), Dôle (a Valais red blend of Pinot Noir and Gamay), Salvagnin (a Vaud red blend), Oeil de Perdrix (Pinot Noir rosé, especially Neuchâtel), Johannisberg (Sylvaner in the Valais) and Malvoisie (Pinot Gris).
countries.climate_soils:
Swiss vineyards are cool to moderate, but warmed by lakes and protected by mountains. Lake Geneva and the Jura lakes reflect light and store heat; the Valais lies in a deep rain shadow between the Bernese and Pennine Alps, with under 600 mm of rain in places and the warm föhn wind; Ticino has a sub-Mediterranean climate south of the Alps with heavy rain and sunshine.

Soils mirror Alpine geology: glacial moraine, limestone and conglomerate in Lavaux and Vaud, schist, gneiss, limestone and alluvial fans in the Valais, Jurassic limestone along Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel, molasse sandstone in the German-speaking cantons, and granite and gneiss with glacial deposits in Ticino.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: The most planted grape (about 3,950 ha), from the Bündner Herrschaft and Neuchâtel to the Valais.

grapes.name: Chasselas
grapes.note: About 3,650 ha; the soul of Vaud, called Fendant in the Valais, and a remarkable conduit for terroir.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.note: About 1,200 ha, mostly in Geneva, Vaud and the Valais.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: About 1,180 ha, the signature of Ticino since 1906.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau (Riesling x Sylvaner)
grapes.note: Bred at Geisenheim by Hermann Müller, a native of Thurgau, and the classic white of German-speaking Switzerland.

grapes.name: Petite Arvine
grapes.note: The Valais' signature white, salty and grapefruit-scented, dry or sweet.

grapes.name: Cornalin and Humagne Rouge
grapes.note: Native or ancient Valais reds; Cornalin (Rouge du Pays) is dark and cherry-fruited.

grapes.name: Heida (Savagnin)
grapes.note: Grown at over 1,100 m at Visperterminen in the Upper Valais.

grapes.name: Amigne
grapes.note: An ancient variety almost confined to Vétroz, made dry to sweet with a bee symbol showing sweetness.

grapes.name: Completer and Räuschling
grapes.note: Old German-Swiss rarities, Completer in Graubünden and Räuschling on Lake Zurich.

further_reading: Wine Grapes, Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz

countries.name: Luxembourg
countries.tagline: Forty kilometres of Moselle riverbank where Crémant, Riesling and Auxerrois face Germany across the water.

stats.note: STATEC via FAOSTAT (official figure): 1,200 ha of vines in 2024 (Wikipedia gives about 1,295 ha). Production has been roughly 0.1 mhl in recent years (FAOSTAT carries an outside estimate of 8,100 t for 2023); no 2025 figure was found

countries.overview:
Luxembourg's wine country is a single strip of slopes along the left bank of the Moselle, about 42 km from Schengen in the south to Wasserbillig and Rosport in the north, facing Germany's Obermosel on the opposite bank. Roughly 1,300 hectares of vines are farmed by about 450 growers, and the whole country is one appellation, the AOP Moselle Luxembourgeoise.

The wines are mostly dry whites from grapes that like cool, limestone country: Rivaner (Müller-Thurgau), Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling and the ancient Elbling, plus Gewürztraminer and a growing share of Pinot Noir. Sparkling wine is the country's great success. Crémant de Luxembourg, created on 4 January 1991 for traditional-method wines, accounts for a large share of sales, and houses such as Bernard-Massard in Grevenmacher have made sparkling wine since the 1920s.

The southern half, the canton of Remich, has softer limestone and marl soils and gives rounder wines; the northern half around Grevenmacher and Wormeldange has steeper slopes of shell limestone (Muschelkalk) and gives Luxembourg's best Rieslings, notably from the Koeppchen above Wormeldange. Cooperatives (Domaines Vinsmoselle) produce well over half the wine, private growers about a quarter, and the trade the rest. The village of Schengen, where the 1985 agreement on open borders was signed on a riverboat, is the southern gateway of the wine route.

history.title: Romans on the Moselle
history.text: Roman settlers planted vines on the Moselle, part of the same wine economy that supplied Trier.

history.title: Elbling after the great frost
history.text: After the catastrophic winter of 1709 about 90 percent of replanting was Elbling, sold in bulk to German Mosel blenders for two centuries.

history.title: A national quality push
history.text: After the end of the customs union with Germany, Luxembourg replaced Elbling with better varieties, founded the Institut viti-vinicole in Remich (1925) and created the Marque Nationale (12 March 1935).

history.title: Crémant de Luxembourg
history.text: Crémant de Luxembourg was introduced on 4 January 1991 for traditional-method sparkling wine.

history.title: AOP reform
history.text: The old Vin classé, Premier Cru and Grand Premier Cru tasting grades were dropped in favour of an origin pyramid: Côtes de, Coteaux de and Lieu-dit.

countries.classification: One PDO, Moselle Luxembourgeoise (registered 1973), covering 12 communes. Since the 2014 reform labels use three tiers of origin: 'Côtes de' plus a village (approachable everyday wines), 'Coteaux de' plus a broader terroir (premium wines from defined limestone or marl zones) and 'Lieu-dit' plus a named site (single-vineyard wines with lower yields). Crémant de Luxembourg is a sparkling style within the AOP. The Marque Nationale label (since 1935) certifies wines made from Luxembourg grapes and controlled by the state.
countries.climate_soils: A cool, temperate climate moderated by the Moselle. In the south (canton of Remich) Keuper marl and gypsum give rounder, softer wines; in the north (canton of Grevenmacher) the slopes are steeper and made of shell limestone (Muschelkalk), giving more tension and structure, especially in Riesling.

grapes.name: Rivaner (Müller-Thurgau)
grapes.note: The most planted grape, for easy everyday whites.

grapes.name: Auxerrois
grapes.note: A Luxembourg speciality, soft and creamy, often the base of Crémant.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc
grapes.note: Important for still wine and Crémant.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Best on the shell limestone of the north.

grapes.name: Elbling
grapes.note: The ancient Moselle grape, light and tart.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Rising red and Crémant base.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.tagline: Chalk, climate change and Champagne grapes: the country that invented the idea of sparkling wine is now making it seriously.

stats.note: Vineyard: WineGB Industry Report 2025, 4,841 ha, 1,104 vineyards and 238 wineries (the Food Standards Agency register counted 4,357 ha and 1,158 vineyards in 2025). Production: Food Standards Agency, 124,377 hl (about 16.5 million bottles) from the record 2025 harvest, up from about 10.6 million bottles in 2024, 69 percent of which was sparkling

countries.overview:
Britain has drunk wine since the Romans, but for most of history it bought rather than made it: claret from Bordeaux, sherry, port and Champagne were all, in part, English commercial creations. Its own vineyards are a modern phenomenon. About 4,840 hectares are now planted, mostly in the south-east of England, and the area has more than doubled in ten years. Kent has the most vines, followed by West Sussex, Essex, East Sussex and Hampshire.

The reason is sparkling wine. The chalk that runs from Champagne under the Channel and resurfaces in the North and South Downs, combined with a cool climate that has warmed enough to ripen Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier most years, gives base wines with the high acidity that traditional-method sparkling needs. Nyetimber, planted in West Sussex in 1988, and Ridgeview, planted in 1995, proved the point, and English sparkling wines now beat Champagne in blind tastings and international competitions. About 69 percent of production is sparkling and nearly all of it is made by the traditional method. Champagne houses have invested too: Taittinger at Domaine Evremond in Kent and Pommery in Hampshire.

Still wine is the other half of the story. Bacchus, a German crossing, gives elderflower-scented whites that have become England's answer to Sauvignon Blanc, and riper vintages have produced convincing Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Essex's Crouch Valley, one of the driest places in Britain, is now a source of fine still Pinot. Weather remains the risk: spring frost, wet flowering and cool autumns can halve a crop, as in 2024, while 2018 and 2025 were large.

Legally, the UK has four wine PDOs: English Wine and Welsh Wine (both registered with the EU in 2011 and carried into UK law after Brexit), Darnibole (a single Cornish Bacchus vineyard, 2017) and Sussex (2022), the first regional PDO for sparkling wine.

history.title: Roman vineyards
history.text: Excavations at Wollaston in the Nene valley, Northamptonshire, revealed planting trenches of a Roman vineyard covering several hectares, the largest evidence of Roman viticulture in Britain.

history.title: Domesday vineyards
history.text: The Domesday Book records more than 40 vineyards, many attached to monasteries and producing communion wine.

history.title: Bordeaux becomes English
history.text: Eleanor of Aquitaine's marriage to Henry Plantagenet brought Bordeaux under the English crown for three centuries, and claret became England's wine.

history.title: Christopher Merret's paper
history.text: Merret presented 'Some Observations concerning the Ordering of Wines' to the Royal Society, describing how coopers added sugar and molasses to make wine 'brisk and sparkling', decades before Champagne made sparkling wine deliberately. Strong English coal-fired glass made it possible.

history.title: Painshill's vineyard
history.text: Charles Hamilton planted a vineyard at Painshill in Surrey whose sparkling wine was reportedly passed off as Champagne; it has been replanted.

history.title: Hambledon
history.text: Major-General Sir Guy Salisbury-Jones planted Hambledon in Hampshire, generally counted as the first commercial vineyard of the modern English revival.

history.title: Nyetimber
history.text: Stuart and Sandy Moss planted Champagne varieties at Nyetimber in West Sussex; the first wine, a 1992 Blanc de Blancs, launched English sparkling wine.

history.title: PDOs
history.text: English and Welsh wine were registered as PDOs in 2011, Darnibole in 2017 and Sussex in July 2022.

countries.classification: Four PDOs: English Wine and Welsh Wine (grapes 100 percent from England or Wales, vineyards below 220 m, quality sparkling limited to Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Pinot Noir Précoce, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris), Darnibole (Bacchus from a single Cornish valley) and Sussex (2022, the first regional PDO, with at least 15 months on lees for sparkling). Two PGIs, English Regional Wine and Welsh Regional Wine, allow hybrids such as Seyval Blanc. WineGB's 'Great British Classic Method' hallmark covers traditional-method PDO wines.
countries.climate_soils: A cool maritime climate, warmed by the Gulf Stream, with long, mild growing seasons in good years. The best sites are south-facing slopes on chalk (North and South Downs, Hampshire, Kent), greensand and clay (the Weald), with drier, warmer conditions in Essex and East Anglia. Frost, rain at flowering and autumn rot are the main risks.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: The most planted grape; backbone of sparkling and increasingly fine still wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Sparkling and, in warm years, still red.

grapes.name: Pinot Meunier
grapes.note: The third Champagne grape.

grapes.name: Bacchus
grapes.note: The aromatic still-wine signature, elderflower and nettle.

grapes.name: Seyval Blanc
grapes.note: A hardy hybrid of the early revival, still used for sparkling.

grapes.name: Solaris and Ortega
grapes.note: Early ripeners for marginal sites.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.tagline: A beer country quietly rebuilding a medieval wine tradition, with Chardonnay and Crémant on Meuse slopes and Flemish hills.

stats.note: Statbel via FAOSTAT (official figure): 900 ha of vines in 2024, up from 680 ha in 2023. No reliable current production figure: FAOSTAT's Belgian wine numbers are estimates; production was about 4,000 hl in 2006 and has grown strongly since. See gaps

countries.overview:
Belgium had vineyards long before it became famous for beer. Monks of the Carolingian era planted vines around Liège and Huy on the Meuse, and Leuven had 23 public wine presses in 1411. The Little Ice Age, cheap Burgundy, wars and the rise of beer ended most of that, and by the nineteenth century the country was better known for table grapes grown under glass in the Hoeilaart greenhouses near Brussels.

The modern revival began in the 1960s and accelerated with warmer summers. Belgium now has seven protected designations, four in Flanders and three in Wallonia, and a few hundred hectares of vines. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris grow alongside Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau and fungus-resistant varieties such as Johanniter and Solaris. Sparkling wine, especially Crémant de Wallonie, is the strongest suit, and estates such as Domaine du Chant d'Eole near Mons and Ruffus (Domaine des Agaises) at Haulchin have won international awards with traditional-method wines from chalk soils that continue those of Champagne. In Flanders, Wijnkasteel Genoels-Elderen in Haspengouw and Wijndomein Aldeneyck in the Maas valley are the best-known names.

history.title: Monastic vineyards on the Meuse
history.text: Vineyards at Vivegnis near Liège and at Huy were already old in the ninth century; part of the Huy vineyard belonged to the Bishop of Liège.

history.title: Leuven's 23 presses
history.text: At its medieval peak the city of Leuven had 23 public wine presses, a sign of how widespread viticulture was in Brabant.

history.title: Grapes under glass
history.text: From 1862 table grapes were grown in greenhouses around Hoeilaart and Overijse; by 1960 there were about 35,000.

history.title: Appellations return
history.text: Hageland became Belgium's first wine appellation in 1997, followed by Haspengouw, Côtes de Sambre et Meuse, Heuvelland, Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn and, in 2008 to 2009, Crémant de Wallonie and Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie.

countries.classification: Seven PDOs: in Flanders Hagelandse wijn, Haspengouwse wijn, Heuvellandse wijn and Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn; in Wallonia Côtes de Sambre et Meuse, Crémant de Wallonie and Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie. The cross-border Maasvallei Limburg PDO (2017) is shared with the Netherlands. PGIs are Vlaamse landwijn and Vin de pays des Jardins de Wallonie. National dates (1997 to 2009) and EU registration dates differ; the EU register lists Hagelandse and Haspengouwse wijn from 2004.
countries.climate_soils: Cool maritime to slightly continental. Chalk and marl in Hainaut (continuous with Champagne's chalk), loess in Haspengouw and Hageland, iron-rich sandstone (ijzerzandsteen) hills in Hageland, sandy and gravelly soils in the Maas valley, and clay hills in Heuvelland near the French border.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: The most acclaimed variety, for still and sparkling.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier
grapes.note: Sparkling and light reds.

grapes.name: Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau
grapes.note: Still whites.

grapes.name: Johanniter, Solaris, Regent
grapes.note: Fungus-resistant varieties for organic growers.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.tagline: Limburg marl, Achterhoek farms and fungus-resistant grapes: Dutch wine is young, small and growing fast.

stats.note: CBS via FAOSTAT (official figure): 230 ha of vines in 2024 (250 ha in 2023). Wikipedia (de) put output at about 1.2 million bottles in 2020; no current production figure found

countries.overview:
Wine in the Netherlands is first documented in 968, and medieval vineyards grew on the slopes around Maastricht and along the Maas and Geul, but beer, the Little Ice Age and phylloxera finished them; the last old vineyard near Maastricht closed in 1946. The revival began in the 1970s, when the Apostelhoeve near Maastricht planted Müller-Thurgau and Riesling on the marl slopes of the Louwberg, and has accelerated with warmer summers. By 2020 there were about 250 hectares in some 135 sites, producing around 1.2 million bottles, and the area has kept growing.

Two very different styles have emerged. In South Limburg, on chalky marl (mergel) hills like those across the border in Belgium, classic varieties such as Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir dominate. Elsewhere, on sandy soils in Gelderland, Overijssel and North Brabant, growers rely on fungus-resistant varieties (Solaris, Johanniter, Souvignier Gris, Regent, Cabernet Cortis) that can be farmed with little or no spraying. Each style now has PDOs: Mergelland, Vijlen and the cross-border Maasvallei Limburg in Limburg, and Oolde, Ambt Delden and Achterhoek-Winterswijk in the east, most of them single estates.

history.title: First record of Dutch wine
history.text: The first mention of viticulture in the Netherlands dates to 968; medieval vineyards grew around Maastricht and on Maas and Geul slopes.

history.title: The last old vineyard
history.text: The last historic vineyard near Maastricht closed, ending the old tradition.

history.title: Apostelhoeve replants
history.text: The Hulst family planted vines at the Apostelhoeve on the Louwberg south of Maastricht, the start of modern Dutch wine.

history.title: PDOs arrive
history.text: Maasvallei Limburg (2017, with Belgium), Mergelland (2018), Vijlen and Oolde (2018), Ambt Delden (2019) and Achterhoek-Winterswijk (2020) were registered.

countries.classification: Six PDOs registered between 2017 and 2020: Maasvallei Limburg (cross-border with Belgium), Mergelland, Vijlen, Oolde, Ambt Delden and Achterhoek-Winterswijk. Each province has a PGI-level regional wine. Several PDOs are effectively single estates with strict rules on varieties and yields.
countries.climate_soils: A cool maritime climate. South Limburg's hills of Cretaceous chalky marl (mergel) and loess give the most classic conditions; the east and centre have sand, loam and glacial deposits, where wet summers favour fungus-resistant varieties.

grapes.name: Solaris, Johanniter, Souvignier Gris
grapes.note: Fungus-resistant whites, the most planted grapes in sandy regions.

grapes.name: Regent, Cabernet Cortis, Pinotin
grapes.note: Fungus-resistant reds.

grapes.name: Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Classic varieties in Limburg.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.tagline: Solaris, sea air and long summer light: a twenty-first-century wine country on the edge of the map.

stats.note: About 173 ha and 146 vineyards in 2022 (Wikipedia, Danish wine).

countries.overview:
Danish monasteries made a little wine for their own use from the thirteenth century, but commercial wine-growing only became legal in 1999, when a ban was lifted and 99 hectares were allowed for wine grapes; the 2001 vintage was the first sold. Since then the number of vineyards has grown from about 20 in 2006 to 146 in 2022, on about 173 hectares, most of them on Zealand and Bornholm.

The climate is cool, but long summer days at 55 to 57 degrees north, a sunny Baltic microclimate and warming summers let early-ripening, mostly fungus-resistant grapes succeed: Solaris above all, plus Rondo, Regent, Cabernet Cortis, Souvignier Gris and some Pinot Noir and Chardonnay for sparkling. Skærsøgaard at Dons near Kolding pioneered quality sparkling wine, and its Dons became Denmark's first PDO in 2018. Regional designations exist for Fyn, Jylland, Sjælland and Bornholm. Denmark also has a thriving fruit-wine and cider culture, and Frederiksdal on Lolland is famous for its cherry wine.

history.title: Monastic wine
history.text: Monasteries made small amounts of wine for their own use; it was never commercial.

history.title: Wine-growing becomes legal
history.text: A ban on commercial wine-growing was lifted in 1999 after EU recognition; the 2001 vintage was the first sold legally.

history.title: Dons PDO
history.text: Dons near Kolding, home of Skærsøgaard, was registered as Denmark's first PDO, for quality sparkling wine.

countries.classification: One PDO, Dons (2018, quality sparkling wine from Kolding municipality). The Danish authority publishes product specifications for the regional designations Fyn, Jylland and Sjælland (still, sparkling and quality sparkling, max. 60 hl/ha) and Bornholm; these regional names are commonly described as PGIs, but the specifications themselves only say 'protected designation', so their exact status should be confirmed in eAmbrosia.
countries.climate_soils: Cool maritime with long summer days. Bornholm's granite and Baltic sunshine make it one of the warmest parts of Denmark; elsewhere vines grow on glacial moraine, clay and sand.

grapes.name: Solaris
grapes.note: The dominant white, ripening early with good sugar.

grapes.name: Rondo and Regent
grapes.note: Leading reds.

grapes.name: Cabernet Cortis, Souvignier Gris, Muscaris, Orion
grapes.note: Other fungus-resistant varieties.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
grapes.note: For sparkling wine at Dons and elsewhere.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.tagline: Skåne's southern hills and Baltic islands are making a new wine story at 56 degrees north.

stats.note: Statistics Sweden via FAOSTAT (official figure): 120 ha of vines in 2024; no reliable production statistic

countries.overview: Sweden's wine-growing is a twenty-first-century story, made possible by warmer summers and fungus-resistant grapes. The main area is Skåne, the southernmost province, where vineyards grow on the Kullaberg peninsula near Arild, around Österlen and near Malmö and Lund; there are also vineyards on Gotland and Öland in the Baltic and along the west coast. Solaris dominates, with Rondo, Regent and some Pinot Noir and Chardonnay for sparkling. Kullabergs Vingård and Arilds Vingård on the Kullaberg peninsula, with sea-warmed slopes, are among the best known. Sweden has no EU-registered wine PDO in the dataset used here; any newly registered names should be checked in eAmbrosia.

history.title: Monastic vines
history.text: Monasteries in Skåne grew some vines in the Middle Ages, though wine-growing never became significant.

history.title: Modern start
history.text: Commercial vineyards appeared in Skåne in the early 2000s, helped by warmer summers and fungus-resistant varieties.

countries.classification: No wine PDO is listed for Sweden in the EU geospatial dataset used for this atlas (Candiago et al. 2022). Wines are sold as Swedish wine without a protected origin unless a newer registration exists.
countries.climate_soils: Cool maritime to continental with very long summer days. Skåne has fertile moraine and limestone; the Kullaberg is a granite and gneiss ridge warmed by the sea.

grapes.name: Solaris
grapes.note: The main grape.

grapes.name: Rondo, Regent
grapes.note: Reds.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
grapes.note: For sparkling wine.

countries.name: Norway
countries.tagline: A handful of vines near the 59th parallel.

stats.note: Negligible commercial production; no statistics found.

countries.overview: Norway makes almost no wine. A few small vineyards in the south, notably Lerkekåsa near Gvarv in Telemark at about 59 degrees north, grow early-ripening and fungus-resistant varieties such as Solaris on sheltered, sun-facing slopes. The state retail monopoly (Vinmonopolet) and a large import market define Norwegian wine culture; domestic production is a curiosity. Norway is outside the EU and has no wine appellations.

history.title: First vineyards
history.text: Small experimental and commercial vineyards appeared in southern Norway, especially in Telemark around Gvarv, known for its fruit growing.

countries.climate_soils: Short, cool summers with long daylight; only the most sheltered southern slopes can ripen grapes.

grapes.name: Solaris
grapes.note: The main grape at the few vineyards.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.tagline: Moravian cellar lanes, Pálava limestone and the Elbe hills of Bohemia: a wine culture older than the country's beer fame suggests.

stats.note: Czech Statistical Office via FAOSTAT (official figure): 16,030 ha of vines in 2024; Wikipedia (de) gives about 18,750 ha for 2004. Moravia holds about 94 to 96 percent. FAOSTAT carries an outside estimate of 48,800 t of wine for 2023; OIV estimates Czech consumption at 2.0 mhl in 2025, far above domestic output

countries.overview:
Czechia is famous for beer, but South Moravia is one of central Europe's liveliest wine regions, and its villages are lined with sklepy, rows of small cellars dug into loess where families make and pour their own wine. The country has two wine regions: Morava (Moravia), with about 95 percent of the vineyard, in the warm south-east bordering Austria and Slovakia, and Čechy (Bohemia), a tiny but historic area along the Elbe and Vltava north of Prague around Mělník and Litoměřice.

Moravia's four subregions (Znojemská, Mikulovská, Velkopavlovická and Slovácká) continue the landscapes of Austria's Weinviertel across the border, and the grapes overlap: Grüner Veltliner (Veltlínské zelené), Welschriesling (Ryzlink vlašský), Riesling (Ryzlink rýnský), Müller-Thurgau, Sauvignon Blanc, the Pinot family, Pálava and Gewürztraminer among whites; Saint Laurent (Svatovavřinecké), Blaufränkisch (Frankovka), Zweigelt, Pinot Noir (Rulandské modré) and Czech crossings such as André and Cabernet Moravia among reds. The best wines are fresh, aromatic whites with lively acidity, and an active natural-wine scene, centred on growers of the Autentista group around Mikulov and Velké Pavlovice, has given Moravia an international following.

Czech wine law follows the EU model, with the German-style Prädikat ladder for quality wines, but its most interesting feature is the VOC (víno originální certifikace, 'wine of original certification'), a local appellation run by growers' associations that sets grapes and style for a named area. VOC Znojmo was first in 2009, and by 2019 there were 13. Valtice Castle, part of the Lednice-Valtice UNESCO landscape, houses the national Wine Salon, which each year selects the country's 100 best wines.

history.title: Roman legions on the Dyje
history.text: Roman legions campaigned and camped at Mušov (Burgstall) below the Pálava hills during the Marcomannic Wars; local tradition credits Roman soldiers with the first Moravian vines, though hard evidence is debated.

history.title: Ludmila's vineyards at Mělník
history.text: Legend says Prince Bořivoj and his wife Ludmila planted the first Bohemian vineyards around Mělník; Ludmila, later Bohemia's patron saint, is honoured by the town's wine.

history.title: Charles IV's vineyards
history.text: Emperor Charles IV encouraged planting around Prague with land grants and tax relief and restricted imports; the Prague district of Vinohrady ('vineyards') recalls the era. The 14th to 16th centuries were Bohemian and Moravian wine's golden age.

history.title: Thirty Years' War
history.text: Before the war Bohemia had an estimated 10,000 ha and Moravia 20,000 ha of vines; destruction and the rise of beer shrank both dramatically.

history.title: Valtice wine school
history.text: A wine school was founded at Valtice, the Liechtenstein seat whose vineyards appear in a register of 1414.

history.title: The VOC system
history.text: VOC Znojmo (2009) became the first wine of original certification; 12 more followed by 2019.

countries.classification:
Czech wine follows EU categories: víno (wine), zemské víno (PGI, from the České or Moravské regions), jakostní víno (quality wine from a region or subregion) and jakostní víno s přívlastkem (Prädikat wine: kabinetní víno, pozdní sběr, výběr z hroznů, výběr z bobulí, výběr z cibéb, ledové víno and slámové víno), defined by sugar at harvest. The EU register holds Čechy and Morava, the six subregions, and three local PDOs: Znojmo (the VOC), Šobes and Novosedelské Slámové víno.

VOC (víno originální certifikace) is a growers' appellation for a defined area, with its own varieties, styles and tasting control, closer to the Austrian DAC than to the Prädikat system. The 13 VOCs are Znojmo (2009), Mikulov and Modré Hory (2011), Pálava (2012), Blatnice (2013), Valtice and Mělník (2015), Slovácko and Hustopečsko (2016), Kraví hora and Bzenec (2017), Mutěnice (2018) and Velké Pavlovice (2019).
countries.climate_soils: Moravia has a warm continental climate on the edge of the Pannonian basin, with hot summers, cold winters and modest rainfall; loess dominates, with Jurassic limestone on the Pálava hills, granite and gneiss around Znojmo and the Dyje valley, and sand and flysch in Slovácko. Bohemia is cooler, with vineyards on sheltered south-facing slopes over the Elbe and Vltava on sandstone, marl and basalt (around Velké Žernoseky).

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.tagline: Little Carpathian royal towns, Danube plain reds and a slice of Tokaj that both sides of the border claim.

stats.note: Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic via FAOSTAT (official figure): 9,000 ha of vines in 2024; about 10,000 ha were worked in 2011 (SITA), against up to 57,000 ha in the early nineteenth century. No current production figure found

countries.overview:
Slovakia's vineyards lie along its southern edge, from the foothills of the Little Carpathians above Bratislava to the volcanic hills of Tokaj on the Hungarian and Ukrainian borders, and cover about 9,000 hectares (2024) in six wine regions. For most of history this was Upper Hungary, and in the early nineteenth century the area supplied wine to European courts from as much as 57,000 hectares; phylloxera, war and four decades of state cooperatives shrank and flattened the industry, and the modern revival dates from the 1990s.

The Little Carpathians (Malokarpatská) are the historic heart, with the old royal free towns of Svätý Jur, Pezinok and Modra, where burgher families made wine in courtyards and cellars under their houses, and Bratislava's Rača district, famous for Frankovka. The Danube plain to the south-east (Južnoslovenská) and the hills around Nitra (Nitrianska) give fuller, riper whites and reds, and the smaller Central and East Slovak regions add volcanic and loess sites. Grüner Veltliner and Welschriesling are the most planted grapes, with Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Pinot Blanc and Riesling. Slovak breeders, notably Dorota Pospíšilová, created crossings such as Devín (white) and Dunaj (red) that are now local favourites.

Slovakia's corner of Tokaj, seven villages around Malá Tŕňa and Viničky, makes the same botrytised wines as Hungarian Tokaj, from Furmint, Lipovina (Hárslevelű) and Yellow Muscat, under the name Tokajský výber. Hungary fought for years to stop Slovakia using the name; EU courts rejected Hungary's challenge in 2012 and 2013, and both countries now use it.

history.title: Romans on the Danube limes
history.text: Roman forts such as Gerulata (Bratislava-Rusovce) guarded the Danube, and Emperor Probus is traditionally credited with spreading vines in Pannonia.

history.title: Royal free towns of wine
history.text: Modra, Svätý Jur and Pezinok became royal free towns of the Kingdom of Hungary in the seventeenth century, status bought with the wealth of their wine trade.

history.title: Trianon splits Tokaj
history.text: The Treaty of Trianon left three Tokaj villages and about 175 ha in Czechoslovakia; later laws added villages up to the present seven and about 908 ha.

history.title: The Tokaj dispute
history.text: A 2004 agreement allowed Slovak wine from 565 ha to use the Tokaj name under Hungarian-style rules; Hungary later sought to remove Slovakia's 'Vinohradnícka oblasť Tokaj' from the EU register, but the General Court (2012) and Court of Justice (2013) rejected its case.

countries.classification: Slovak wine follows EU categories. Five regional PDOs (Malokarpatská, Južnoslovenská, Nitrianska, Stredoslovenská, Východoslovenská) and the Vinohradnícka oblasť Tokaj PDO are registered, each with grammatical variants; two more local PDOs are Karpatská perla (2011, a quality label for the Bratislava and Little Carpathian area) and Skalický rubín (2017, a red blend from Skalica). Quality wines with a predicate follow the German ladder (kabinetné, neskorý zber, výber z hrozna, bobuľový výber, hrozienkový výber, cibébový výber, ľadové víno, slamové víno). Special terms include mladé víno (young wine sold from the first Monday in November), archívne víno (aged three years) and panenská úroda (first harvest of a new vineyard).
countries.climate_soils: Continental with warm summers. The Little Carpathians have granite and schist on the slopes and loess below; the Danube plain has sand, gravel and loess; Nitra and Central Slovakia have loess, clay and volcanic andesite in places; Tokaj and the East have volcanic tuff, andesite and loess.

countries.name: Poland
countries.tagline: A medieval wine country, then Germany's northernmost Sekt town, now one of Europe's fastest-growing young vineyards.

stats.note: Statistics Poland via FAOSTAT (official figure): 1,400 ha of vines in 2024, up from about 500 ha in 2011 (Wikipedia de); no reliable current production figure

countries.overview:
Wine is part of Polish history from the start. Grape seeds found on Wawel hill in Kraków suggest vines around the year 1000, a papal bull of 1136 mentions vineyards near Płock and Włocławek, and Cistercian monks at Paradyż (Paradies) were making wine near Zielona Góra by 1250. In the fourteenth century there were vineyards from Silesia and Greater Poland to Toruń, Sandomierz and Kraków. The Little Ice Age and cheap Hungarian wine, especially Tokaji, which Polish nobles adored, pushed most of them out.

The great exception was Zielona Góra (German Grünberg) in Lower Silesia, then part of Prussia. Its slopes held thousands of small vineyards, and in 1826 the firm Häusler, Förster und Grempler began making sparkling wine by the Champagne method there, among the first in Germany; the town's harvest festival has been held since 1852. After 1945 the German population was expelled, and Silesian viticulture almost vanished; the communist state favoured fruit wines. The Barossa Valley's Henschke and Lehmann families trace their roots to the region.

The revival began with hobby growers and a 2008 wine law that made commercial sale practical. Hundreds of small vineyards now grow fungus-resistant varieties such as Solaris, Johanniter, Regent and Rondo, along with Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Seyval Blanc. Leading areas are Lubuskie around Zielona Góra, Lower Silesia, Małopolska around Kraków (Srebrna Góra, 28 ha, in the city), the Vistula valley around Sandomierz and Kazimierz Dolny, Podkarpacie near Jasło, and even West Pomerania, where Winnica Turnau is one of the country's largest estates. Poland has no EU-registered wine PDO in the dataset used here.

history.title: Vines on Wawel hill
history.text: Archaeobotanical finds suggest grapes were grown on Wawel hill in Kraków around the year 1000.

history.title: Cistercians and Grünberg
history.text: Monks of the Cistercian abbey of Paradyż made wine by 1250, and vineyards around Zielona Góra are recorded from 1314.

history.title: Grünberg sparkling wine and the Winobranie
history.text: Häusler, Förster und Grempler began traditional-method sparkling wine in Grünberg in 1826; the town's annual wine festival dates from 1852.

history.title: Expulsion and decline
history.text: With the expulsion of the German population of Silesia, its viticulture almost disappeared; the communist economy turned to fruit wine.

history.title: A modern wine law
history.text: A wine law adopted in 2008 (and later amended) let small producers sell wine commercially, triggering rapid growth.

countries.classification: Poland lies in EU wine zone A. Growers may sell wine with a Polish origin and varietal and vintage labelling; the country has defined grape-growing areas, but no wine PDO appears in the EU dataset used for this atlas (Candiago et al. 2022). Check eAmbrosia for any newer registrations.
countries.climate_soils: Cool continental with cold winters and warm summers; the south and west (Lower Silesia, Lubuskie, Małopolska, Podkarpacie) are warmest. Soils include loess (Sandomierz, Kazimierz), limestone (Kraków), glacial sands and clays (Lubuskie, Pomerania) and flysch (Podkarpacie).

regions.name: Mosel
regions.tagline: Slate cliffs, river loops and Riesling of impossible lightness.
regions.summary:
The Mosel is the most recognisable wine landscape in Germany: a river that coils back on itself between the Hunsrück and Eifel, with vineyards rising from the water's edge at gradients that make farming a mountain sport. It is Germany's oldest wine region and its third largest, with about 8,500 hectares, and Riesling covers more than 5,300 of them. The region includes the tributary valleys of the Saar and Ruwer, which until 2007 shared the official name Mosel-Saar-Ruwer.

Mosel Riesling is famous for doing more with less. Alcohol can be as low as 7.5 or 8 percent in a Kabinett, yet the wines have racy acidity, flavours of green apple, peach and white flowers, and a smoky, stony note that drinkers associate with slate. The residual sweetness in traditional Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese is balanced by that acidity, which is why a 30-year-old Mosel Spätlese can taste fresher than a five-year-old Chardonnay. Dry wines and Grosses Gewächs have improved dramatically since the 1990s, but the Mosel remains the heartland of fruity-sweet Riesling.

The region divides into the Terrassenmosel (Lower Mosel) from Koblenz to Zell, with its terraced cliffs and the Calmont; the Middle Mosel from Zell to Trier, home to the most famous names (Bernkastel, Wehlen, Graach, Zeltingen, Ürzig, Erden, Brauneberg, Piesport); the Saar and Ruwer near Trier; and the Upper Mosel on limestone along the Luxembourg border, where Elbling and Burgundian grapes grow.
regions.history: Romans planted the slopes to supply Trier, an imperial capital; the poet Ausonius described them around 371, and press houses from the fourth century have been excavated at Piesport, Brauneberg, Erden and Graach. Through the Middle Ages the Archbishop-Electors of Trier and the great abbeys (St. Maximin, St. Matthias, the Carthusians) owned the best land. In 1787 Elector Clemens Wenzeslaus ordered inferior vines replaced with good ones, which in practice meant Riesling. Under Prussian rule after 1815 the region was mapped and taxed; the 1868 Prussian tax map of the Trier district ranked sites in classes that still read like a list of grand crus. Around 1900 the best Mosel wines fetched prices equal to or above first-growth Bordeaux. The twentieth century brought decline: phylloxera, wars, the 1971 Großlagen and a flood of cheap sweet wine. Since the 1990s a generation of growers (Ernst Loosen, Markus Molitor, Clemens Busch, Reinhard Löwenstein, Roman Niewodniczanski at Van Volxem and many others) has restored the old steep sites, and abandoned terraces are being replanted.
regions.terroir: The Mosel cuts through Devonian slate of the Rhenish Massif, 400 million years old. Blue-grey slate dominates the Middle Mosel and Ruwer; the Lower Mosel's harder slate is mixed with quartzite and sandstone; Ürzig and Erden have patches of red Permian (Rotliegend) slate and volcanic material that give spicier wines; the Saar has grey slate with diabase intrusions. Slate warms quickly, stores heat, and drains well, letting vines root deep on slopes that would otherwise be too cool. The river meanders create south-facing amphitheatres (Piesport, Trittenheim, Brauneberg) that trap sunlight, while the Saar and Ruwer, colder and more exposed, give the most nervy, high-acid wines in Germany.
regions.grapes: Riesling (about 62 percent), Müller-Thurgau, Elbling (Upper Mosel), Weißburgunder, Spätburgunder, Kerner, Dornfelder. Red wine has been permitted only since 1987 and remains a small share.
regions.styles: Fruity-sweet Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese; dry and off-dry (feinherb) Riesling; Grosses Gewächs; botrytised BA and TBA; Eiswein; Elbling Sekt and still Elbling from the Upper Mosel.
regions.classification: Six Bereiche: Burg Cochem, Bernkastel, Obermosel, Moseltor, Saar and Ruwertal. Famous Großlagen (Bernkasteler Kurfürstlay, Piesporter Michelsberg, Zeller Schwarze Katz, Kröver Nacktarsch) must carry the word 'Region' from the 2026 vintage. The VDP's Grosse Lage list draws heavily on the 1868 Prussian classification, and the Grosser Ring auction in Trier each September is one of the price benchmarks of the wine world. Three Uhlen sub-sites at Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf are separate EU PDOs.

regions.name: Saar
regions.tagline: The Mosel's coldest, steeliest tributary, home of Scharzhofberg.
regions.summary: The Saar joins the Mosel at Konz just above Trier, and its last 25 kilometres carry some of the most coveted Riesling vineyards on earth: Scharzhofberg, Bockstein, Rausch, Kupp, Altenberg, Gottesfuß. The valley is cooler and windier than the Middle Mosel, and for much of the twentieth century only three or four vintages a decade ripened properly. In those years the wines were the most electric in Germany: diamond-hard acidity, low alcohol, and a perfume of citrus blossom and wet stone. Climate change has made ripeness reliable, and the Saar has become one of the hottest addresses in German wine, both for traditional sweet Kabinett and Auslese and for dry Riesling.
regions.history: Vineyards were held by Trier's abbeys and the cathedral chapter; the Scharzhof was church property until the French secularised it, and in 1797 Jean-Jacques Koch, ancestor of the Müller family, bought it at auction. In the late nineteenth century Saar Rieslings appeared on the grandest wine lists in Europe. Recent decades have seen a renaissance driven by Egon Müller, Hanno Zilliken, Florian Lauer, Dorothee Zilliken, Van Volxem, von Othegraven and newcomers who have rescued abandoned slopes.
regions.terroir: Grey and blue Devonian slate with intrusions of greenish volcanic diabase (notably at Saarburg's Rausch). Many slopes face south to south-west and rise from the river at steep angles; the valley's exposure to cold air from the Hunsrück lengthens the season and keeps acidity high.
regions.grapes: Riesling almost exclusively.
regions.styles: Fruity Kabinett and Spätlese, Auslese with gold capsules, BA, TBA and Eiswein; increasingly dry Riesling and GG.
regions.classification: A Bereich of the Mosel region. The Scharzhof, Ayler Kupp parcels and others carry long-standing reputations reflected in the VDP Grosse Lage list.

regions.name: Ruwer
regions.tagline: A tiny side valley of monastery vineyards and ethereal Riesling.
regions.summary: The Ruwer is a small stream that enters the Mosel just downstream of Trier, and its valley holds only a couple of hundred hectares of vines. It punches far above its size because of two historic monopole estates, Maximin Grünhaus and the Karthäuserhof, and the village of Kasel. Ruwer Rieslings are the most delicate of the Mosel family: very low alcohol, blackcurrant leaf and herbal notes, and a fine-boned acidity that ages for decades.
regions.history: Maximin Grünhaus belonged to the Benedictine abbey of St. Maximin in Trier from 966 until secularisation; the von Schubert family has owned it since 1882. The Karthäuserhof at Eitelsbach was a Carthusian property from 1335. Both estates still bottle wine from the slopes that rise directly behind their buildings.
regions.terroir: Blue Devonian slate on steep south-facing slopes; the Ruwer valley is cool and the wines ripen late.
regions.grapes: Riesling.
regions.styles: Fruity and dry Riesling, from featherweight Kabinett to rare Eiswein.
regions.classification: The Ruwertal Bereich of the Mosel region. Grünhaus's Abtsberg, Herrenberg and Bruderberg and the Karthäuserhofberg are monopoles.

regions.name: Rheingau
regions.tagline: A single south-facing slope that became the cradle of fine Riesling.
regions.summary:
Between Wiesbaden and Lorch the Rhine, blocked by the Taunus hills, turns west for about 30 kilometres, and the north bank becomes one long, south-facing slope. That geographical accident made the Rheingau, with about 3,200 hectares, the aristocrat of German wine. Riesling covers about three quarters of the vineyard, and Spätburgunder from Assmannshausen is a historic red island. The style is fuller and rounder than the Mosel, with peach, apricot and a spicy, firm finish, and the region was an early champion of dry Riesling through the Charta association (1983) and its Erstes Gewächs classification (1999).

The landmarks read like a history of Riesling: Kloster Eberbach and the walled Steinberg; Schloss Johannisberg, where the Spätlese was born; Schloss Vollrads, which claims wine sales back to 1211; the Marcobrunn spring at Erbach; Rüdesheim's steep Berg; and Hochheim on the Main, whose wines gave the English the word 'hock' after Queen Victoria visited in 1845.
regions.history: Charlemagne's palace at Ingelheim faced the Rheingau across the Rhine, and the Archbishops of Mainz owned the region for centuries. The Cistercians of Eberbach (1136) organised the vineyards and shipped wine down the river. The first written mention of Riesling (1435) comes from nearby Rüsselsheim, and Schloss Johannisberg's Riesling planting around 1720 and the late-harvest legend of 1775 made the region the reference point for quality. The Geisenheim research institute (1872) trained generations of winemakers and bred grapes. After decades of reliance on big names, the Charta growers (1983) and later the VDP pushed dry, terroir-driven Riesling; today Robert Weil, Georg Breuer, Peter Jakob Kühn, Künstler, Leitz, Spreitzer, Schloss Johannisberg and the state domain at Eberbach lead.
regions.terroir: The slope runs from about 80 to 300 metres. Near the river the soils are loess, sand and marl that give rounder wines; higher up, at Kiedrich, Rauenthal and Rüdesheim, quartzite and slate give tension and minerality. The Taunus forest blocks cold north winds, the broad Rhine reflects light and moderates temperature, and Rüdesheim's Berg, where the river turns north into the gorge, has steep terraces of quartzite and slate. Hochheim, east of Wiesbaden on the Main, is warmer and on deeper soils.
regions.grapes: Riesling (about 76 percent), Spätburgunder (Assmannshausen, Lorch), small amounts of other varieties.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and Erstes Gewächs/GG, fruity Kabinett and Spätlese, noble sweet BA/TBA, Spätburgunder, Riesling Sekt.
regions.classification: One Bereich, Johannisberg, covering the whole region. The Rheingau defined its own Erstes Gewächs in 1999 and the state's vineyard map ('Gütekarte') of roughly 1,100 hectares underpins the new national use of Grosses and Erstes Gewächs from the 2024 vintage.
