regions.name: Nahe
regions.tagline: Germany's geological patchwork, where volcano meets slate.
regions.summary:
The Nahe flows north from the Hunsrück to meet the Rhine at Bingen, and its 4,250 hectares hold more kinds of rock than any other German region. That variety shows in the glass: Rieslings from porphyry (rhyolite) taste smoky and taut, those from slate are lifted and floral, those from sandstone and loess are softer and fruitier. Riesling covers about 1,250 hectares and leads the quality end; Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder and the Pinots fill the rest.

The Nahe was long treated as a hinterland of Rheinhessen and the Mosel and only became an Anbaugebiet in its own right in 1971. Its reputation rests on a handful of estates: Dönnhoff in Oberhausen, Emrich-Schönleber in Monzingen, Schäfer-Fröhlich in Bockenau, Kruger-Rumpf, Diel and the revived state domain at Niederhausen. The middle Nahe between Bad Münster and Monzingen, with Niederhausen's Hermannshöhle and the old copper mine at Schlossböckelheim, is the heart.
regions.history: The Romans planted vines around Bad Kreuznach. In the early twentieth century the Prussian state cleared rocky slopes at Niederhausen and Schlossböckelheim, using convict labour, to create the Domäne Niederhausen (1902), which made the region's name for decades before falling into decline; it was privatised in 1998 and later revived as Gut Hermannsberg. Helmut Dönnhoff's wines from the 1980s on put the Nahe on the international map.
regions.terroir: The Nahe valley sits on the boundary between the Rhenish slate massif and the Saar-Nahe basin, so slate and quartzite in the north and west meet Permian volcanic rocks (porphyry, melaphyre) and red sandstones in the middle and south. The climate is dry and sunny, sheltered by the Hunsrück; sites like the Hermannshöhle face south over the river.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Silvaner.
regions.styles: Dry and fruity Riesling, GG, noble sweet wines, Pinot whites, Sekt.
regions.classification: One Bereich, Nahetal. Monzinger Niederberg is a separate EU PDO registered in 2018.

regions.name: Rheinhessen
regions.tagline: Germany's largest region, reinvented by a generation of young growers.
regions.summary:
Rheinhessen is a rolling plateau of fields and vineyards inside the Rhine's great bend between Mainz, Bingen and Worms, and with about 27,500 hectares it is the largest wine region in Germany, almost twice the vineyard area of all Switzerland. For decades it stood for volume: Liebfraumilch, Müller-Thurgau and bulk wine. Since the late 1990s it has become the most dynamic region in the country, as growers like Klaus Peter Keller, Philipp Wittmann, Kai Schätzel and the 'Message in a Bottle' generation showed that its limestone and red slate could rival anything on the Rhine.

Two areas carry most of the fame. The Roter Hang between Nackenheim and Nierstein is a steep cliff of red slate and sandstone above the Rhine that gives spicy, mineral Riesling (Pettenthal, Hipping, Ölberg, Brudersberg, Rothenberg). The Wonnegau in the south, around Westhofen and Flörsheim-Dalsheim, sits on limestone and gives powerful, chalky dry Riesling from Morstein, Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Hubacker. Rheinhessen also holds the largest share of German Silvaner (about 43 percent of the national total) and Ingelheim's historic red wine.
regions.history: Charlemagne built his palace at Ingelheim, and Worms and Mainz were medieval centres of church wine. The Liebfrauenkirche in Worms is surrounded by the Liebfrauenstift vineyards whose wine gave its name to Liebfraumilch, which by the 1980s was a blended brand of millions of cases from four regions. The 1971 Großlage Niersteiner Gutes Domtal and Liebfraumilch together did great damage to the region's reputation. The comeback began with growers who cut yields, farmed organically and priced their wines against grand cru Burgundy; Keller's G-Max is now one of the most expensive dry white wines in the world.
regions.terroir: A sheltered plateau in the rain shadow of the Hunsrück, Taunus and Donnersberg, one of the driest and warmest parts of Germany. Soils are mostly loess and marl over limestone; the Roter Hang is Rotliegend (Permian red slate and sandstone); the Wonnegau and the area near Bingen add limestone and quartzite (Bingen's Scharlachberg).
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling (about 5,400 ha), Dornfelder, Silvaner, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Spätburgunder, Portugieser, Scheurebe.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and GG, Silvaner, Pinot whites, Spätburgunder, fruity Riesling and noble sweet wines, Sekt; plus large volumes of everyday wine.
regions.classification: Three Bereiche: Bingen, Nierstein and Wonnegau. The 'RS' Rheinhessen Silvaner designation was created in 2002 to rebuild Silvaner's image.

regions.name: Pfalz
regions.tagline: Germany's Tuscany: warm, generous, and home to the 'three Bs' of Riesling.
regions.summary:
The Pfalz runs about 85 kilometres north to south along the eastern foot of the Haardt mountains, from Bockenheim to the French border at Schweigen, where it simply continues into Alsace. With about 23,800 hectares it is the second largest region, and the warmest and driest of the classic ones: almonds, figs and even lemons grow in sheltered gardens. Riesling (about 6,000 hectares) gives full, ripe and often dry wines, and red grapes cover nearly a third of the vineyard.

The Mittelhaardt between Kallstadt and Neustadt is the historic core, with the villages of Ungstein, Bad Dürkheim, Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg and the great estates Bürklin-Wolf, Bassermann-Jordan and von Buhl (the 'three Bs'). Forst's Kirchenstück, Jesuitengarten, Pechstein and Ungeheuer are among Germany's most famous dry Riesling sites. The Südliche Weinstraße to the south was long a land of cooperatives but now has stars such as Rebholz, Dr. Wehrheim, Becker in Schweigen and Kranz, with excellent Pinot and Riesling from red sandstone and limestone.
regions.history: Roman villas dotted the area, and the Speyer bottle, the oldest bottle of wine in the world, was found here. The region was Bavarian from 1816 to 1945; the Bavarian land-tax survey of 1828 ranked sites by value, with Forst's Kirchenstück at the top. The Deutsche Weinstraße tourist route was created in 1935, with the Deutsches Weintor at Schweigen built in 1936, a Nazi-era project to boost a struggling region. Bad Dürkheim's Riesenfass (1934), a barrel-shaped restaurant, and its Wurstmarkt festival are local institutions.
regions.terroir: The Haardt (northern Palatinate Forest) shields the vineyards from westerly rain, leaving 500 to 600 mm a year. Soils are a mosaic: red sandstone (Buntsandstein) on the hills, limestone at Kallstadt (Saumagen) and Ungstein, basalt from the Pechsteinkopf at Forst, loess and clay on the plain.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Dornfelder, Müller-Thurgau, Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Portugieser, Chardonnay, Scheurebe, Gewürztraminer, Sankt Laurent.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and GG, Pinot family whites and reds, Sekt, everyday wines; some outstanding noble sweet wines from Forst and Deidesheim.
regions.classification: Two Bereiche: Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstraße and Südliche Weinstraße. Bürklin-Wolf has used its own Burgundy-style G.C./P.C. labels since the 1990s, inspired by the 1828 Bavarian classification.

regions.name: Baden
regions.tagline: Germany's warm south, from Lake Constance to Tauberfranken, ruled by Pinot.
regions.summary:
Baden is a 400-kilometre ribbon of vineyards along the Upper Rhine and beyond, from the Tauber valley in the north to Lake Constance in the south, with about 15,700 hectares in nine Bereiche. It is the only German region in the EU's warmer wine-growing zone B, and the Burgundian family (Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay) covers about 62 percent of the vineyard. Baden's Pinot Noir in particular now ranks with the best outside Burgundy.

The Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano rising from the Rhine plain near Freiburg, is the warmest place in Germany, with volcanic terraces at Ihringen, Achkarren, Oberrotweil and Oberbergen and estates such as Dr. Heger, Salwey, Franz Keller and Bercher. The Ortenau around Durbach grows Riesling (called Klingelberger) and Pinot on granite; the Breisgau, home of Bernhard Huber's estate at Malterdingen, has limestone; the Markgräflerland between Freiburg and Basel is the land of Gutedel (Chasselas). Cooperatives produce most of the wine, led by the Badischer Winzerkeller in Breisach.
regions.history: Romans grew vines here; monasteries such as St. Gallen and Reichenau spread viticulture around Lake Constance. Grand Duke Ludwig of Baden's era promoted quality varieties, and Freiburg's state viticulture institute (founded 1920) bred grapes and later pioneered fungus-resistant varieties. A famous exception allows the Bocksbeutel flask in Baden's Taubertal and in the Neuweier area near Baden-Baden.
regions.terroir: Sheltered between the Black Forest and the Vosges, the Upper Rhine plain is sunny and warm. Soils range from granite and gneiss in the Ortenau to volcanic tuff and loess on the Kaiserstuhl, shell limestone in the Breisgau and Kraichgau, Keuper in the north and glacial moraine at Lake Constance.
regions.grapes: Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Riesling, Gutedel, Chardonnay, Silvaner, Auxerrois.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc in dry styles, Chardonnay, Gutedel, Riesling, Weißherbst rosé, Sekt.
regions.classification: Nine Bereiche: Tauberfranken, Badische Bergstraße, Kraichgau, Ortenau, Breisgau, Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg, Markgräflerland and Bodensee.

regions.name: Franken
regions.tagline: Silvaner in a flattened flask, from the shell limestone of the Main.
regions.summary:
Franken follows the zigzag of the Main through northern Bavaria, around Würzburg, Volkach, Iphofen and Klingenberg, with about 6,200 hectares. Its climate is continental, with cold winters and frost risk, and its wines are traditionally dry, earthy and firm. Silvaner (about 1,560 hectares) and Müller-Thurgau dominate, and Franken Silvaner, with its notes of hay, herbs and stone, is the classic partner for asparagus and the local carp. Riesling, Weißburgunder, Bacchus and Scheurebe also grow, and the red sandstone slopes of Churfranken near Bürgstadt and Klingenberg produce some of the finest Spätburgunder in Germany.

Franken's wine comes in the Bocksbeutel, a flattened, round-bellied bottle with EU protection. Würzburg holds three historic institutional estates whose cellars run beneath the baroque city: the Juliusspital (1576), the Bürgerspital (1316) and the Staatlicher Hofkeller under the Residenz.
regions.history: Charlemagne's donation of Hammelburg to Fulda in 777 records the earliest vineyards. Prince-bishops of Würzburg fostered wine for centuries; on 5 April 1659 the first Silvaner was planted at Castell, the earliest record of the grape in Germany. In the 1720s Würzburg's city council ordered its best wines to be filled into sealed Bocksbeutel to fight fraud. Goethe ordered Würzburger Steinwein to Weimar. Bottles of the legendary 1540 Steinwein survived into the twentieth century; Hugh Johnson tasted one in 1961 and found it still alive. Franken's vineyard collapsed after phylloxera and was rebuilt after the Second World War.
regions.terroir: Franken's soils follow the Triassic layers: Buntsandstein (red sandstone) in the west around Miltenberg, Klingenberg and Bürgstadt; Muschelkalk (shell limestone) in the central Maindreieck around Würzburg, Randersacker and Escherndorf; and Keuper marl and gypsum in the Steigerwald around Iphofen, Rödelsee and Castell. The continental climate brings dry, warm summers but severe frosts.
regions.grapes: Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau, Bacchus, Riesling, Domina, Spätburgunder, Weißburgunder, Kerner, Scheurebe.
regions.styles: Mostly dry whites, Silvaner and Riesling GG, Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder from red sandstone, Sekt, some noble sweet Rieslaner and Silvaner.
regions.classification: Traditionally three Bereiche (Mainviereck, Maindreieck, Steigerwald); in recent years Franken has promoted smaller landscape names such as Churfranken and Volkacher Mainschleife. Würzburger Stein-Berg (2020) and Bürgstadter Berg (2017) are separate EU PDOs.

regions.name: Württemberg
regions.tagline: Red-wine country on the Neckar, where Stuttgart has vineyards inside the city.
regions.summary:
Württemberg follows the Neckar and its tributaries (Rems, Enz, Kocher, Jagst) around Stuttgart and Heilbronn, with about 11,400 hectares, two thirds of them red. Trollinger (Schiava) is the everyday local red, pale and light and drunk by the quarter-litre 'Viertele'; Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Schwarzriesling (Pinot Meunier) and Spätburgunder are the serious ones. Riesling is the leading white. Cooperatives make most of the wine, and much of it never leaves Swabia.

A wave of ambitious estates (Aldinger in Fellbach, Schnaitmann, Dautel in Bönnigheim, Graf Neipperg in Schwaigern, Haidle, Wöhrwag, Fürst Hohenlohe-Oehringen and others) now makes Lemberger and Pinot of real depth. Stuttgart itself has about 400 hectares of vines within its city limits.
regions.history: Vines spread here under monastic and ducal patronage. The Weinsberg viticulture school, founded in 1868, bred Kerner (1929, named after the local poet Justinus Kerner) and Dornfelder (1955). Schillerwein, a rosé-like blend of red and white grapes fermented together, is a regional speciality.
regions.terroir: Steep slopes along the Neckar's meanders, some on terraced Muschelkalk cliffs such as the Hessigheimer Felsengärten, others on colourful Keuper marls. Sheltered by the Black Forest and Swabian Alb, the climate is warm in summer.
regions.grapes: Trollinger, Riesling, Lemberger, Schwarzriesling, Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Kerner, Samtrot, Dornfelder.
regions.styles: Light and full reds, Schillerwein, dry Riesling, Sekt.
regions.classification: Bereiche include Remstal-Stuttgart, Württembergisch Unterland, Kocher-Jagst-Tauber, Oberer Neckar and the Bodensee areas.

regions.name: Ahr
regions.tagline: A narrow slate canyon making Pinot Noir at the 50th parallel, rebuilt after the 2021 flood.
regions.summary:
The Ahr is a short river flowing east to the Rhine south of Bonn, and its gorge holds only about 530 hectares of vines, almost 80 percent red. Spätburgunder covers about two thirds, giving perfumed, mineral reds that are among the finest in Germany, with Frühburgunder as a speciality. The steep slate slopes at Walporzheim, Dernau, Mayschoß and Altenahr store heat like a radiator, which is why red grapes ripen this far north.

On 14 and 15 July 2021 a cloudburst turned the Ahr into a wall of water that killed more than 130 people in the valley, destroyed bridges, houses and cellars, and swept away barrels and entire vintages. Meyer-Näkel, Jean Stodden, Deutzerhof, Kreuzberg, J.J. Adeneuer and the cooperatives all suffered. Helpers from across Germany shovelled mud, and a 'Flutwein' campaign selling mud-caked bottles raised millions. The vineyards on the slopes mostly survived, and the 2021 to 2024 vintages carry that story.
regions.history: The Mayschoß cooperative, founded in 1868, is Germany's oldest winegrowers' cooperative. Red wine became the Ahr's identity in the nineteenth century, and day-trippers from Cologne and Bonn made the valley a tourist magnet.
regions.terroir: Devonian slate and greywacke on steep, terraced slopes in a narrow valley; the rock absorbs warmth by day and releases it at night. The lower valley around Bad Neuenahr has loess and deeper soils.
regions.grapes: Spätburgunder, Frühburgunder, Riesling, Portugieser, Dornfelder.
regions.styles: Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder reds, Blanc de Noirs, rosé, some Riesling.
regions.classification: Single Bereich Walporzheim/Ahrtal. Top sites: Walporzheimer Kräuterberg, Dernauer Pfarrwingert, Ahrweiler Rosenthal, Recher Herrenberg, Mayschosser Mönchberg.

regions.name: Mittelrhein
regions.tagline: Castles, the Loreley and steep slate Riesling in a UNESCO gorge.
regions.summary: The Mittelrhein follows the Rhine gorge from Bingen to Bonn, the stretch of castles and legends that inspired the Romantic movement. Its 460 hectares are mostly steep slate terraces, two thirds planted with Riesling, and the core lies in the Upper Middle Rhine Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site (2002) between Bingen and Koblenz. The wines are crisp and mineral, somewhere between the Mosel and the Rheingau. Hard work on steep slopes and a shortage of successors have shrunk the vineyard dramatically over the last century, but estates such as Toni Jost in Bacharach, Ratzenberger in Steeg, Matthias Müller and Florian Weingart in Spay and Lanius-Knab in Oberwesel keep the great sites alive: Bacharacher Hahn, Steeger St. Jost, Oberweseler Ölsberg and the Bopparder Hamm in the Rhine's largest loop.
regions.history: Monasteries and Rhine tolls made the gorge rich in the Middle Ages, and its wines shipped downriver to Cologne and the Low Countries. Nineteenth-century Romantic tourism (Turner, Victor Hugo, the Loreley poem of Heinrich Heine) made it famous, but phylloxera and industrialisation emptied the slopes.
regions.terroir: Devonian slate, greywacke and quartzite on terraced slopes of up to 60 percent; the river and rock retain warmth.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Grauburgunder.
regions.styles: Dry and fruity Riesling, Sekt, a little Pinot.
regions.classification: Two Bereiche: Loreley and Siebengebirge.

regions.name: Hessische Bergstraße
regions.tagline: Germany's springtime garden on the edge of the Odenwald.
regions.summary: The Hessische Bergstraße is a strip of vineyards along the western edge of the Odenwald between Darmstadt and Heppenheim, about 460 hectares in all. Spring arrives here earlier than almost anywhere in Germany, with almond and cherry blossom in March, and the climate is warm and sheltered. Riesling covers about a third, with Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder behind. The Hessian State Wine Estates run a domain at Bensheim whose monopole Heppenheimer Centgericht is the region's best-known site, alongside the Heppenheimer Steinkopf and Bensheimer Kalkgasse.
regions.history: The Romans built a road (strata montana) along the foot of the hills, which gave the region its name. Monasteries at Lorsch and the Electors of Mainz owned the vineyards; the area became a separate region in 1971 after being split from Baden's Bergstraße.
regions.terroir: Granite and weathered crystalline rocks of the Odenwald with loess on the lower slopes; the hills shelter the vines from east winds.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Grauburgunder, Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Silvaner.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and Pinot whites, some reds and Sekt.
regions.classification: Two Bereiche: Starkenburg and Umstadt.

regions.name: Saale-Unstrut
regions.tagline: Germany's northernmost classic region, on shell-limestone terraces.
regions.summary:
Saale-Unstrut lies around Freyburg and Naumburg in Saxony-Anhalt, along the Saale and Unstrut rivers, at about 51 degrees north. Its roughly 850 hectares (including outposts in Thuringia and at Werder in Brandenburg) are mostly on terraced Muschelkalk slopes, and the wines are dry, fresh and pure: Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Silvaner, Riesling and the Bacchus cross, plus some Pinot and Portugieser. Low yields after hard winters and tourism mean most wine is drunk locally.

The region holds Rotkäppchen in Freyburg, East Germany's famous Sekt house (founded 1856 as Kloss and Foerster, named Rotkäppchen in 1894), which bought Mumm in 2002 and became Germany's largest sparkling wine company, and the Landesweingut Kloster Pforta, on lands the Cistercians began farming in the twelfth century. At Großjena, a vineyard cliff carries the 'Steinernes Bilderbuch', a series of eighteenth-century reliefs carved into the rock.
regions.history: Viticulture was introduced by monks around a thousand years ago; the Cistercians of Pforta (1137) were key. After 1945 the region lay in East Germany; it became an Anbaugebiet after reunification in 1990.
regions.terroir: Muschelkalk and red sandstone terraces, some loess; a dry continental climate in the rain shadow of the Harz with cold winters and frost risk.
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Silvaner, Riesling, Bacchus, Kerner, Grauburgunder, Spätburgunder, Portugieser.
regions.styles: Dry whites, light reds, Sekt.
regions.classification: Three Bereiche: Schloss Neuenburg, Thüringen and Mansfelder Seen.

regions.name: Sachsen
regions.tagline: Baroque palaces and granite terraces on the Elbe around Dresden.
regions.summary: Sachsen is the easternmost wine region of Germany, about 520 hectares along the Elbe between Pirna, Dresden, Radebeul, Meißen and Diesbar-Seußlitz. Vineyards climb steep terraces of granite, gneiss and syenite, often crowned by baroque summer houses built for the Saxon court. The wines are mostly dry: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Traminer and Goldriesling, a local crossing hardly grown anywhere else, plus some Spätburgunder. Schloss Wackerbarth (the state Sekt house), Schloss Proschwitz, Klaus Zimmerling, Martin Schwarz and Vincenz Richter are leading names.
regions.history: Viticulture near Meißen is first recorded in 1161. The Wettin rulers expanded it; Hoflößnitz in Radebeul was their wine estate, and Augustus the Strong's court made Saxon wine a status symbol. Phylloxera arrived in 1887 and devastated the slopes, and in East Germany the region shrank further. It became an Anbaugebiet in 1990.
regions.terroir: Granite, syenite and gneiss weathered on south-facing terraces above the Elbe; the river valley moderates a continental climate with cold winters.
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Traminer, Goldriesling, Spätburgunder, Kerner.
regions.styles: Dry whites, Sekt, some Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Two Bereiche: Meißen and Elstertal.

regions.name: Niederösterreich
regions.tagline: The Danube's terraces and the Weinviertel's loess: Austria's white-wine heartland.
regions.summary:
Lower Austria holds 26,732 hectares, about 60 percent of the country's vineyard, and produced 1.7 million hectolitres in 2025. It contains eight specific wine areas, each now a DAC. Along the Danube west of Vienna lie the famous three: the Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal, plus the smaller Traisental and the Wagram's loess terraces. North of the river, the vast Weinviertel ('wine quarter') stretches to the Czech border and alone produced almost a million hectolitres in 2025. South-east of Vienna lie Carnuntum, with its Roman ruins and Zweigelt, and the Thermenregion, the spa country of Baden bei Wien with its rare white grapes and Pinot.

Grüner Veltliner rules here, from the 'Pfefferl' of the Weinviertel to the Smaragd of the Wachau, with Riesling in the stony Danube sites. The region's wine culture is visible everywhere in its Kellergassen, lanes of small press houses and cellars dug into loess at the edge of villages.
regions.history: Roman forts on the Danube (Favianis, Carnuntum), then monasteries (Klosterneuburg, Göttweig, Melk, Zwettl, Herzogenburg) and Bavarian abbeys shaped the vineyards. Krems and Stein were medieval wine-trading towns. The twentieth century brought Lenz Moser's high-trained vines at Rohrendorf, then the post-1985 quality revolution led by growers like Josef Jamek, F.X. Pichler, Emmerich Knoll and Willi Bründlmayer.
regions.terroir: Crystalline rocks of the Bohemian Massif on the Danube terraces, loess everywhere else, limestone at Falkenstein and in the Thermenregion; a meeting of cool Waldviertel air and warm Pannonian influence.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Zweigelt, Welschriesling, Weißburgunder, Blauer Portugieser, Roter Veltliner, Zierfandler, Rotgipfler, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Dry whites dominate; reds in Carnuntum, the Thermenregion and the Weinviertel; Sekt (much Austrian Sekt g.U. comes from here).
regions.classification: Eight DACs: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal, Traisental, Wagram, Weinviertel, Carnuntum, Thermenregion. Wines outside DAC rules are labelled Niederösterreich. ÖTW Erste Lagen cover the Danube regions.

regions.name: Burgenland
regions.tagline: Pannonian heat, a steppe lake and Austria's greatest reds and sweet wines.
regions.summary:
Burgenland runs down Austria's eastern border with Hungary and has 11,538 hectares of vines. It became Austrian only in 1921, and its culture still faces east. Around Lake Neusiedl the Pannonian climate is the warmest and driest in the country, and the lake's autumn mists make it one of the most reliable places on earth for noble rot. The region is Austria's red-wine heartland: Zweigelt around the lake, Blaufränkisch in Mittelburgenland, on the Leithaberg and at Eisenberg, plus Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir.

Its five wine areas are Neusiedlersee (the eastern shore and Seewinkel), Leithaberg (the western shore and the Leitha hills), Rosalia, Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg in the south, along with the sweet-wine DAC of Ruster Ausbruch. In 2025 Burgenland produced 582,900 hectolitres, slightly more than half of it red.
regions.history: Hallstatt-era grape seeds at Zagersdorf, Roman villas, and the Hungarian nobility (the Esterházy family still owns large estates) shaped the region. Rust's Ausbruch was among Europe's most prized sweet wines in the seventeenth century. Burgenland was the epicentre of the 1985 glycol scandal and then of the recovery, through growers such as Alois Kracher, Ernst Triebaumer, Hans Igler, Josef Umathum and the Gols group Pannobile.
regions.terroir: Flat sand, gravel, black earth and salty Seewinkel soils east of the lake; Leitha limestone and mica schist on the Leithagebirge; heavy clay in Mittelburgenland; greenschist and iron-rich loam at Eisenberg.
regions.grapes: Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch, Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Weißburgunder, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Furmint (revived at Rust).
regions.styles: Dry reds and red blends, dry whites, rosé, and noble sweet wines (Ausbruch, BA, TBA, Eiswein, Schilfwein).
regions.classification: DACs: Neusiedlersee, Leithaberg, Rosalia, Mittelburgenland, Eisenberg, Ruster Ausbruch. Other wines are labelled Burgenland.

regions.name: Steiermark
regions.tagline: Steep green hills on the Slovenian border, built for Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.summary:
Styria has 5,109 hectares of vines on some of the steepest slopes in Austria, a landscape of forested hills, wooden rattles (Klapotetz) to scare off birds and Buschenschank taverns. The climate is warmer and wetter than the Danube, with Mediterranean influence from the south and strong day-night swings, and the wines are aromatic, crisp and dry. Sauvignon Blanc is the star, alongside Gelber Muskateller, Morillon (Chardonnay), Weißburgunder and Welschriesling. Three DACs divide the region: Südsteiermark, Vulkanland Steiermark and Weststeiermark, home of Schilcher rosé.

A generation of growers (Tement, Polz, Gross, Sattlerhof, Lackner-Tinnacher, Wohlmuth) built an international reputation for Styrian Sauvignon from the 1990s on, while a group of natural-wine pioneers (Sepp and Maria Muster, Ewald Tscheppe of Werlitsch, Andreas Tscheppe, Franz Strohmeier) made the region a reference for skin-contact and biodynamic wines.
regions.history: The Styrian vineyard grew under the Habsburgs and the Archduke Johann (1782 to 1859), who promoted modern viticulture. Much of southern Styria lost its vineyards to the new border with Yugoslavia in 1919, and some estates still own vines on the Slovenian side.
regions.terroir: Opok (calcareous marl and sandstone), sand, gravel and schist in the south; basalt and volcanic tuff in the south-east; gneiss and schist in the west. High rainfall is offset by steep, well-drained slopes.
regions.grapes: Welschriesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Weißburgunder, Morillon, Gelber Muskateller, Grauburgunder, Traminer, Blauer Wildbacher, Zweigelt.
regions.styles: Dry aromatic whites, Schilcher rosé and Schilcher sparkling, skin-contact and natural wines.
regions.classification: Three DACs from the 2018 vintage, each with Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers; the STK producers' group classifies its own Große and Erste STK Rieden.

regions.name: Wien
regions.tagline: A world capital with 588 hectares of vines and a tavern on every hill.
regions.summary:
Vienna has 588 hectares of vineyards inside the city limits, on the slopes of the Kahlenberg, Nussberg and Bisamberg north of the Danube and at Mauer in the south. The city's signature is the Wiener Gemischter Satz, a white field blend of several varieties grown, picked and fermented together, which became a DAC in 2013. The Heurigen of Grinzing, Sievering, Nussdorf, Heiligenstadt, Stammersdorf and Neustift serve young wine with cold cuts under the 'ausg'steckt' pine branch, a tradition founded by Joseph II's decree of 17 August 1784.

Fritz Wieninger, Rainer Christ, Richard Zahel and the Mayer am Pfarrplatz estate (in the house where Beethoven lived in 1817) led a revival that turned Vienna from tourist wine into a serious appellation. In 2025 the city produced 30,200 hectolitres.
regions.history: Vines have grown in Vienna since Roman Vindobona. Medieval Vienna was surrounded by vineyards, and Duke Rudolf IV taxed tavern wine from 1359.
regions.terroir: Limestone and loess on the Nussberg and Kahlenberg, flysch sandstone, gravel and loess on the Bisamberg, and warm Pannonian influence.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Gemischter Satz field blends (often with Neuburger, Traminer, Welschriesling), Zweigelt, Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Gemischter Satz field blends, dry whites, some reds, Sekt.
regions.classification: Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC (2013): at least three white varieties planted together, the largest no more than 50 percent and the third at least 10 percent; a Ried name may be given. Other wines are labelled Wien.

regions.name: Bergland
regions.tagline: Small, ambitious vineyards in the Alpine provinces.
regions.summary: Bergland groups the five western and southern provinces of Kärnten (Carinthia), Oberösterreich (Upper Austria), Salzburg, Tirol and Vorarlberg, with about 243 hectares of vines in all. Each is a separate PDO. Carinthia, with vineyards on sunny slopes around the Wörthersee and in the Lavant valley, has grown fastest since its wine law was relaxed in the 2000s; Upper Austria has small vineyards along the Danube near Linz; Tirol and Vorarlberg grow a few hectares in sheltered valleys.
regions.history: Monasteries such as St. Paul im Lavanttal made wine in Carinthia in the Middle Ages, but the Little Ice Age and competition from the east pushed viticulture back. Modern revival began after 1970.
regions.terroir: Varied Alpine soils on sunny, sheltered slopes, often near lakes; cool nights and high frost risk.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir, Zweigelt, fungus-resistant varieties (Solaris, Muscaris).
regions.styles: Mostly dry whites and some sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Five PDOs: Kärnten, Oberösterreich, Salzburg, Tirol, Vorarlberg.

regions.name: Valais
regions.tagline: A sun-trap valley of the Rhône with dozens of Alpine grapes and some of Europe's highest vineyards.
regions.summary:
The Valais is Switzerland's largest wine canton, with about 4,600 hectares, roughly a third of the national vineyard, stretched for about 100 km along the upper Rhône from Martigny to Visp. The valley lies in the rain shadow of high Alps on both sides, and the vineyards on the south-facing right bank, between 450 and 800 metres, are among the sunniest and driest places in the Alps. Irrigation channels called bisses, some centuries old, once carried glacier water across cliffs to the vines.

No other wine region of its size grows so many varieties. Chasselas, here called Fendant, and Pinot Noir dominate in volume, along with Gamay and the traditional red blend Dôle. But the Valais' fame now rests on its specialities: Petite Arvine (salty, rhubarb and grapefruit, from dry to late-harvest), Amigne from Vétroz, Humagne Blanche, Heida (Savagnin) from Visperterminen, Johannisberg (Sylvaner), Malvoisie (Pinot Gris, often sweet), Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Syrah, which has thrived on the warm slopes since the 1920s. In the Val d'Anniviers, villages such as Grimentz keep the Vin des Glaciers, an oxidative, solera-aged wine from the old Rèze grape kept in larch barrels.
regions.history: Celtic and Roman wine is attested here, from the Sembrancher bottle to Roman Octodurus (Martigny). The canton built its wine economy on Fendant for the Swiss market, then rebuilt its image from the 1990s around native grapes and quality rules; the 1990 cantonal quality hierarchy was Switzerland's first. Leading names include Marie-Thérèse Chappaz in Fully, Domaine Jean-René Germanier, Simon Maye, Denis Mercier, Provins (the big cooperative), Domaine Cornulus and Chanton in Visp.
regions.terroir: Schist, gneiss and limestone on steep right-bank slopes; alluvial fans and glacial deposits, often stony and well drained. Very dry (under 600 mm in parts), with intense sunlight, high diurnal range and the föhn wind.
regions.grapes: Chasselas (Fendant), Pinot Noir, Gamay, Petite Arvine, Syrah, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne, Heida, Johannisberg, Malvoisie, Chardonnay, Merlot.
regions.styles: Dry whites, light and serious reds, Dôle, sweet late-harvest and botrytised wines (Petite Arvine, Malvoisie, Amigne), Vin des Glaciers.
regions.classification: AOC Valais, with communal and local names and Grand Cru rules set by communes such as Salgesch, Vétroz, Fully and Saint-Léonard. Fendant and Dôle are protected traditional names.

regions.name: Vaud
regions.tagline: The terraces of Chasselas above Lake Geneva.
regions.summary:
Vaud, with about 3,800 hectares, is the heart of Chasselas and of Swiss wine culture. Its vineyards ring Lake Geneva from the city of Geneva's border to the Rhône delta and continue up the Rhône into the Chablais, with smaller areas near Lakes Neuchâtel and Murten. Chasselas covers most of the white vineyard, and the Vaudois approach is to let the grape transmit place: wines are named after villages and sites rather than grapes.

Four great areas define Vaud. Lavaux, between Lausanne and Vevey, is 830 hectares of terraces dropping to the lake, inscribed by UNESCO in 2007, with the Grand Cru appellations Dézaley and Calamin. The Chablais upstream, with Yvorne, Aigle, Ollon and Bex, has steeper, warmer slopes and gravelly soils. La Côte, between Lausanne and Nyon, is gentler and larger, with Féchy, Mont-sur-Rolle and Morges. Nord Vaudois (Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars, Vully) lies near the Jura lakes.
regions.history: Monks of the eleventh and twelfth centuries and the bishops of Lausanne built Lavaux's terraces; Bern ruled Vaud from 1536 to 1798, and after the Reformation church estates such as the Clos des Abbayes and Clos des Moines passed to the city of Lausanne, which still owns them. The Confrérie des Vignerons in Vevey has inspected vineyards and staged its festival since the eighteenth century.
regions.terroir: Glacial moraine, limestone, marl and conglomerate in Lavaux; scree and alluvial gravel in the Chablais; deeper moraine and molasse on La Côte. In Lavaux the 'three suns' (sky, lake reflection and warmth from the stone walls) ripen grapes on gradients of up to about 40 degrees.
regions.grapes: Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Gamaret, Garanoir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Merlot.
regions.styles: Dry Chasselas from light to deep and age-worthy, Salvagnin and Pinot-Gamay reds, some sparkling and sweet wines.
regions.classification: Eight cantonal AOCs: Chablais, Lavaux, Calamin (Grand Cru), Dézaley (Grand Cru), La Côte, Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars and Vully (shared with Fribourg). Premier Grand Cru recognises individual estates. Communal names such as Yvorne, Aigle, Epesses, Saint-Saphorin, Féchy and Mont-sur-Rolle appear within the AOCs.

regions.name: Genève
regions.tagline: Switzerland's third canton, a flat crescent of Gamay and Chasselas around the city.
regions.summary: Geneva has about 1,340 hectares of vines, almost entirely surrounded by France, in three areas: the Mandement around Satigny (one of the largest wine communes in Switzerland), the land between the Arve and the Rhône, and between the Arve and the lake. The canton was the first to introduce French-style AOC rules in the late 1980s and is now a laboratory for new varieties: Gamaret and Garanoir (Swiss crossings of Gamay and Reichensteiner) do well here, and Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Merlot are all important. Premier Cru communes such as Satigny, Dardagny and Russin allow higher-grade labels.
regions.history: Monasteries and Geneva's merchants planted vines around the city from the Middle Ages. Today the canton's growers, including Domaine des Balisiers, Domaine de la Vigne Blanche and the Cave de Genève cooperative, have built a reputation for clean, modern wines.
regions.terroir: Glacial moraine and alluvial deposits on gentle slopes; a relatively warm, sunny climate moderated by the lake.
regions.grapes: Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamaret, Chardonnay, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Garanoir.
regions.styles: Dry whites and reds, rosé, sparkling.
regions.classification: AOC Genève with 22 Premier Cru areas.

regions.name: Three Lakes
regions.tagline: Pinot Noir, Oeil de Perdrix and Chasselas on Jurassic limestone.
regions.summary: Swiss Wine Promotion's Three Lakes region joins the vineyards along Lake Neuchâtel (canton of Neuchâtel, about 600 ha), Lake Biel (Bielersee, canton of Bern) and Lake Murten (Vully, shared by Fribourg and Vaud), about 945 hectares in all. The soils are Jurassic limestone like Burgundy's, and Pinot Noir and Chasselas dominate. Neuchâtel claims to have invented Oeil de Perdrix ('partridge eye'), a pale rosé of Pinot Noir, and is known for unfiltered Chasselas released in January. The Bielersee villages of Ligerz, Twann and Schafis grow Chasselas and Pinot on steep slopes above the lake.
regions.history: The Château d'Auvernier and the Château de Boudry (which houses a wine museum) recall Neuchâtel's long viticultural history under the Prussian kings, who ruled the principality until 1848.
regions.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl at the foot of the Jura, moraine and molasse at Vully; lakes moderate the climate.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chasselas, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Gamay.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, Oeil de Perdrix, Chasselas (including unfiltered), sparkling.
regions.classification: AOC Neuchâtel, AOC Bielersee (Lac de Bienne), AOC Vully (Vaud/Fribourg).

regions.name: Ticino
regions.tagline: Merlot under the palms, south of the Alps.
regions.summary: Ticino, Switzerland's Italian-speaking canton, has about 1,030 hectares of vines on hills and terraces from the Leventina to the Mendrisiotto near Como. After phylloxera wiped out the old local varieties, Merlot was planted from 1906 and now covers about 80 percent of the vineyard, giving everything from light reds to oak-aged wines of Bordeaux structure and, increasingly, white Merlot (vinified without skin contact). Rainfall is heavy but sunshine abundant, and the north (Sopraceneri, around Bellinzona and Locarno) has granite and gneiss while the south (Sottoceneri) has limestone and clay. Gialdi, Tamborini, Guido Brivio, Luigi Zanini's Castello di Morcote, Cantina Kopp von der Crone Visini and Christian Zündel are leading names.
regions.history: The canton has been growing wine since Roman times, but phylloxera ended the old tradition around 1900. In 2025 Ticino and Misox produced 3.4 million litres, down 8 percent, partly because of Japanese beetle in the Mendrisiotto.
regions.terroir: Granite, gneiss and glacial deposits north of Monte Ceneri; limestone, clay and moraine to the south; sub-Mediterranean climate with heavy rain.
regions.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bondola (a local survivor), Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Merlot reds, white Merlot, rosato.
regions.classification: AOC Ticino; the Ticino VITI label marks wines approved by a tasting panel.

sources.title: swissinfo.ch / FOAG: 2025 judged an excellent year for Swiss wine

regions.name: German-speaking Switzerland
regions.tagline: Small lake and valley vineyards, from Basel to the Bündner Herrschaft's Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: About 2,600 hectares of vines spread across 17 German-speaking cantons, from Basel and Aargau to Zurich, Schaffhausen, Thurgau, St. Gallen and Graubünden. Pinot Noir (Blauburgunder) is the main grape, and Müller-Thurgau, named after its Swiss breeder, the main white. The star is the Bündner Herrschaft in Graubünden, four villages (Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins and Malans) in the upper Rhine valley where the warm föhn wind ripens Pinot Noir of Burgundian finesse; Daniel and Martha Gantenbein, Georg Fromm, Thomas Studach and the Donatsch family make some of Switzerland's most sought-after reds. Graubünden is also home to Completer, an ancient white revived at Malans. Schaffhausen's Hallau and Zurich's lake villages make the bulk of the rest; the Wädenswil research station on Lake Zurich (now Agroscope) has its roots in the 1890 founding of an experimental station there.
regions.history: Monasteries and city councils spread the vine; Hermann Müller from Tägerwilen in Thurgau bred Müller-Thurgau at Geisenheim in 1882 and later directed Wädenswil. In 2025 German-speaking Switzerland's harvest rose by almost a third to 13.7 million litres.
regions.terroir: Molasse sandstone and marl, glacial moraine, limestone; föhn winds in Graubünden and the Rhine valley.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Müller-Thurgau, Räuschling, Completer, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Blanc.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, light whites, some sparkling.
regions.classification: One cantonal AOC per canton (Graubünden, Zürich, Schaffhausen, Aargau, Thurgau, St. Gallen, Basel-Landschaft and others).

sources.title: swissinfo.ch / FOAG: 2025 judged an excellent year for Swiss wine

regions.name: Moselle Luxembourgeoise
regions.tagline: One river, one appellation, and a sparkling-wine country in miniature.
regions.summary: The Luxembourg Moselle runs from Schengen to Wasserbillig along a 42 km wine route, with villages such as Remerschen, Wellenstein, Remich, Stadtbredimus, Ehnen, Wormeldange, Machtum and Grevenmacher. Riesling, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Rivaner dominate, and Crémant is the national pride.
regions.history: Roman, then monastic, then a bulk Elbling supplier to Germany, Luxembourg rebuilt its wine identity after 1919, with the Institut viti-vinicole at Remich and the Marque Nationale in 1935. The cooperative movement (Domaines Vinsmoselle) dominates production; private growers such as Alice Hartmann, Domaine Thill, Schumacher-Knepper and Abi Duhr's Château Pauqué lead quality.
regions.terroir: Keuper marl in the south, Muschelkalk in the north; south-east-facing slopes above the river.
regions.grapes: Rivaner, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Elbling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Dry whites, Crémant, some reds and late-harvest wines.
regions.classification: AOP Moselle Luxembourgeoise with Côtes de, Coteaux de and Lieu-dit levels; Crémant de Luxembourg.

regions.name: South East England
regions.tagline: Kent, Sussex and Surrey: chalk downs and the heart of English sparkling wine.
regions.summary: Kent (the largest planted county), West and East Sussex and Surrey hold most of the UK's vineyards. The North and South Downs are chalk, the Weald between them clay and greensand. Nyetimber, Ridgeview, Rathfinny, Wiston, Bolney, Chapel Down, Gusbourne, Hush Heath, Domaine Evremond (Taittinger) and Denbies are here. Sussex gained its own PDO in 2022.
regions.history: Kent and Sussex had medieval monastic vineyards; Bolney (1972) and Breaky Bottom (1974) were early modern pioneers, and Nyetimber (1988) and Ridgeview (1995) proved that Champagne varieties could make world-class sparkling wine here. Champagne houses followed: Taittinger planted Domaine Evremond in Kent from 2017.
regions.terroir: Chalk of the North and South Downs, Wealden clay and greensand between them; maritime climate, warm summers close to the Channel.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs; Sussex PDO (2022)

regions.name: Wessex
regions.tagline: Hampshire's chalk and the cradle of the modern revival at Hambledon.
regions.summary: Hampshire, Dorset and Wiltshire share chalk downland similar to Champagne. Hambledon (1952) began the modern revival; Hattingley Valley, Exton Park, Coates and Seely and Louis Pommery England are leading names.
regions.history: Hambledon's planting in 1952 began the English revival, and Hampshire's chalk drew investment in the 2000s from Hattingley Valley, Exton Park and the Pommery partnership.
regions.terroir: Chalk downland with flint, similar to Champagne; slightly cooler and higher than Sussex.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs

regions.name: East Anglia
regions.tagline: Dry, sunny Essex and the rise of still English Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: Essex is now the third county by planted area, and the Crouch Valley near Burnham-on-Crouch, one of the driest parts of Britain on London clay, supplies fruit for some of the best still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, including for Gusbourne and other wineries.
regions.history: Essex and Suffolk had monastic vineyards in the Middle Ages; the modern Crouch Valley plantings date mostly from the 1990s on and expanded fast after 2015.
regions.terroir: London clay and gravels in Essex, one of the driest and sunniest parts of Britain.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs

regions.name: South West England
regions.tagline: Cornish valleys, Devon slate and the Darnibole PDO.
regions.summary: Cornwall, Devon, Somerset and Gloucestershire have smaller, often tourist-led vineyards. Camel Valley in Cornwall, founded by Bob and Annie Lindo in 1989, won international awards for sparkling wine and created the Darnibole PDO for its Bacchus.
regions.history: Roman and medieval vineyards existed in the west country; Camel Valley (1989) is the best-known modern estate.
regions.terroir: Slate, sandstone and clay; mild, wet and windy, so sheltered valleys matter.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs; Darnibole PDO (2017)

regions.name: Wales
regions.tagline: A small but fast-growing wine country with its own PDO.
regions.summary: Wales has about 91 hectares of vines, mostly in the south-east (Monmouthshire, the Vale of Glamorgan) and along the border. Ancre Hill, a biodynamic estate near Monmouth, and Llanerch are the best known. Welsh Wine has been a PDO since 2011.
regions.history: Vines were grown at Castell Coch for the Marquess of Bute in the 1870s; the modern Welsh wine revival dates from the 1970s and accelerated in the 2010s.
regions.terroir: Old red sandstone, limestone and clay; wetter and cooler than south-east England.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Bacchus, Seyval Blanc, Solaris and others
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling (most of the output), still white, rosé and some red
regions.classification: PDO English Wine (or Welsh Wine in Wales) and the English/Welsh Regional Wine PGIs

regions.name: Wallonia
regions.tagline: Chalk slopes of Hainaut and the Meuse valley, home of Crémant de Wallonie.
regions.summary: Wallonia's vineyards are concentrated in Hainaut near Mons and Binche, the Sambre and Meuse valleys around Namur, Dinant and Huy, and near Liège. The three Walloon PDOs cover still wine (Côtes de Sambre et Meuse) and sparkling wine (Crémant de Wallonie, Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie) across the whole region.
regions.history: The Meuse valley at Huy and Liège had vineyards from Carolingian times. Château de Bioul near Anhée revived a historic estate in the 2000s.
regions.terroir: Chalk and marl in Hainaut, slate and limestone in the Meuse valley.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Johanniter, Solaris.
regions.styles: Sparkling, dry whites, light reds.
regions.classification: Three PDOs: Côtes de Sambre et Meuse, Crémant de Wallonie, Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie; PGI Vin de pays des Jardins de Wallonie.
appellations: Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie

regions.name: Flanders
regions.tagline: Haspengouw's loess, Hageland's ironstone hills and the Maas valley.
regions.summary: Flanders has four PDOs and shares a fifth with the Netherlands. Hageland in Flemish Brabant, on iron-rich sandstone hills around Aarschot, Diest and Leuven, was the first Belgian appellation in 1997; Haspengouw (Hesbaye) in Limburg is fruit-orchard country on loess; Heuvelland, near Ypres on the French border, is a small hilly area; and Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn covers Flemish sparkling wine. The Maasvallei Limburg PDO crosses the Maas into the Netherlands.
regions.history: Leuven's medieval presses and the Hageland's monastic vineyards are the historic roots.
regions.terroir: Loess, sand, ironstone and clay; cool maritime climate.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder, Regent, Johanniter.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, light reds.
regions.classification: PDOs: Hagelandse wijn, Haspengouwse wijn, Heuvellandse wijn, Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn, Maasvallei Limburg (with the Netherlands); PGI Vlaamse landwijn.

sources.title: Candiago et al. (2022), geospatial inventory of EU wine PDOs (registration dates, varieties, communes)

regions.name: Limburg (NL)
regions.tagline: Marl hills, the Maas and the classic varieties.
regions.summary: South Limburg is the most hilly part of the Netherlands and the historic heart of Dutch wine, with vineyards on chalky marl and loess near Maastricht, Valkenburg, Gulpen and Vaals. The Mergelland and Vijlen PDOs cover it, and the Maasvallei Limburg PDO covers the river valley further north around Thorn and Roermond.
regions.history: Medieval vineyards on the Maas slopes, revived from 1970 by the Apostelhoeve.
regions.terroir: Cretaceous marl and loess, Maas gravels.
regions.grapes: Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Solaris, Johanniter.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, light reds.
regions.classification: PDOs Mergelland, Vijlen, Maasvallei Limburg.

sources.title: Candiago et al. (2022), geospatial inventory of EU wine PDOs (registration dates, varieties, communes)

regions.name: Eastern Netherlands
regions.tagline: Farm estates on sand, built on fungus-resistant grapes.
regions.summary: The eastern provinces of Gelderland and Overijssel have some of the largest Dutch vineyards, on sandy and loamy soils, with three single-estate PDOs: Oolde near Lochem, Ambt Delden in Twente and Achterhoek-Winterswijk.
regions.history: A twenty-first-century development, driven by farmers diversifying from dairy and arable crops.
regions.terroir: Sand, loam and glacial deposits; cool, wet maritime climate.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Souvignier Gris, Cabernet Blanc, Regent, Pinotin, Cabernet Cortis.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, reds, some fortified and dried-grape wines.
regions.classification: PDOs Oolde, Ambt Delden, Achterhoek-Winterswijk.

regions.name: Denmark
regions.tagline: Vineyards on Jutland, Funen, Zealand and Bornholm.
regions.summary: Danish vineyards are scattered across the country, with the largest concentration on Zealand (especially North Zealand) and Bornholm, plus Funen and Jutland. Dons near Kolding in south-east Jutland has the only PDO.
regions.history: Legal commercial wine-growing dates only from 1999.
regions.terroir: Moraine, clay, sand; granite on Bornholm.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Rondo, Regent, Cabernet Cortis, Souvignier Gris, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds, fruit wines.
regions.classification: PDO Dons; regional designations Fyn, Jylland, Sjælland, Bornholm.

regions.name: Skåne
regions.tagline: Sweden's southern tip, where most of its vines grow.
regions.summary: Skåne, the southernmost Swedish province, has most of Sweden's vineyards, from the Kullaberg peninsula in the north-west to Österlen in the south-east.
regions.history: A modern development since the early 2000s.
regions.terroir: Moraine, limestone and granite; maritime influence.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Rondo, Regent, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: White, sparkling, rosé.
regions.classification: No PDO.

regions.name: Morava
regions.tagline: South Moravia: cellar lanes, loess and Pálava limestone on the Austrian border.
regions.summary: Moravia holds about 95 percent of Czech vineyards in four subregions along the Austrian and Slovak borders. The largest wine villages are Velké Bílovice (766 ha), Valtice (578 ha), Mikulov (516 ha) and Čejkovice (515 ha). Fresh, aromatic whites dominate, with reds in Velkopavlovická and Slovácko.
regions.history: Roman, Great Moravian and monastic roots; the Liechtensteins of Valtice and Lednice and the Dietrichsteins of Mikulov shaped the landscape. Communism nationalised the industry; since 1989 family wineries and cellar villages have revived it.
regions.terroir: Loess, limestone (Pálava), granite and gneiss (Znojmo), sand and flysch (Slovácko); warm continental climate.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Pálava, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot varieties, Saint Laurent, Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt.
regions.styles: Dry and off-dry whites, Prädikat wines, reds, rosé, sparkling, straw and ice wine.

regions.name: Čechy
regions.tagline: A sliver of vines on the Elbe, where Czech wine began in legend.
regions.summary: Bohemia has only about 4 to 5 percent of Czech vineyards, in the Mělnická and Litoměřická subregions on the Elbe and Vltava north of Prague, plus small plots in Prague itself and around Most. Müller-Thurgau, Riesling and Saint Laurent lead, and Mělník's château winery and the old cellars of Velké Žernoseky are the landmarks.
regions.history: Ludmila's legendary planting at Mělník and Charles IV's support for vineyards around Prague in the fourteenth century.
regions.terroir: Sandstone, marl and basalt on south-facing river slopes; cooler and drier than Moravia.
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Saint Laurent, Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc, Gewürztraminer.
regions.styles: Dry whites and light reds.

regions.name: Malokarpatská
regions.tagline: Royal wine towns on the slopes above Bratislava.
regions.summary: The Little Carpathian region runs north-east from Bratislava along the foothills, through Rača, Svätý Jur, Pezinok and Modra to Trnava and Skalica, and is Slovakia's most historic and largest wine region. Courtyard wineries, the annual Open Cellar days and the Little Carpathian Wine Route link the towns; Rača's Frankovka, Pezinok's Grüner and Riesling and Modra's research station (home of Slovak grape breeding) are its pillars.
regions.history: Vines were grown on these slopes under the Romans and in the Middle Ages by German-speaking settlers; Svätý Jur, Pezinok and Modra grew rich on wine and became royal free towns of the Kingdom of Hungary in the seventeenth century. Under communism the large state cooperatives dominated; family wineries returned after 1989.
regions.terroir: Granite and crystalline schist on the slopes, loess and alluvium below; sheltered from north winds by the mountains.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín
regions.styles: Dry whites, reds, rosé, Prädikat wines
regions.classification: Regional PDO Malokarpatská

regions.name: Južnoslovenská
regions.tagline: The warm Danube plain, rich whites and reds.
regions.summary: The South Slovak region spreads across the Danube lowland from Šamorín and Dunajská Streda to Galanta, Komárno, Strekov and Štúrovo, largely in the Hungarian-speaking south. It is warm and dry, giving ripe whites and reds; Château Belá near Štúrovo, run with the Saar's Egon Müller, made Slovak Riesling internationally known.
regions.history: The Danube plain was part of Hungary's wine economy for centuries; Strekov and Štúrovo (opposite Esztergom) have medieval roots. Modern investment since the 1990s, including Château Belá, revived quality.
regions.terroir: Sand, gravel and loess on the plain, with loess and clay hills near Strekov and Štúrovo.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín
regions.styles: Dry whites, reds, rosé, Prädikat wines
regions.classification: Regional PDO Južnoslovenská

regions.name: Nitrianska
regions.tagline: Loess hills around the old capital of Nitra.
regions.summary: The Nitra region is the largest by area, around Nitra, Hlohovec, Zlaté Moravce, Vráble and Topoľčianky, with loess hills and some volcanic sites in the south-east. Château Topoľčianky, in the Habsburg estate town with its national stud, is a major producer.
regions.history: Nitra, seat of a Great Moravian prince and Slovakia's oldest town, has a wine history going back over a thousand years; Topoľčianky was a Habsburg estate.
regions.terroir: Loess and clay, with andesite near the Štiavnica hills.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín

regions.summary: The Central Slovak region lies along the Hungarian border around Modrý Kameň, Fiľakovo, Rimavská Sobota and Tornaľa, with scattered vineyards on loess and volcanic soils.
regions.history: Small peasant vineyards in the Hungarian-speaking south, long overshadowed by neighbouring Eger and Tokaj across the border.
regions.terroir: Loess, clay and volcanic rock; warm summers.
regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín

regions.tagline: Volcanic hills of the east, next to Tokaj.
regions.summary: The East Slovak region covers vineyards around Košice, Moldava nad Bodvou and the Trebišov and Michalovce areas outside the Tokaj delimitation, on volcanic and loess soils.
regions.history: Viticulture around Košice and the Zemplín shares its history with Tokaj; the region was cut off from Hungarian markets after 1920.

regions.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín

regions.name: Tokaj (Slovakia)
regions.tagline: Seven villages of volcanic Tokaj on the Slovak side of the border.
regions.summary: Slovak Tokaj covers about 908 hectares of classified vineyards in seven villages of the Trebišov district (Bara, Čerhov, Černochov, Malá Tŕňa, Slovenské Nové Mesto, Veľká Tŕňa and Viničky), on the northern edge of the Zemplén hills that form Hungarian Tokaj. The same grapes (Furmint, Lipovina and Yellow Muscat) and the same botrytis styles are made, including Tokajský výber, graded in puttony, and Tokajská esencia. Medieval cellars cut into volcanic tuff riddle the hills of Malá Tŕňa and Veľká Tŕňa.
regions.history: The region was split from Hungarian Tokaj by the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. The long dispute over the name was settled in Slovakia's favour by EU courts in 2012 and 2013.
regions.terroir: Volcanic tuff, andesite and loess on south-facing slopes above the Bodrog plain; autumn mists from the Bodrog and Latorica bring noble rot.
regions.grapes: Furmint, Lipovina (Hárslevelű), Muškát žltý (Yellow Muscat).
regions.styles: Dry and sweet Tokaj wines, samorodné, výber (aszú), esencia, mášláš, fordítáš.
regions.classification: PDO Vinohradnícka oblasť Tokaj (EU reg. 2006).

regions.name: Lubuskie (Zielona Góra)
regions.tagline: Poland's historic wine capital.
regions.summary: Zielona Góra, the 'city of wine', had thousands of vineyards at its peak and made Prussian sparkling wine from 1826. Today the Lubuskie wine route links dozens of new vineyards, including the large Zabór estate (about 35 ha), and the Palm House on Wine Hill and the September Winobranie festival keep the tradition alive.
regions.history: Vineyards from at least 1314 and a Prussian sparkling-wine industry from 1826 made Grünberg the northernmost notable wine town of its time.
regions.terroir: Glacial sands and clays on gentle hills; cool continental climate.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds
regions.classification: No PDO.

regions.name: Dolny Śląsk (Lower Silesia)
regions.tagline: Young vineyards in the warm south-west.
regions.summary: Lower Silesia around Wrocław, Trzebnica and the Sudeten foothills has some of Poland's oldest modern vineyards, such as Winnica Jaworek, and a warm, sheltered climate.
regions.history: Cistercians and Silesian towns grew vines in the Middle Ages; Trzebnica's hills were among the first replanted after 1990.
regions.terroir: Loess and clay in the Trzebnica hills, varied soils in the Sudeten foothills; one of Poland's warmest areas.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds
regions.classification: No PDO.

regions.name: Małopolska
regions.tagline: Limestone vineyards around Kraków.
regions.summary: Małopolska has medieval roots on Wawel hill and a modern cluster of vineyards on Jurassic limestone around Kraków, led by Srebrna Góra (about 28 ha) below the Camaldolese monastery at Bielany, and Winnica Garlicki.
regions.history: Grape seeds on Wawel suggest vines around 1000; monasteries and the royal court in Kraków kept vineyards in the Middle Ages.
regions.terroir: Jurassic limestone and loess around Kraków.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds
regions.classification: No PDO.

regions.name: Vistula Valley (Sandomierz and Kazimierz)
regions.tagline: Loess hills above the Vistula.
regions.summary: The Vistula valley around Sandomierz and Kazimierz Dolny has loess hills with a long wine history; Winnica Płochockich near Sandomierz is a well-known estate.
regions.history: Sandomierz had medieval vineyards on its loess hills, and the area was among the first in modern Poland to replant.
regions.terroir: Deep loess on hills above the Vistula; warm, sunny summers.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds
regions.classification: No PDO.

regions.name: Podkarpacie
regions.tagline: The south-eastern foothills near Jasło.
regions.summary: Podkarpacie in the south-east, around Jasło, Krosno and Przemyśl, revived its vineyards from the 1980s and hosts an annual wine festival in Jasło.
regions.history: Krosno and Przemyśl had medieval vineyards and traded in Hungarian wine; the modern revival began in the 1980s.
regions.terroir: Carpathian flysch, clay and loess in the foothills.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds
regions.classification: No PDO.

appellations.name: Mosel
appellations.grapes: Riesling (about 62%), Müller-Thurgau, Elbling, Weißburgunder, Spätburgunder, Kerner
appellations.summary:
The Mosel PDO covers the river from the Luxembourg border to Koblenz plus the Saar and Ruwer valleys: about 8,500 hectares in 131 municipalities, most of them on slopes too steep for machines. It is the benchmark for Riesling at low alcohol and high acidity. A Mosel Kabinett might have 8 percent alcohol and 40 grams of sugar yet taste dry-ish and electric; a Spätlese is richer, an Auslese honeyed, and the region's TBA and Eiswein are among the most expensive sweet wines in the world. Dry Riesling, often labelled trocken or Grosses Gewächs, is now just as important, and grower Sekt from Riesling or Elbling is rising.

The best sites cluster in the Middle Mosel between Trittenheim and Ürzig, at Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen and Zeltingen, and on the Saar around Wiltingen and Ockfen. Abandoned terraces on the Lower Mosel and side valleys are being replanted by young growers, a sign of a region in revival.
appellations.terroir: Devonian slate in blue, grey and red forms, steep south-facing slopes over a river that reflects light and buffers frost.
appellations.nerd_note: The Mosel's traditional gold capsule (Goldkapsel) and long gold capsule mark an estate's best Auslese, a private code that predates the 1971 law.
contains: Uhlen Blaufüsser Lay / Uhlen Blaufüßer Lay

appellations.name: Saar
appellations.summary: The Saar Bereich covers the lower Saar valley from Serrig to Konz, with the villages of Saarburg, Ockfen, Ayl, Wiltingen, Kanzem, Wawern and Oberemmel. It is cooler and later-ripening than the Middle Mosel, and its Rieslings have the highest acidity and some of the most precise flavours in Germany. Scharzhofberg is the most famous site; Bockstein, Rausch, Kupp and Altenberg are close behind.
appellations.terroir: Grey slate and diabase on steep, wind-exposed slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Peter Lauer labels its wines by 'Fass' numbers that correspond to historic parcels within the Ayler Kupp.

appellations.name: Ruwertal
appellations.summary: The Ruwertal Bereich covers the little Ruwer valley east of Trier, with Kasel, Waldrach, Mertesdorf and Eitelsbach. The Rieslings are delicate and herbal, with very low alcohol and long ageing potential. Two monastic estates, Maximin Grünhaus and the Karthäuserhof, own their slopes as monopoles.
appellations.terroir: Blue Devonian slate on steep south-facing slopes in a cool valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Karthäuserhof's bottles carry only a neck label and no body label, a tradition dating to the nineteenth century.

appellations.name: Bernkastel
appellations.summary: Bereich Bernkastel is the Middle Mosel from Zell to Trier-area villages, the heartland of the region's fame: Piesport, Brauneberg, Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen, Zeltingen, Ürzig and Erden. A wine labelled only with the Bereich name is a blend from anywhere in that stretch; the excitement lies in the single villages and vineyards inside it.
appellations.terroir: Blue slate in the main river bends, red slate at Ürzig and Erden.
appellations.nerd_note: The famous Großlage Bernkasteler Kurfürstlay sits inside this Bereich and must now be labelled 'Region Kurfürstlay'.

appellations.name: Burg Cochem
appellations.summary: Burg Cochem is the Lower Mosel or Terrassenmosel, from Zell to Koblenz, with Bremm's Calmont, Cochem's castle and the terraced cliffs of Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf. Growers like Heymann-Löwenstein and Knebel have shown that its terraces give powerful, dry Rieslings.
appellations.terroir: Hard slate, quartzite and sandstone on dry-stone terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: The Uhlen at Winningen was split into three separately registered EU PDOs in 2018 according to its soils.

appellations.name: Obermosel
appellations.summary: The Upper Mosel faces Luxembourg across the river south of Trier and sits on Muschelkalk limestone, not slate. It is the last stronghold of Elbling, one of Europe's oldest varieties, which gives light, tart wines and good Sekt, alongside the Pinot family.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and marl, the same geology as Luxembourg's Moselle.
appellations.nerd_note: Elbling is thought to have been grown on the Mosel since Roman times.

appellations.name: Moseltor
appellations.summary: Moseltor is the small Saarland end of the Mosel around Perl and Nennig, opposite Schengen in Luxembourg, where three countries meet. Limestone soils and Pinot varieties link it to Luxembourg and Lorraine.
appellations.terroir: Muschelkalk limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: A Roman villa at Nennig preserves one of the largest mosaics north of the Alps, a reminder that wine and wealth arrived here early.

appellations.name: Uhlen Blaufüsser Lay / Uhlen Blaufüßer Lay
match: Uhlen Blaufüsser Lay / Uhlen Blaufüßer Lay
appellations.summary: One of three EU PDOs carved from the Winninger Uhlen on the Lower Mosel in 2018, at the initiative of Reinhard Löwenstein, who argued that the amphitheatre-shaped Uhlen contains three distinct soils. Blaufüßer Lay is the blue-grey slate section with calcareous inclusions; its Riesling is the most fine-boned and saline of the three. Rules require Riesling, a maximum yield of 70 hl/ha and hand harvesting.
appellations.terroir: Blue-grey Devonian slate with lime-rich fossil layers on terraced cliffs above the Mosel.
appellations.nerd_note: Among the first single-vineyard PDOs in Germany; the name means 'blue-foot slate'.

appellations.name: Uhlen Laubach
appellations.summary: The Laubach section of the Winninger Uhlen, registered as an EU PDO in 2018, lies on grey slate rich in fossils. Its Rieslings are broad and smoky, often with more body than Blaufüßer Lay. Like its siblings it requires Riesling, hand harvest and low yields.
appellations.terroir: Grey slate with fossil-bearing layers.
appellations.nerd_note: Löwenstein's three Uhlen bottlings side by side are a textbook lesson in soil and taste.

appellations.name: Uhlen Roth Lay
appellations.summary: Roth Lay, the reddish, iron-rich slate section of the Uhlen straddling Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf, became an EU PDO in 2018. It gives the most powerful, spicy wines of the Uhlen trio.
appellations.terroir: Red, iron-bearing slate.
appellations.nerd_note: The only one of the three Uhlen PDOs whose area extends into Kobern-Gondorf.

appellations.name: Rheingau
appellations.summary:
The Rheingau PDO covers about 3,200 hectares in eleven municipalities from Flörsheim and Hochheim on the Main to Lorch at the start of the Rhine gorge. It is the most Riesling-dominated region in Germany and the historic home of German fine wine: the place of Kloster Eberbach, Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads and the Geisenheim institute. Rheingau Riesling is broader than Mosel Riesling, with peach and citrus fruit, spice and a firm, dry backbone, and the region led the movement back to dry Riesling with the Charta (1983) and its Erstes Gewächs (1999). Spätburgunder from the slate slopes of Assmannshausen is a celebrated red.

The great sites run along the slope: Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg and Rottland, Johannisberger Hölle, Winkeler Jesuitengarten, Erbacher Marcobrunn and Siegelsberg, the Steinberg, Kiedricher Gräfenberg, Rauenthaler Baiken and Hochheimer Hölle and Domdechaney.
appellations.terroir: A south-facing slope sheltered by the Taunus with the wide Rhine as a mirror; loess and marl near the river, slate and quartzite higher up.
appellations.nerd_note: The word 'hock' for Rhine wine comes from Hochheim; after Queen Victoria visited in 1845 a vineyard there was renamed Königin-Victoriaberg.

appellations.name: Johannisberg
appellations.summary: Bereich Johannisberg is the single district covering the whole Rheingau. A wine with only this name is a regional blend; it should not be confused with Schloss Johannisberg or the village of Johannisberg, both far more specific.
appellations.nerd_note: Wines labelled 'Bereich Johannisberg' must from the 2026 vintage show the word 'Region' in front of the name.

appellations.name: Nahe
appellations.summary: The Nahe PDO covers about 4,250 hectares in 91 municipalities along the Nahe and its side valleys, from Monzingen to Bingen. It is Germany's most geologically varied region, and its best Rieslings combine the Mosel's lift with the Rheingau's body. The middle Nahe holds the stars: Dönnhoff's Hermannshöhle and Brücke, the Kupfergrube and Felsenberg at Schlossböckelheim, Emrich-Schönleber's Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen at Monzingen, and Schäfer-Fröhlich's Felseneck at Bockenau.
appellations.terroir: Slate, quartzite, porphyry, melaphyre, sandstone and loess in a sunny, dry valley.
appellations.nerd_note: The Nahe was split from the Rheinhessen and Mosel orbit only in 1971; before that its wines were often sold under neighbours' names.

appellations.name: Nahetal
appellations.created: After 1971 (merger of Bereiche Kreuznach and Schloss Böckelheim)
appellations.summary: The single Bereich covering the whole Nahe, created when the two older Bereiche (Kreuznach and Schloss Böckelheim) were merged. A wine labelled only Nahetal is a regional blend; from the 2026 vintage it must be printed as 'Region Nahetal', and the region's real interest lies in its villages and single sites.

appellations.name: Monzinger Niederberg
appellations.summary: A small single-site PDO at Monzingen on the upper Nahe, registered by the EU in 2018 for Riesling with a maximum yield of 75 hl/ha. It is one of the handful of German vineyards to seek protection at EU level outside the Anbaugebiet system, a sign of growers wanting to anchor quality to a precise place.
appellations.terroir: Slate and weathered volcanic rock on a slope near Monzingen.
appellations.nerd_note: Monzingen is better known for the Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen, Emrich-Schönleber's two Grosse Lagen.

appellations.name: Rheinhessen
appellations.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Dornfelder, Silvaner, Grauburgunder, Spätburgunder
appellations.summary: Germany's largest PDO at about 27,500 hectares in 133 municipalities, Rheinhessen produced over two million hectolitres in 2025 and makes everything from bulk wine to some of the world's most expensive dry Riesling. Its best sites are on the Roter Hang at Nierstein and Nackenheim, the limestone of the Wonnegau around Westhofen and Dalsheim, Bingen's Scharlachberg and the Rheinhessische Schweiz around Siefersheim. Silvaner, Weißburgunder and Spätburgunder are all excellent here.
appellations.terroir: A warm, dry plateau; loess and marl over limestone, red Rotliegend slate at the Roter Hang.
appellations.nerd_note: Keller's G-Max, from undisclosed old vines in the Wonnegau, has fetched thousands of euros per bottle at auction.

appellations.name: Bingen
appellations.summary: The north-western Bereich of Rheinhessen around Bingen, Ingelheim and the Rheinhessische Schweiz. It includes Bingen's quartzite Scharlachberg, Ingelheim's red wine tradition and the porphyry soils of Siefersheim, where Wagner-Stempel works.
appellations.terroir: Quartzite, porphyry, loess and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Ingelheim calls itself the 'Rotweinstadt', a red-wine tradition dating to Charlemagne's palace.

appellations.name: Nierstein
appellations.summary: The eastern Bereich along the Rhine from Mainz to Worms-north, including Nackenheim, Nierstein and Oppenheim. Its jewel is the Roter Hang, a cliff of red Permian slate and sandstone above the river. The infamous Großlage Niersteiner Gutes Domtal also sits here.
appellations.terroir: Red Rotliegend slate and sandstone on the river cliff; loess inland.
appellations.nerd_note: Oppenheim's Deutsches Weinbaumuseum documents the region's long history.

appellations.name: Wonnegau
appellations.summary: The southern Bereich around Worms, Westhofen, Flörsheim-Dalsheim and Monsheim, whose limestone hills have become the epicentre of modern Rheinhessen. Keller and Wittmann made Morstein, Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Hubacker famous.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, marl and loess.
appellations.nerd_note: The Liebfrauenstift vineyards around Worms' Liebfrauenkirche lie in this Bereich.

appellations.name: Pfalz
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Dornfelder, Müller-Thurgau, Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder
appellations.summary: The Pfalz PDO runs along the Haardt from Bockenheim to Schweigen with about 23,800 hectares in 142 municipalities. It is warm, dry and diverse, making the country's fullest dry Rieslings, fine Pinot, and good everyday reds. The Mittelhaardt's Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim, Ungstein and Kallstadt hold the greatest Riesling sites; the Südliche Weinstraße around Birkweiler, Siebeldingen and Schweigen excels with Pinot and Riesling on red sandstone and limestone.
appellations.terroir: Sheltered by the Haardt forest; sandstone, limestone, loess and basalt.
appellations.nerd_note: The region was officially called Rheinpfalz until the 1990s; Bavarian rule (1816 to 1945) left the 1828 land-tax classification that still informs site rankings.

appellations.name: Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstraße
appellations.summary: The northern Bereich of the Pfalz from Bockenheim to Neustadt, containing the classic Riesling villages of Kallstadt, Ungstein, Bad Dürkheim, Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg. This is where the 'three Bs' and Christmann farm their grand crus.
appellations.terroir: Sandstone, limestone, loess and the basalt of Forst.

appellations.name: Südliche Weinstraße
appellations.summary: The southern Bereich from Neustadt to the French border. Long a cooperative stronghold, it has become a source of exceptional Pinot Noir, Weißburgunder and Riesling from estates in Birkweiler, Siebeldingen, Leinsweiler, Ilbesheim and Schweigen, some of whose vineyards lie across the border in Alsace.
appellations.terroir: Red sandstone, Rotliegend, limestone and loess.
appellations.nerd_note: Friedrich Becker's best Pinot Noir comes from vineyards in Wissembourg, France, which German law lets him label as Pfalz.

appellations.name: Baden
appellations.grapes: Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Riesling, Gutedel
appellations.summary: Baden's PDO covers about 15,700 hectares in roughly 400 municipalities, stretched across nine Bereiche from Tauberfranken to Lake Constance. As the only German region in EU wine zone B, it has slightly different rules on alcohol and enrichment, and it is the home of German Pinot: Spätburgunder is the leading variety and the Burgundian family covers well over half the vineyard. The volcanic Kaiserstuhl, the granite Ortenau and the limestone Breisgau and Markgräflerland each have a distinct style.
appellations.terroir: Warm Upper Rhine plain between Black Forest and Vosges; granite, volcanic tuff, loess, limestone and moraine.
appellations.nerd_note: Baden's 'Weißherbst' is a rosé made from a single red variety and stated as such on the label.

appellations.name: Kaiserstuhl
appellations.summary: The Kaiserstuhl is an extinct volcano about 15 km across that rises from the Rhine plain north-west of Freiburg, and its Bereich is the warmest part of Germany.
