Terraces of volcanic tuff and deep loess at Ihringen, Achkarren, Oberrotweil, Burkheim and Oberbergen give powerful Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder and Weißburgunder; Ihringen regularly records Germany's highest temperatures.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic tephrite and tuff overlain in places by loess up to tens of metres deep.
appellations.nerd_note: Loess terraces were bulldozed into huge flat platforms in the 1970s land consolidation, a scar still visible from the air.

appellations.name: Tuniberg
appellations.summary: A small limestone ridge west of Freiburg, next to the Kaiserstuhl, planted mostly with Spätburgunder and Pinot whites and dominated by cooperatives.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone under loess.

appellations.name: Ortenau
appellations.summary: The Ortenau between Baden-Baden and Offenburg grows Riesling (locally 'Klingelberger') and Spätburgunder on steep granite slopes at Durbach, Neuweier and Oberkirch. Neuweier is one of the few places outside Franken allowed to use the Bocksbeutel.
appellations.terroir: Weathered granite and gneiss of the Black Forest.
appellations.nerd_note: In Durbach Riesling is called Klingelberger after a vineyard at Schloss Staufenberg.

appellations.name: Breisgau
appellations.summary: The Breisgau north of Freiburg is limestone and loess country whose star is Malterdingen, where Bernhard Huber (died 2014; now Julian Huber) showed that Muschelkalk can give Pinot Noir of Burgundian finesse. Cistercians from Tennenbach are said to have brought Pinot here.
appellations.terroir: Shell limestone, Keuper and loess.

appellations.name: Markgräflerland
appellations.summary: Between Freiburg and Basel, the Markgräflerland is the home of Gutedel (Chasselas), introduced in 1780 by Margrave Karl Friedrich from Vevey. It also makes fine Pinot and Chardonnay on limestone and loess, with stars such as Ziereisen and the Wassmer brothers.
appellations.terroir: Loess and limestone, warm and sunny below the Black Forest.
appellations.nerd_note: Gutedel is the same grape as Switzerland's Chasselas and covers about a third of the Markgräflerland vineyard.

appellations.name: Bodensee
appellations.summary: Baden's Lake Constance vineyards around Meersburg and Hagnau, at around 400 to 500 metres, benefit from the lake's warmth. Müller-Thurgau and Spätburgunder dominate, including Weißherbst rosé.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine and molasse.
appellations.nerd_note: The Meersburg state winery traces its roots to the Prince-Bishops of Konstanz.

appellations.name: Kraichgau
appellations.summary: A hilly loess and Keuper landscape between Heidelberg and Heilbronn, the 'land of a thousand hills', with mixed plantings of Riesling, Pinot and Müller-Thurgau, much of it handled by cooperatives, and a few ambitious estates in villages such as Sulzfeld and Eichtersheim.
appellations.terroir: Loess, Keuper marl, shell limestone.

appellations.name: Badische Bergstraße
appellations.summary: The Baden continuation of the Bergstraße south of Heidelberg, around Weinheim, Schriesheim and Wiesloch, with Riesling and Pinot on granite and loess at the foot of the Odenwald; it shares the early spring and almond blossom of its Hessian neighbour.
appellations.terroir: Granite and loess.

appellations.name: Tauberfranken
appellations.summary: Baden's northernmost Bereich in the Tauber valley around Tauberbischofsheim and Lauda, culturally Franconian, with Muschelkalk slopes, a continental climate, Bocksbeutel bottles and the old red Tauberschwarz grape, which almost vanished before local growers revived it.
appellations.terroir: Shell limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Tauberschwarz, nearly extinct by the 1950s, was revived here.

appellations.name: Franken
appellations.grapes: Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau, Bacchus, Riesling, Domina, Spätburgunder
appellations.summary: The Franken PDO covers about 6,200 hectares in 141 municipalities along the Main, mostly in Lower Franconia. It is the home of dry Silvaner and the protected Bocksbeutel bottle. The Würzburger Stein, Randersackerer Pfülben, Escherndorfer Lump, Iphöfer Julius-Echter-Berg and Rödelseer Küchenmeister make the region's great whites, while the red sandstone of Bürgstadt and Klingenberg gives some of Germany's finest Spätburgunder from Rudolf Fürst and Benedikt Baltes.
appellations.terroir: Triassic layers of red sandstone, shell limestone and Keuper; continental climate with frost risk.
appellations.nerd_note: Franken growers still use the term 'Frankenwein ist Männerwein'; the region's dry tradition is old enough that many wines never bothered with the word trocken.

appellations.name: Würzburger Stein-Berg
appellations.summary: Registered by the EU in 2020, this single-site PDO covers the Würzburger Stein and adjacent Steinberg slopes above the city. The rules are strict: Silvaner, Riesling or Weißburgunder only, 50 hl/ha maximum and dry wines. It turns the most famous vineyard of Franken into a legally protected origin of its own, a model of how German growers are using EU law to fix quality to place.
appellations.terroir: Shell limestone (Muschelkalk) on a south-facing slope above the Main, with the warmth of the city.
appellations.nerd_note: Würzburg's Steinwein gave the name 'Stein' to Franconian wine in general in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

appellations.name: Bürgstadter Berg
appellations.summary: An EU PDO registered in 2017 for the red sandstone hillside of Bürgstadt on the lower Main, the first German single-site PDO. Bürgstadt is the home of Rudolf Fürst, whose Centgrafenberg and Hundsrück Spätburgunder are among Germany's greatest reds.
appellations.terroir: Buntsandstein (red sandstone) on steep south-facing slopes over the Main.
appellations.nerd_note: The Centgrafenberg is named after the medieval 'Centgraf', a district judge.

appellations.name: Württemberg
appellations.summary: Württemberg's PDO covers about 11,400 hectares in 375 municipalities around the Neckar and Stuttgart, and is Germany's red-wine region par excellence, with red grapes on two thirds of the land. Light Trollinger and Schwarzriesling are local staples; Lemberger and Spätburgunder from ambitious estates now rival the best in Germany. The region also covers the Bavarian shore of Lake Constance around Lindau.
appellations.terroir: Steep Neckar slopes of Muschelkalk and Keuper marl; warm summers.
appellations.nerd_note: Württemberg Schillerwein is a protected Rotling: red and white grapes pressed and fermented together.

appellations.name: Ahr
appellations.summary: The Ahr PDO is a narrow slate gorge of about 530 hectares in seven municipalities, and one of the most northerly places in the world for serious Pinot Noir. Spätburgunder covers about two thirds of the vineyard and Frühburgunder is a speciality. After the catastrophic flood of July 2021 the growers rebuilt cellars and wineries; production in 2025 rose sharply from the depressed post-flood years.
appellations.terroir: Devonian slate and greywacke on steep terraces that store heat in a sheltered valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Meyer-Näkel's sisters Meike and Dörte Näkel clung to a tree for hours during the 2021 flood before being rescued, then rebuilt and released the 2021 vintage.

appellations.name: Mittelrhein
appellations.summary: The Mittelrhein PDO covers about 460 hectares in 51 municipalities in the Rhine gorge from Bingen to near Bonn, mostly on steep slate. Riesling dominates, giving crisp, mineral wines. Bacharach, Steeg, Oberwesel and Boppard are the key villages, and much of the area lies in the Upper Middle Rhine Valley World Heritage Site.
appellations.terroir: Slate and greywacke terraces above the Rhine.
appellations.nerd_note: Bacharach takes its name, according to tradition, from Bacchus' altar (Bacchi ara), a rock in the river.

appellations.name: Hessische Bergstraße
appellations.summary: One of Germany's smallest regions at about 460 hectares in ten municipalities between Darmstadt and Heppenheim. Riesling and Pinot Gris grow on granite and loess along the Odenwald, in a climate so mild that spring blossom arrives weeks before the rest of Germany.
appellations.terroir: Granite and loess on the western edge of the Odenwald.
appellations.nerd_note: The state estate's Heppenheimer Centgericht is a monopole named after a medieval court.

appellations.name: Saale-Unstrut
appellations.summary: The Saale-Unstrut PDO covers about 850 hectares in 51 municipalities in Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Brandenburg, around 51 degrees north. Dry whites from shell-limestone terraces dominate, and Freyburg is home to Rotkäppchen-Mumm, Germany's largest sparkling wine company.
appellations.terroir: Muschelkalk and sandstone terraces in a dry continental climate.
appellations.nerd_note: The Werder area near Potsdam in Brandenburg belongs to Saale-Unstrut for legal purposes despite lying 150 km away.

appellations.name: Sachsen
appellations.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Traminer, Goldriesling
appellations.summary: Sachsen's PDO covers about 520 hectares along the Elbe from Pirna to Diesbar-Seußlitz in 55 municipalities, the easternmost region in Germany. Granite terraces, baroque estates and dry, aromatic whites define it; Goldriesling is a local curiosity.
appellations.terroir: Granite, syenite and gneiss on south-facing Elbe terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: Goldriesling, a 1893 Alsatian crossing, survives almost only in Saxony.

appellations.name: Wachau
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling (Riedenwein only these two); 17 varieties for Gebietswein
appellations.summary:
The Wachau is a 36-kilometre stretch of the Danube between Melk and Krems where the river cuts through granite and gneiss hills, and its terraced vineyards, castles and baroque abbeys make it one of the loveliest wine landscapes in Europe (UNESCO World Heritage, 2000). Only about 1,285 hectares of vines grow here, mostly on narrow terraces held up by dry-stone walls, but they produce some of the world's finest dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

The wines are dry and unchaptalised, and since 1983 the growers' association Vinea Wachau has graded them by ripeness: Steinfeder (light, up to 11.5 percent alcohol, named after a feathery grass on the terraces), Federspiel (11.5 to 12.5 percent, named after a falconry lure) and Smaragd (above 12.5 percent, named after the emerald lizards that bask on the walls). A Smaragd Riesling from the Achleiten or Kellerberg combines ripe stone fruit with a cool, stony core and can age for decades. Since the 2020 vintage the Wachau has been a DAC with three tiers: Gebietswein (17 varieties), Ortswein (nine varieties) and Riedenwein, reserved for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from 157 named Rieden and always hand-picked.

The pioneers include Josef Jamek, who made dry Wachau wines famous in the 1950s and 1960s, and the generation of F.X. Pichler, Franz Hirtzberger, Emmerich Knoll and Franz Prager that followed. The Domäne Wachau cooperative in Dürnstein farms about a third of the area.
appellations.terroir: Primary rock (gneiss, amphibolite, mica schist and granulite) on the terraces, loess and sand at the foot of the slopes. The Danube moderates temperatures, warm Pannonian air drifts up the valley from the east and cold air drains from the Waldviertel at night; the Spitzer Graben side valley is notably cooler. Irrigation is often needed on the thin terrace soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The Smaragd category is named after the emerald lizard that suns itself on the terrace walls; Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd are trademarks of Vinea Wachau, not legal categories, so only members may use them.

appellations.name: Kremstal
appellations.summary: Kremstal surrounds the old wine town of Krems at the eastern exit of the Wachau, with about 2,240 hectares. West of the town, around Stein and on the Pfaffenberg, the soils are the same primary rock as the Wachau and the Rieslings are equally fine; east and north of Krems, around Rohrendorf, Gedersdorf and Senftenberg, deep loess terraces give rich, spicy Grüner Veltliner. South of the Danube the vineyards around Furth and Palt lie below the great baroque abbey of Göttweig. The DAC (2007) allows Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, with Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers.
appellations.terroir: Gneiss and mica schist at Stein and Senftenberg, deep loess at Krems, Rohrendorf and Gedersdorf.
appellations.nerd_note: The Kremser Sandgrube, recorded in 1208, is the oldest documented vineyard name in Austria.

appellations.name: Kamptal
appellations.summary: The Kamptal follows the little Kamp river from the Waldviertel down to the Danube plain, with about 3,570 hectares around Langenlois, Austria's largest wine town, and the villages of Zöbing, Gobelsburg, Kammern, Strass and Schönberg. Its fame rests on the Heiligenstein, a ridge of 270-million-year-old desert sandstone that gives some of Austria's greatest Rieslings, and on loess slopes such as the Lamm, Spiegel and Renner that give deep, spicy Grüner Veltliner. Cool air from the Waldviertel cools the vineyards on summer nights, keeping the wines fresh. The DAC (2008) covers Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, with Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers; the ÖTW classification of Erste Lagen began here and in Kremstal.
appellations.terroir: Permian sandstone and conglomerate with volcanic fragments on the Heiligenstein; gneiss and amphibolite on the Gaisberg; loess on the Lamm, Spiegel and Käferberg.
appellations.nerd_note: Schloss Gobelsburg, run by Michael Moosbrugger, belonged to the Cistercians of Zwettl Abbey, and its 'Tradition' wines recreate nineteenth-century cellar methods.

appellations.name: Traisental
appellations.summary: The Traisental, south of the Danube around Traismauer, Herzogenburg and Nußdorf ob der Traisen, is the smallest of Lower Austria's Danube regions. Its vines grow on chalky conglomerate and gravel terraces that give Grüner Veltliner and Riesling with unusual tension and a firm, almost salty finish. The DAC dates from 2006.
appellations.terroir: Calcareous conglomerate, gravel and loess on narrow terraces; cool air from the Alpine foothills to the south.
appellations.nerd_note: Unlike the crystalline Wachau and Kamptal, the Traisental's best sites are on limestone-rich conglomerate, a reason its Grüner often tastes leaner and more mineral.

appellations.name: Wagram
appellations.created: DAC from 2021 vintage (PDO 1996 as Donauland; renamed 2007)
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Roter Veltliner, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir and others by tier
appellations.summary: The Wagram is a long loess escarpment rising up to 40 metres above the Danube plain north of the river, between Krems and Vienna, together with the Klosterneuburg area south of the river. Its roughly 2,400 hectares are built on loess many metres deep, which gives Grüner Veltliner of creamy weight and spice. The region is also the home of Roter Veltliner, an old and difficult variety (unrelated to Grüner) that here gives rich, nutty whites. Bernhard Ott's biodynamic Grüner from Feuersbrunn made the Wagram's name. The area was called Donauland until 2007 and became a DAC from the 2021 vintage, with Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers.
appellations.terroir: Deep loess over gravel and marine sediments on a south-facing escarpment above the Danube.
appellations.nerd_note: The name Wagram comes from 'Wogenrain', the bank of the waves, referring to the ancient shoreline of the Danube.

appellations.name: Weinviertel
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner (DAC); many others under Niederösterreich
appellations.summary:
The Weinviertel, the 'wine quarter' between the Danube, the Manhartsberg and the Czech and Slovak borders, is Austria's largest wine area with about 13,700 hectares, a third of the national vineyard, and in 2025 it produced 989,300 hectolitres. Rolling loess hills, sunflower fields and villages with cellar lanes (Kellergassen) define it. The Weinviertel became Austria's first DAC with the 2002 vintage and limited it to Grüner Veltliner in a fresh, fruity, peppery style (the famous 'Pfefferl'), with Reserve (from 2009) and Große Reserve (since 2020) for richer wines.

The region is diverse: Poysdorf in the north-east is Austria's Sekt base, Falkenstein has limestone cliffs and old castles, Röschitz near the Manhartsberg has granite, and the far north-east near the March river is warm enough for reds.
appellations.terroir: Loess dominates, with limestone at Falkenstein and the Waschberg, granite near the Manhartsberg; a dry, Pannonian-continental climate.
appellations.nerd_note: The Weinviertel was Austria's first DAC: its growers chose Grüner Veltliner as the region's sole flagship and launched the appellation with the 2002 vintage.

appellations.name: Carnuntum
appellations.grapes: Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch; Grüner Veltliner, Chardonnay, Weißburgunder
appellations.summary: Carnuntum lies east of Vienna between the Danube and the Leitha hills, named after the Roman legionary town and provincial capital whose ruins dominate Petronell. Its 800-odd hectares of loess, gravel and limestone at Göttlesbrunn, Höflein, Prellenkirchen and on the Spitzerberg are warm and windy, ideal for red wine. Zweigelt is the signature (sold by a growers' group as 'Rubin Carnuntum'), and Blaufränkisch from the Spitzerberg's limestone is the region's most serious wine. The DAC (2019 vintage) covers Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch, Grüner Veltliner, Chardonnay and Weißburgunder, with cuvées at least two-thirds from these.
appellations.terroir: Loess and gravel terraces, limestone on the Spitzerberg and Hundsheimer Berg; Pannonian warmth with constant wind.
appellations.nerd_note: Dorli Muhr (Muhr-van der Niepoort) helped revive the Spitzerberg's half-abandoned limestone terraces for Blaufränkisch.

appellations.name: Thermenregion
appellations.grapes: Zierfandler, Rotgipfler, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Sankt Laurent, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: The Thermenregion runs south from Vienna along the edge of the Vienna Woods to Bad Vöslau, a landscape of spa towns (Baden bei Wien's hot springs give the name) and old monastery estates. Around Gumpoldskirchen, Pfaffstätten and Traiskirchen it grows two rare white grapes found almost nowhere else: Zierfandler (Spätrot) and Rotgipfler, which give rich, spicy, long-lived whites, dry or sweet. Further south, around Tattendorf, Sooß and Bad Vöslau, the hot gravel plain gives fine Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir. The Thermenregion became Austria's eighteenth and last DAC with the 2023 vintage, with Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and calcareous gravel at the foot of the Vienna Woods, warm Pannonian climate, plus the hot, stony Steinfeld plain to the south.
appellations.nerd_note: Freigut Thallern has belonged to the Cistercian abbey of Heiligenkreuz since 1141, one of the oldest continuously run wine estates in Austria.

appellations.name: Niederösterreich
appellations.summary: The federal-state PDO for Lower Austria, used for quality wines from anywhere in its eight DAC areas that do not meet (or do not seek) DAC rules: a Kamptal Zweigelt or a Wachau Chardonnay, for example, is labelled Niederösterreich. With 26,732 hectares, it is by far Austria's largest origin.
appellations.nerd_note: Austrian Sekt g.U. (with Klassik, Reserve and Große Reserve tiers since 2015) is often labelled with the Niederösterreich origin.

appellations.name: Neusiedlersee
appellations.created: DAC from 2011 vintage (sweet wines added 2020; PDO 1996)
appellations.grapes: Zweigelt (dry DAC); white varieties for sweet DAC
appellations.summary: Neusiedlersee covers the north and east shores of Lake Neusiedl, from Gols and Mönchhof to Podersdorf, Illmitz and Apetlon in the Seewinkel, about 6,000 hectares. The shallow steppe lake (315 square kilometres but under 2 metres deep), the salty Seewinkel ponds and the Pannonian heat create two great wine styles. In summer and early autumn, warm days produce juicy Zweigelt and powerful red blends around Gols, where the Pannobile growers (Heinrich, Nittnaus, Achs, Beck, Pittnauer, Preisinger, Renner) set the tone. Then autumn mists off the lake bring noble rot, and Illmitz and Apetlon make Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese of world class; the late Alois Kracher made them famous in the 1990s with his numbered 'Zwischen den Seen' and 'Nouvelle Vague' TBAs. The DAC (2011) is for Zweigelt, classic or Reserve; since 2020 sweet wines from white grapes also qualify.
appellations.terroir: Sand, gravel, loam and black earth (Tschernosem); salty soils in the Seewinkel; the lake moderates frost and feeds autumn mist.
appellations.nerd_note: Gerhard Nekowitsch in Illmitz pioneered Schilfwein, sweet wine from grapes dried on mats woven from the lake's reeds.

appellations.name: Leithaberg
appellations.created: DAC red from 2008, white from 2009 (EU reg. 2009)
appellations.grapes: Blaufränkisch (red); Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Neuburger, Grüner Veltliner and blends (white)
appellations.summary: Leithaberg covers the western shore of Lake Neusiedl and the slopes of the Leitha hills (Leithagebirge), with Jois, Winden, Breitenbrunn, Purbach, Donnerskirchen, Schützen, Eisenstadt, Großhöflein and St. Georgen. Its soils of Leitha limestone and mica schist give wines with a cool, chalky structure: Blaufränkisch that is fine-boned rather than heavy, and whites from Pinot Blanc, Chardonnay, Neuburger and Grüner Veltliner that are dry, mineral and lightly oaked at most. The DAC was a growers' initiative, launched for reds in 2008 and whites in 2009, and it explicitly asks for 'minerality' rather than power.
appellations.terroir: Leitha limestone (fossil-rich coral and shell limestone) and mica schist and gneiss on the slopes of the Leithagebirge; the lake's warmth below.
appellations.nerd_note: A single ancient vine found in 2000 near St. Georgen, in the Leithaberg area, turned out to be a parent of Grüner Veltliner; it was propagated and is now grown again as 'St. Georgen'.

appellations.name: Ruster Ausbruch
appellations.grapes: One or more white varieties: Furmint, Welschriesling, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Gelber Muskateller and others
appellations.summary: Ruster Ausbruch is one of the world's great historic sweet wines, made only in the town of Rust on the western shore of Lake Neusiedl. Botrytised berries are picked by hand, berry by berry, and must reach at least 30 degrees KMW, the same as a Trockenbeerenauslese, but the traditional method of soaking or pressing the shrivelled berries in fresh must gives a wine with more acid lift and less cloying sweetness. In the seventeenth century Ausbruch was famous across Europe, and Rust is said to have paid part of the price of its freedom as a royal town in 1681 in barrels of it. A DAC since 2020, it is a tiny production carried by a handful of families who still keep storks nesting on their chimneys.
appellations.terroir: Rust's slopes of Leitha limestone and schist face the lake, whose mists bring noble rot in autumn.
appellations.nerd_note: Michael Wenzel and Heidi Schröck helped revive Furmint in Rust, the grape of Tokaji, which had almost disappeared from Austria.

appellations.name: Rosalia
appellations.grapes: Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt (red); rosé from one or more red varieties
appellations.summary: Rosalia, Austria's smallest DAC at about 230 hectares, lies on the eastern slopes of the Rosalia hills in the Mattersburg district of northern Burgenland, between the Leithaberg and Mittelburgenland. Its cool, forested hills give Blaufränkisch and Zweigelt with freshness and spice. Rosalia is the only DAC with a protected rosé category, which recognises the area's long tradition of pink wines.
appellations.terroir: Gravel, sand, loam and crystalline rock on the slopes of the Rosaliengebirge, cooler than the lake shore.
appellations.nerd_note: The region takes its name from a chapel to St. Rosalia on the hilltop.

appellations.name: Mittelburgenland
appellations.summary: Mittelburgenland, which calls itself 'Blaufränkischland', covers about 2,000 hectares around Deutschkreutz, Horitschon, Neckenmarkt and Lutzmannsburg on the Hungarian border. Sheltered from the north by the Ödenburg (Sopron) hills and open to Pannonian warmth, its deep, heavy clay soils give Blaufränkisch of dark fruit, firm tannin and spice. It was Austria's second DAC (2005 vintage) and is limited to Blaufränkisch, with Ortswein, Riedenwein and Reserve categories. Roland Velich's Moric, from very old vines at Lutzmannsburg and Neckenmarkt, showed that Mittelburgenland Blaufränkisch could be ethereal rather than merely powerful.
appellations.terroir: Deep, heavy clay and loam with gravel and sand; warm and sheltered.
appellations.nerd_note: Franz Weninger also farms vines across the border in Hungary's Sopron, the same Blaufränkisch landscape split by the 1921 frontier.

appellations.name: Eisenberg
appellations.grapes: Blaufränkisch; Welschriesling only with a Ried name
appellations.summary: Eisenberg is the southern Burgenland area around the Eisenberg hill and the villages of Deutsch-Schützen, Höll and Moschendorf, near the Hungarian border, with about 525 hectares. The 'iron mountain' has greenschist and iron-rich loam soils that give Blaufränkisch of rare finesse, with dark cherry, pepper and a mineral, slightly bloody note. Since 2023 the Reserve category has gone and the DAC focuses on Blaufränkisch, with Welschriesling allowed for Riedenwein. South Burgenland is also the home of Uhudler, a rustic wine from American hybrid grapes that has its own protected status.
appellations.terroir: Greenschist (phyllite), iron-rich loam and clay on the Eisenberg and the Deutsch-Schützen hills; warmer and wetter than northern Burgenland.
appellations.nerd_note: Uhudler, made from American hybrid grapes, spent decades in legal limbo before Burgenland re-authorised it in the 2010s; it is now a regional cult.

appellations.name: Burgenland
appellations.summary: The federal-state PDO for Burgenland, used for quality wine from any of its areas that falls outside the DAC rules, for example Cabernet blends, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and most sweet wines from beyond Rust and the Seewinkel DAC rules.
appellations.nerd_note: Many of Burgenland's most famous red blends, such as Gernot Heinrich's Pannobile, appear under the Burgenland origin rather than a DAC.

appellations.name: Südsteiermark
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon, Gelber Muskateller, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Welschriesling, Riesling, Traminer
appellations.summary: Südsteiermark is a landscape of steep, green hills along the Slovenian border south of Graz, with about 2,800 hectares around Gamlitz, Ehrenhausen, Leutschach, Spielfeld and the Sausal hills at Kitzeck. Vines grow on gradients of up to about 70 percent, among the steepest in Austria, and the Südsteirische Weinstraße winds along ridges where the vineyards of Austria and Slovenia touch. The wines are dry and aromatic: Sauvignon Blanc with gooseberry, elderflower and cassis-leaf intensity, the piercing grapey Gelber Muskateller, and Morillon (the local name for Chardonnay) that can be as complex as Burgundy from the best Rieden. The DAC (2018 vintage) has Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein tiers and requires hand harvesting.
appellations.terroir: Opok (marl and calcareous sandstone), sand, gravel and coral limestone in the south; slate and schist in the Sausal, where Kitzeck's vineyards reach over 600 metres. Rainfall is higher than elsewhere in Austria, offset by steep drainage and warm days.
appellations.nerd_note: Tement's Zieregg vineyard straddles the border; the family's Slovenian holdings are bottled as Ciringa.

appellations.name: Vulkanland Steiermark
appellations.grapes: Welschriesling, Weißburgunder, Morillon, Grauburgunder, Riesling, Gelber Muskateller, Sauvignon Blanc, Traminer
appellations.summary: The Vulkanland in south-eastern Styria is a hilly landscape of extinct volcanoes, with castles on basalt plugs at Riegersburg and Kapfenstein, about 1,650 hectares of vines and a scattered pattern of small vineyards among orchards and fields. Volcanic basalt and tuff, mixed with sand and loam, give whites of spice and warmth; the Traminer of Klöch is the area's most famous speciality, intensely perfumed with rose petals. Neumeister in Straden and Winkler-Hermaden at Kapfenstein are the leading names. The DAC (2018 vintage) has three tiers; the region was called Süd-Oststeiermark until the change to Vulkanland.
appellations.terroir: Basalt, volcanic tuff and ash over sand and clay; warmer and drier than Südsteiermark, with Pannonian influence.
appellations.nerd_note: Klöch's Weinbaumuseum and Traminer route celebrate a grape planted on the volcano's slopes for centuries.

appellations.name: Weststeiermark
appellations.grapes: Blauer Wildbacher (Schilcher); white varieties at Ort and Ried level
appellations.summary: West Styria, south-west of Graz around Stainz, Deutschlandsberg, Ligist and Wies, is the land of Schilcher, a pale onion-skin to salmon rosé from the Blauer Wildbacher grape. Schilcher has piercing acidity and notes of redcurrant and rhubarb, a love-it-or-hate-it wine drunk locally with cold cuts in the Buschenschanken along the Schilcherweinstraße; modern producers also make it as sparkling wine and as a more structured Ried wine. About 650 hectares grow on gneiss and schist at up to 600 metres. The DAC (2018 vintage) requires hand harvest and covers Schilcher and selected white varieties.
appellations.terroir: Gneiss and schist, often steep, at the edge of the Koralpe; cooler and wetter than the rest of Styria.
appellations.nerd_note: Blauer Wildbacher may only be labelled Schilcher if it comes from Styria; the word is protected.

appellations.name: Steiermark
appellations.summary: The federal-state PDO for Styria, covering quality wines that fall outside the three Styrian DACs, including reds such as Zweigelt and Blauburger and many sparkling wines.
appellations.nerd_note: Styria is known for the Klapotetz, a wooden wind-rattle that scares birds from the ripening grapes.

appellations.name: Wien
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay, Gemischter Satz varieties, Zweigelt, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Vienna's own PDO covers about 588 hectares within the city limits, on the Nussberg, Kahlenberg, Bisamberg and Maurer Berg. The wines, mostly white, are drunk largely in the city's Heurigen. Varietal wines and reds are labelled Wien, while field blends that meet the rules become Wiener Gemischter Satz DAC.
appellations.terroir: Limestone, loess, gravel and flysch on the hills around the city; Pannonian warmth.
appellations.nerd_note: Vienna claims to be the only capital in the world with significant vineyards inside its borders.

appellations.name: Wiener Gemischter Satz
appellations.grapes: At least three white varieties from one vineyard, planted together
appellations.summary: Gemischter Satz means a 'mixed planting': vineyards where different varieties grow side by side and are picked and fermented together, as was normal before single-variety planting took over. Vienna kept the tradition alive, and Fritz Wieninger and a group of growers turned it into a quality wine and Austria's tenth DAC in 2013. At least three white varieties must be planted together in a Viennese vineyard; the largest may not exceed 50 percent and the third largest must reach at least 10 percent. The wines range from light Heuriger whites to complex single-vineyard blends from the Nussberg or Bisamberg.
appellations.terroir: Vineyards on the Nussberg (limestone), Bisamberg (loess, gravel) and other Viennese hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Some Nussberg field blends include up to twenty varieties, among them old Viennese grapes such as Grüner Sylvaner, Rotgipfler and Zierfandler.

appellations.name: Kärnten
appellations.summary: Carinthia's PDO, registered in 2004, covers small vineyards on sunny, often lakeside slopes around the Wörthersee, Millstätter See, the Lavant valley and near St. Paul's abbey. Plantings have grown fast since 2000, mostly Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir and fungus-resistant varieties.
appellations.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

appellations.name: Oberösterreich
appellations.summary: Upper Austria's PDO (2004) covers a handful of vineyards along the Danube and in the Alpine foreland, with fresh whites and some sparkling wine.
appellations.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

appellations.name: Salzburg
appellations.summary: The PDO for the province of Salzburg, registered in 2004, has only a few hectares, notably near Salzburg city; it exists mainly so that growers can sell quality wine with a local origin.
appellations.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

appellations.name: Tirol
appellations.summary: Tyrol's PDO (1999) covers small, sheltered vineyards in the Inn valley and its side valleys, including some of the highest in Austria.
appellations.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

appellations.name: Vorarlberg
appellations.summary: The westernmost PDO (1999), with a few hectares near Lake Constance and in the Rhine valley, close to Swiss and German neighbours.
appellations.terroir: Alpine slopes with cool nights; frost risk.

appellations.name: Valais
appellations.created: 1990 (cantonal quality hierarchy); AOC rules updated since
appellations.grapes: Chasselas (Fendant), Pinot Noir, Gamay, Petite Arvine, Syrah, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne, Heida and many others
appellations.summary: The cantonal AOC of the Valais covers about 4,600 hectares along the upper Rhône and is the most varied appellation in Switzerland, with dozens of permitted varieties. It contains famous communal names (Fully, Chamoson, Vétroz, Conthey, Sion, Saint-Léonard, Sierre, Salgesch, Leuk, Visperterminen) and Grand Cru rules defined commune by commune. Fendant (Chasselas) and Dôle (a blend in which Pinot Noir dominates, with Gamay) are the classics, but Petite Arvine, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne and Heida have made the canton internationally interesting. Chamoson is the largest wine commune of the Valais and a Johannisberg (Sylvaner) stronghold; Fully, on a granite fan, is the capital of Petite Arvine and Gamay; Salgesch, at the language border, is known for Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Schist, gneiss, limestone and alluvial fans on steep slopes in a dry, sunny valley.
appellations.nerd_note: The Valais has a bee-shaped sweetness scale for Amigne de Vétroz: one bee is dry, three bees sweet.

appellations.name: Lavaux
appellations.summary: AOC Lavaux covers the terraced vineyards between Lausanne and Vevey (and up to Montreux), the most spectacular wine landscape in Switzerland and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007. About 830 hectares of walls and terraces drop steeply to Lake Geneva in the communes of Lutry, Villette, Epesses, Cully, Saint-Saphorin, Chexbres and Chardonne, around the two Grand Cru enclaves of Dézaley and Calamin. Chasselas is supreme, giving wines of floral delicacy at Lutry and of depth and minerality at Saint-Saphorin and Epesses.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine, marl, limestone and conglomerate on terraces with stone walls; the lake reflects light and warmth (the 'three suns').
appellations.nerd_note: A thirty-kilometre hiking route through the Lavaux terraces links the villages from Lutry to Chillon.

appellations.name: Dézaley
appellations.summary: Dézaley is a Grand Cru AOC of about 54 hectares on the steepest terraces of Lavaux, between Epesses and Rivaz, founded by Cistercian monks of Hautcrêt and Montheron in the twelfth century. Its Chasselas is the most powerful and long-lived in Switzerland, smoky and honeyed with age, and the city of Lausanne's Clos des Abbayes and Clos des Moines lie here. Dézaley Rouge is a rare red.
appellations.terroir: Conglomerate (poudingue) and marl on terraces facing due south above the lake.
appellations.nerd_note: A well-kept Dézaley can taste fresh after thirty years; the Bovard family has kept a vertical library going back decades.

appellations.name: Calamin
appellations.summary: Calamin is the smallest Swiss AOC, about 16 hectares of terraces at Epesses in Lavaux, inside the commune next to Dézaley. Its deeper, clay-limestone soils, which slip slowly downhill, give a Chasselas that is fuller and more earthy than Dézaley.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone moraine with landslide movement on steep terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: The name may come from 'calamine', a zinc ore, or a local word for the area's clay soils.

appellations.name: Chablais
appellations.summary: AOC Chablais covers the Vaud vineyards of the upper Rhône valley between Lake Geneva and Saint-Maurice, with the communes of Villeneuve, Yvorne, Aigle, Ollon and Bex. Yvorne's vineyards grow on a massive landslide deposit of 1584, and Aigle's terraces surround a medieval castle that houses a wine museum. Chablais Chasselas is fuller and warmer than Lavaux's, with notes of flint and smoke.
appellations.terroir: Scree, landslide debris, limestone and gypsum on the Rhône valley floor and slopes; warmed by the föhn.
appellations.nerd_note: Henri Badoux's Aigle 'Les Murailles' label with its lizard is one of the best-known Swiss wine brands.

appellations.name: La Côte
appellations.summary: La Côte is Vaud's largest appellation, on gentle slopes between Lausanne and Nyon, with the communes of Morges, Aubonne, Féchy, Mont-sur-Rolle, Rolle, Begnins, Luins and Vinzel. Its Chasselas is light, fresh and easy, while Féchy and Mont-sur-Rolle give more structured examples, and Pinot Noir, Gamay and Gamaret are important reds.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine and molasse on broad, gentle slopes facing the lake and the Alps.
appellations.nerd_note: Raymond Paccot's biodynamic Domaine de la Colombe in Féchy is one of Switzerland's most respected estates.

appellations.name: Côtes de l'Orbe
appellations.summary: A small Vaud appellation around Orbe and Arnex in the north of the canton, at the foot of the Jura, known for Chasselas, Pinot Noir and Gamay.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and moraine.

appellations.name: Bonvillars
appellations.summary: A Vaud appellation on the north-west shore of Lake Neuchâtel around Grandson and Concise, where Jurassic limestone gives fresh Chasselas and Pinot Noir.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone at the foot of the Jura.

appellations.name: Vully
appellations.summary: Vully is the vineyard on the slopes of Mont Vully between Lake Murten and Lake Neuchâtel, shared by Vaud and Fribourg, and part of the Three Lakes region. Chasselas, Pinot Noir and the aromatic Traminer are the main wines.
appellations.terroir: Molasse sandstone and moraine.
appellations.nerd_note: Vully is one of the few Swiss AOCs that crosses a cantonal border.

appellations.name: Genève
appellations.grapes: Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamaret, Chardonnay, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: AOC Genève covers about 1,340 hectares around the city, in the Mandement (Satigny, Dardagny, Russin), between the Arve and the Rhône and between the Arve and the lake. Geneva pioneered cantonal AOC rules in Switzerland and has 22 Premier Cru areas. Gamay is the leading grape, with Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamaret and Garanoir, and the canton has a reputation for modern, well-made wines.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine and alluvium on gentle slopes; sunny and relatively warm.
appellations.nerd_note: Satigny is one of the largest wine-growing communes in Switzerland.

appellations.name: Neuchâtel
appellations.grapes: Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
appellations.summary: AOC Neuchâtel covers about 600 hectares on Jurassic limestone along the north-west shore of Lake Neuchâtel, from Le Landeron to Vaumarcus, with Auvernier, Cortaillod and Boudry at its heart. Chasselas and Pinot Noir dominate. Neuchâtel's Oeil de Perdrix, a pale salmon rosé of Pinot Noir, is a local invention, and unfiltered Chasselas released on the third Wednesday of January is a cult.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl, like the Côte d'Or, under the Jura escarpment.
appellations.nerd_note: Oeil de Perdrix is a protected name in Neuchâtel for Pinot Noir rosé.

appellations.name: Bielersee
appellations.summary: The canton of Bern's lake appellation covers terraced vineyards along the north shore of Lake Biel at Ligerz, Twann, Schafis and La Neuveville and the island of St. Petersinsel. Chasselas and Pinot Noir grow on limestone below the Jura; the wine villages are among the prettiest in Switzerland. Bern also has a tiny vineyard on Lake Thun (AOC Thunersee).
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone on steep terraces above the lake.

appellations.name: Ticino
appellations.summary: AOC Ticino covers about 1,030 hectares in the Italian-speaking canton, split by Monte Ceneri into the Sopraceneri (granite, around Bellinzona, Locarno and the Gudo and Giubiasco slopes) and the Sottoceneri (limestone and clay, around Lugano and Mendrisio). Merlot, planted since 1906, is the defining grape, from fresh, cherry-scented reds to Bordeaux-like reserve wines, plus white Merlot. The VITI label marks wines approved by a tasting panel.
appellations.terroir: Granite and gneiss north of Monte Ceneri, limestone and moraine south; humid, sunny, sub-Mediterranean.
appellations.nerd_note: Bondola, a local red grape that survived phylloxera, is still made by a few growers as a curiosity.

appellations.name: Graubünden
appellations.summary: AOC Graubünden covers vineyards mostly in the Bündner Herrschaft (Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins, Malans) on the upper Rhine, plus the Misox valley (south of the Alps, Merlot). The warm föhn wind ripens Pinot Noir of great elegance, and Malans keeps the ancient white Completer alive.

appellations.name: Zürich
appellations.summary: AOC Zürich covers about 640 hectares on the shores of Lake Zurich and in the Zürcher Weinland near Schaffhausen. Pinot Noir (Blauburgunder), Müller-Thurgau and the old local white Räuschling dominate.

appellations.name: Schaffhausen
appellations.summary: AOC Schaffhausen grows mostly Pinot Noir on limestone and molasse near the Rhine Falls; Hallau is the largest wine commune of German-speaking Switzerland.

appellations.name: Aargau
appellations.summary: AOC Aargau has just under 400 hectares of vines on the Jura foothills and along the Aare, Limmat and Reuss, with Pinot Noir and Müller-Thurgau.

appellations.name: Thurgau
appellations.summary: AOC Thurgau, home canton of Hermann Müller, grows Müller-Thurgau and Pinot Noir on about 250 hectares along the Thur and Lake Constance.

appellations.name: St. Gallen
appellations.summary: AOC St. Gallen, mostly in the Rhine valley near the Austrian border, grows Pinot Noir in the warm föhn corridor.

appellations.name: Moselle Luxembourgeoise
appellations.grapes: Rivaner, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Elbling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Saint Laurent
appellations.summary: Luxembourg's single wine PDO covers the 12 Moselle communes from Schengen to Rosport. Since 2014 it has worked as an origin pyramid: Côtes de (village wines), Coteaux de (premium terroir zones) and Lieu-dit (single vineyards such as Wormeldinger Koeppchen). Dry whites are the norm, and Crémant de Luxembourg, defined in 1991, is the commercial engine. Notable sites include the Koeppchen (Wormeldange), Primerberg (Remerschen), Göllebour (Remich) and the Fels at Grevenmacher.
appellations.terroir: Marl and gypsum in the south, steep shell limestone in the north, all moderated by the Moselle.
appellations.nerd_note: The EU register allows a theoretical maximum yield of 140 hl/ha for the AOP base level, but Lieu-dit wines are held to much lower yields.

appellations.name: English Wine
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Pinot Noir Précoce, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris for sparkling; many vinifera varieties for still wine
appellations.summary: The English Wine PDO covers wine made entirely from grapes grown in England in vineyards no higher than 220 metres, with a maximum yield of 80 hl/ha. Quality sparkling wine may come only from the six Champagne and Burgundy grapes, and still wine from a long list of vinifera varieties but not hybrids (which must use the English Regional Wine PGI). Most of England's best wine carries this label, from Nyetimber and Ridgeview to Chapel Down's Bacchus.
appellations.terroir: Chalk downs, Wealden clay and greensand, Essex clay, Devon and Cornish slate; cool maritime climate.
appellations.nerd_note: About 91 percent of UK sparkling wine in 2024 was made by the traditional method.

appellations.name: Sussex
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and other classic varieties
appellations.summary: Sussex became the UK's first regional PDO in July 2022 after a campaign by producers including Ridgeview, Wiston, Rathfinny and Bolney. It covers East and West Sussex, with about 1,130 hectares of vines, and sets stricter rules than the English Wine PDO, including at least 15 months on the lees for sparkling wine. The South Downs chalk ridge, Wealden greensand and clay give the county a range of sites, from Rathfinny's chalk bowl near the sea to Nyetimber's greensand at West Chiltington.
appellations.terroir: Chalk of the South Downs, greensand and Wealden clay; maritime climate close to the Channel.
appellations.nerd_note: Breaky Bottom, in a fold of the Downs near Lewes, has made sparkling Seyval Blanc since the 1970s, one of the oldest wineries in Sussex.

appellations.name: Darnibole
appellations.summary: Darnibole is a single valley-side vineyard of Camel Valley, near Bodmin in Cornwall, registered as a PDO in 2017 for still Bacchus. The rules cap yields at 56 hl/ha and require Bacchus grown on the site's slate soils. It was Britain's first single-vineyard PDO and a statement that English still wine could express place.
appellations.terroir: Slate soils on a sheltered, south-facing slope above the River Camel.
appellations.nerd_note: The name is the old Cornish field name for the site.

appellations.name: Welsh Wine
appellations.grapes: Vinifera varieties; classic varieties for sparkling
appellations.summary: The Welsh Wine PDO mirrors the English rules for grapes grown entirely in Wales. With about 91 hectares in 2025, Wales is small but growing, with vineyards mainly in Monmouthshire and the Vale of Glamorgan.
appellations.terroir: Varied soils on sheltered slopes in south-east Wales; wetter and cooler than south-east England.
appellations.nerd_note: Ancre Hill's sparkling wine won a top award at an international sparkling-wine competition in Italy in 2012, a breakthrough for Welsh wine.

appellations.name: Côtes de Sambre et Meuse
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau, Regent, Johanniter and others
appellations.summary: Wallonia's still-wine PDO covers the valleys of the Sambre and Meuse and much of the surrounding provinces (199 municipalities in the EU register). It has the broadest grape list of any Belgian appellation, including Chasselas, Merlot, Regent, Johanniter and old Seibel hybrids, which reflects the experimental nature of Walloon viticulture.
appellations.terroir: Slate, limestone and alluvium on Meuse and Sambre slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: The cooperative Vin de Liège, founded in 2010, replanted the hills of the Meuse where Liège's medieval vineyards once stood.

appellations.name: Crémant de Wallonie
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc (white); Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier
appellations.summary: Traditional-method sparkling wine from anywhere in Wallonia, with at least nine months on lees. Chalk soils in Hainaut give Crémant of real finesse, and Domaine du Chant d'Eole and Ruffus have won international medals.
appellations.terroir: Chalk and marl in Hainaut; slate and limestone in the Meuse valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Chant d'Eole stands among wind turbines, which gave the estate its name ('song of the wind').

appellations.name: Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie
match: Vin mousseux de qualité de Wallonie
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris and others
appellations.summary: A broader Walloon sparkling-wine PDO than Crémant, allowing more grape varieties and less strict methods, used for quality sparkling wines that fall outside the Crémant rules.

appellations.name: Hagelandse wijn
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau, Kerner, Pinot Noir, Dornfelder and others
appellations.summary: Hageland, east of Leuven in Flemish Brabant, was Belgium's first modern wine appellation in 1997. Its rolling hills of iron-rich sandstone (ijzerzandsteen) around Aarschot, Diest, Tienen and Hoegaarden, a region once dotted with medieval vineyards, give fresh whites and light reds. Yields are capped at 67 hl/ha.
appellations.terroir: Ferruginous sandstone hills, sand and loam.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hageland's ironstone was also the building stone of its Gothic churches.

appellations.name: Haspengouwse wijn
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir, Riesling and others
appellations.summary: Haspengouw, the fruit-orchard country of Belgian Limburg around Sint-Truiden, Borgloon and Tongeren, has deep loess soils over chalk and is home to Belgium's best-known winery, Wijnkasteel Genoels-Elderen at Riemst, whose Chardonnay is aged in oak.
appellations.terroir: Loess over chalk and marl; gentle slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Clos d'Opleeuw near Borgloon makes a Chardonnay sometimes compared to good Burgundy.

appellations.name: Heuvellandse wijn
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Johanniter, Regent and others
appellations.summary: A small appellation in the West Flemish hills near Kemmel and Dranouter, close to the French border and the First World War battlefields of Ypres. Wijngoed Monteberg and Entre-Deux-Monts are the best-known estates.
appellations.terroir: Clay and sand hills of the Flemish heights.
appellations.nerd_note: Heuvelland's vineyards grow on ground fought over in the First World War.

appellations.name: Vlaamse mousserende kwaliteitswijn
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois, Riesling
appellations.summary: The PDO for quality sparkling wine from the whole of Flanders (300 municipalities in the EU register), registered nationally in 2005. It allows the Champagne and Pinot family grapes plus Auxerrois and Riesling, and is used by most Flemish estates that make traditional-method sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Maasvallei Limburg
appellations.grapes: Auxerrois, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Siegerrebe, Pinot Noir, Dornfelder, Acolon
appellations.summary: Maasvallei Limburg is the first cross-border PDO in the EU: 11 municipalities on both banks of the Maas, in Belgian Limburg (Maaseik, Kinrooi, Dilsen-Stokkem, Maasmechelen, Lanaken) and Dutch Limburg (Maasgouw, Echt-Susteren, Roermond, Leudal, Sittard-Geleen, Stein). Gravel and sand terraces deposited by the river give crisp whites; Wijndomein Aldeneyck at Maaseik and Wijngoed Thorn are key producers.
appellations.terroir: Maas river gravel, sand and loam terraces; mild climate in the river valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Thorn, the Dutch 'white village', gave its name to Wijngoed Thorn on the Dutch bank.

appellations.name: Mergelland
appellations.grapes: Auxerrois, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Pinot Noir Précoce, Dornfelder
appellations.summary: Mergelland, registered in 2018, covers nine municipalities of South Limburg around Maastricht, Valkenburg and Gulpen, on the chalky marl (mergel) that is quarried for building stone here. It allows only classic vinifera varieties, capped at 85 hl/ha, and includes the Apostelhoeve, the oldest modern Dutch vineyard.
appellations.terroir: Cretaceous marl and loess on slopes of the Maas, Geul and Jeker valleys.
appellations.nerd_note: The marl caves (grotten) around Maastricht, such as those under Château Neercanne, have long served as natural wine cellars.

appellations.name: Vijlen
appellations.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Souvignier Gris, Cabernet Blanc, Muscaris, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Cortis, Monarch, Baron, Pinotin
appellations.summary: Vijlen is a single-estate PDO (2018) near Vaals, at about 200 metres on the slopes of the highest hills in the Netherlands, close to the German and Belgian borders. It is farmed by Wijngaard St. Martinus with a mix of classic and fungus-resistant grapes; yields are capped at 55 hl/ha.
appellations.terroir: Loess and gravel on south-facing slopes near the Vaalserberg.
appellations.nerd_note: Among the highest vineyards in the Netherlands.

appellations.name: Oolde
appellations.grapes: Solaris, Cabernet Blanc, Regent, Pinotin, Cabertin
appellations.summary: Oolde is the single-estate PDO of Wijngoed Hof te Oolde near Laren (Lochem) in Gelderland, registered in 2018. It allows only fungus-resistant varieties, a statement of organic intent, and includes still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wines.
appellations.terroir: Sand and loam on the moraine ridge near Lochem.
appellations.nerd_note: One of the first PDOs anywhere based entirely on fungus-resistant (PIWI) varieties.

appellations.name: Ambt Delden
appellations.grapes: Johanniter, Solaris, Souvignier Gris, Regent, Pinotin
appellations.summary: A single-estate PDO in Hof van Twente, Overijssel, registered in 2019 for Wijngaard Hof van Twente, using only fungus-resistant varieties, including wine from raisined grapes.
appellations.terroir: Sandy and loamy soils of Twente.

appellations.name: Achterhoek - Winterswijk
appellations.grapes: Acolon, Cabernet Cortis, Cabertin, Johanniter, Merzling, Monarch, Pinotin, Regent, Solaris, Souvignier Gris
appellations.summary: The PDO for Winterswijk in the eastern Achterhoek near the German border, registered in 2020, with fungus-resistant varieties grown on unusual soils that include Muschelkalk limestone, rare in the Netherlands. Wijngaard Hesselink is the main producer.
appellations.terroir: Sand, loam and pockets of shell limestone at Winterswijk.
appellations.nerd_note: Winterswijk has one of the very few Muschelkalk outcrops in the Netherlands, quarried for its stone and famous for its Triassic fossils.

appellations.name: Maasvallei Limburg
appellations.grapes: Auxerrois, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Dornfelder, Acolon
appellations.summary: The EU's first cross-border PDO, shared with Belgian Limburg along the Maas. On the Dutch side it includes Maasgouw (Thorn), Echt-Susteren, Roermond, Leudal, Sittard-Geleen and Stein.
appellations.terroir: Maas gravel and sand terraces.
appellations.nerd_note: Entry also listed under Belgium; the polygon spans both countries.

appellations.name: Dons
appellations.grapes: Solaris, Madeleine Angevine, Orion, Zalas Perle, Pinot Noir, Rondo, Regent, Cabernet Cortis
appellations.summary: Dons, in Kolding municipality in south-east Jutland, became Denmark's first PDO in 2018, and the first protected appellation for sparkling wine in Northern Europe. It exists because of Skærsøgaard, where Sven Moesgaard planted vines in 1998 and began making traditional-method sparkling wine; the estate's Dons Cuvée won international medals from the 2006 vintage on. Rules are strict: a maximum yield of 30 hl/ha and quality sparkling wine only.
appellations.terroir: Glacial moraine around the lakes of Dons in south-east Jutland.
appellations.nerd_note: The EU register caps Dons yields at 5,000 kg of grapes per hectare, among the lowest of any PDO in Europe.

appellations.name: Fyn
appellations.grapes: Solaris, Rondo, Regent, Pinot Noir and other permitted varieties
appellations.summary: The regional designation for wine from Funen and its surrounding islands, covering still, sparkling and quality sparkling wine with yields up to 60 hl/ha. Its status (PGI-level) should be confirmed in eAmbrosia.
appellations.terroir: Moraine and clay.

appellations.name: Jylland
appellations.grapes: Solaris, Rondo, Regent, Pinot Noir and other permitted varieties
appellations.summary: The regional designation for Jutland (the Midtjylland, Nordjylland and Syddanmark regions, excluding Funen), for still and sparkling wine with yields up to 60 hl/ha.
appellations.terroir: Moraine, sand and clay.

appellations.name: Sjælland
appellations.summary: The regional designation for Zealand and nearby islands, where most Danish vineyards are, notably in North Zealand and on the Røsnæs peninsula, home of Dyrehøj Vingaard.
appellations.terroir: Moraine and clay.

appellations.name: Bornholm
appellations.summary: The Baltic island of Bornholm has granite soils and the sunniest climate in Denmark, and several vineyards, including Lille Gadegård at Pedersker. Its designation status should be confirmed in eAmbrosia.
appellations.terroir: Granite and sandstone; sunny Baltic microclimate.

appellations.name: Morava
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Saint Laurent, Blaufränkisch and many others
appellations.summary: The regional PDO for Moravia, covering 301 municipalities in the EU register and about 95 percent of Czech vineyards. It is used for quality and Prädikat wine from anywhere in the four Moravian subregions.

appellations.name: Znojemská
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Blanc
appellations.summary: The western Moravian subregion around Znojmo on the Dyje (Thaya), facing Austria's Weinviertel across the border. Granite and gneiss in the Dyje canyon and loess elsewhere give aromatic, crisp whites, especially Grüner Veltliner, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling. It includes the Šobes vineyard and the villages of Hnanice, Nový Šaldorf, Vrbovec (344 ha) and Dobšice.
appellations.terroir: Granite, gneiss and loess; the coolest and most aromatic of the Moravian subregions.
appellations.nerd_note: Znojmo's medieval underground labyrinth was used for wine storage.

appellations.name: Mikulovská
appellations.grapes: Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Pálava
appellations.summary: Mikulovská surrounds the Pálava hills, a limestone ridge rising sharply from the plain south of Brno, with the towns of Mikulov and Valtice and villages such as Dolní Dunajovice, Pavlov and Novosedly. Its Jurassic limestone and loess give the most structured Czech whites, especially Welschriesling, Riesling and Pinot Gris. The subregion is also the centre of Moravia's natural-wine movement.
appellations.terroir: Jurassic limestone of the Pálava hills, loess and sand; warm and dry.
appellations.nerd_note: The Pálava hills are a UNESCO biosphere reserve whose rare steppe flora grows between the vines.

appellations.name: Velkopavlovická
appellations.grapes: Blaufränkisch, Saint Laurent, Zweigelt, André, Pinot Noir, Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner
appellations.summary: The central Moravian subregion around Velké Pavlovice, Velké Bílovice (the largest wine village in the country, about 766 ha), Hustopeče, Čejkovice, Bořetice and Kobylí. Rolling loess hills with apricot orchards make it the red-wine heart of Czechia, home of Frankovka, Saint Laurent and the André crossing, bred here in 1961.
appellations.terroir: Deep loess, sand and marl on rolling hills; warm summers.
appellations.nerd_note: The red crossing André (Blaufränkisch x Saint Laurent) was bred in this part of Moravia and remains a local favourite.

appellations.name: Slovácká
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Welschriesling, Müller-Thurgau, Grüner Veltliner, Saint Laurent, Blaufränkisch
appellations.summary: The eastern Moravian subregion (Moravian Slovakia), around Mutěnice, Bzenec, Strážnice, Blatnice and Uherské Hradiště, a folk-culture landscape of painted cellars and wine festivals. Sandy soils at Bzenec give famous Riesling, and the slopes of the White Carpathians near Blatnice give fresh whites.
appellations.terroir: Sand, loess and Carpathian flysch; slightly wetter and cooler near the hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Blatnice's St. Anthony chapel on its hill is a pilgrimage site above the vines.

appellations.name: Čechy
appellations.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Saint Laurent, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: The regional PDO for Bohemia's small vineyards, covering 67 municipalities in the EU register along the Elbe, Vltava and Ohře and in Prague.

appellations.name: Mělnická
appellations.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Saint Laurent, Pinot Blanc
appellations.summary: The subregion around Mělník at the confluence of the Elbe and Vltava, including Prague's historic vineyards. Mělník's Lobkowicz château winery and its terraced slopes above the rivers are the emblem of Bohemian wine, linked to St. Ludmila and Charles IV.
appellations.terroir: Sandstone and marl slopes at the river confluence.
appellations.nerd_note: Tradition credits Charles IV with bringing Burgundian vines to Mělník; Pinot Noir is still a local speciality.

appellations.name: Litoměřická
appellations.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Blanc, Saint Laurent
appellations.summary: The northern Bohemian subregion along the Elbe around Litoměřice, Velké Žernoseky, Roudnice nad Labem and Most, in the volcanic landscape of the České středohoří hills. Velké Žernoseky's deep cellars are among the oldest wine cellars in Bohemia.
appellations.terroir: Basalt, volcanic tuff, sandstone and marl on Elbe slopes.

appellations.name: Znojmo
appellations.summary: The first Czech VOC (2009) and the only one registered separately as an EU PDO (2011). It covers 22 villages around Znojmo and allows only Veltlínské zelené, Ryzlink rýnský and Sauvignon, in a fresh, aromatic dry style. The Znojmo growers' initiative became the model for later VOCs.
appellations.terroir: Granite, gneiss and loess in the Dyje valley.
appellations.nerd_note: The EU register caps VOC Znojmo at 12,000 kg of grapes per hectare.

appellations.name: Šobes / Šobeské víno
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Grüner Veltliner, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Welschriesling, Pálava, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Šobes is a single vineyard of about 13 hectares on a south-facing slope inside a meander of the Dyje river in the Podyjí National Park near Znojmo, reachable by foot or boat. Often called one of the oldest vineyards in central Europe, it has its own EU PDO (2011) and gives fine Riesling and Sauvignon from gneiss and granite.
appellations.terroir: Weathered gneiss and granite on a sun-trap slope enclosed by the river canyon.
appellations.nerd_note: The vineyard lies opposite the Austrian Thayatal National Park across the river.

appellations.name: Novosedelské Slámové víno
appellations.summary: A PDO for straw wine (slámové víno) from the village of Novosedly near Mikulov, made from grapes dried on straw or hung for months before pressing, giving intensely sweet wines. Novosedly is one of the largest wine villages in Moravia (about 421 ha).
appellations.terroir: Loess and sand below the Pálava hills.
appellations.nerd_note: One of very few straw-wine PDOs in Europe.

appellations.name: Mikulov
appellations.summary: VOC for the area around Mikulov and the Pálava hills, focused on dry whites such as Welschriesling, Grüner Veltliner, Riesling and the Pinots. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Modré Hory
appellations.summary: 'Blue Mountains', a VOC for red wines from villages around Bořetice, Kobylí, Němčičky and Velké Pavlovice, with Frankovka, Saint Laurent, Zweigelt and Portugieser. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Pálava
appellations.summary: VOC for wines from the villages around the Pálava limestone ridge (Pavlov, Dolní Věstonice, Perná, Bavory, Klentnice), known for structured whites. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Blatnice
appellations.summary: VOC for Blatnice pod Svatým Antonínkem and nearby villages in Slovácko, best known for a traditional white blend. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Valtice
appellations.summary: VOC for the Valtice area, seat of the Liechtenstein château and the National Wine Salon. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Mělník
appellations.summary: Bohemia's only VOC, for the historic vineyards around Mělník on the Elbe and Vltava. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Slovácko
appellations.summary: VOC for wines from the Slovácko subregion's villages, emphasising local character. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Hustopečsko
appellations.summary: VOC for the area around Hustopeče, a town of almond orchards and wine. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Kraví hora
appellations.summary: VOC for the Kraví hora hill at Bořetice, a sunny loess and sandstone slope with a famous cellar village and lookout tower. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Bzenec
appellations.summary: VOC for Bzenec, whose sandy soils have long been famous for Riesling (Ryzlink rýnský). Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Mutěnice
appellations.summary: VOC for Mutěnice, a large wine village with a viticulture research station and cellar lanes. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Velké Pavlovice
appellations.summary: VOC for Velké Pavlovice, the red-wine and apricot town of central Moravia. Like all VOCs it is run by a local growers' association that fixes varieties, style and a tasting check; it sits inside the subregion PDO rather than having its own EU registration.

appellations.name: Malokarpatská / Malokarpatské / Malokarpatský
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín and others
appellations.summary: The Little Carpathian PDO (EU reg. 2006), covering 143 municipalities from Bratislava to Skalica. It includes the wine towns of Rača, Svätý Jur, Pezinok and Modra, whose burghers made the region's fortune, and modern producers who have revived Grüner Veltliner, Riesling and Frankovka from granite slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Rača in Bratislava has been famous for Frankovka (Blaufränkisch) for centuries; its annual harvest festival celebrates the grape.

appellations.name: Južnoslovenská / Južnoslovenské / Južnoslovenský
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín and others
appellations.summary: The South Slovak PDO (EU reg. 2006) for the Danube plain, 120 municipalities from Šamorín to Štúrovo. Warm, dry and sandy, it gives ripe whites and reds; Strekov and Belá have become sources of some of the country's most talked-about wines.
appellations.nerd_note: Château Belá's Riesling, made with Egon Müller of the Saar, put Slovakia on serious wine lists from the early 2000s.

appellations.name: Nitrianska / Nitrianske / Nitriansky
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín and others
appellations.summary: The Nitra PDO (EU reg. 2006), the largest Slovak region by municipalities (192), around Nitra, Hlohovec, Zlaté Moravce and Vráble. Loess hills give balanced whites and reds; Château Topoľčianky is a key producer.

appellations.name: Stredoslovenská / Stredoslovenský / Stredoslovenské
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín and others
appellations.summary: The Central Slovak PDO (EU reg. 2006), 133 municipalities along the southern border around Modrý Kameň, Fiľakovo and Rimavská Sobota, with small family vineyards.

appellations.name: Východoslovenská / Východoslovenský / Východoslovenské
appellations.grapes: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Blaufränkisch, Müller-Thurgau, Saint Laurent, Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Devín and others
appellations.summary: The East Slovak PDO (EU reg. 2006), 99 municipalities around Košice, Moldava nad Bodvou and the Zemplín outside the Tokaj delimitation. Volcanic and loess soils near the Tokaj hills give aromatic whites, including Furmint and Lipovina sold without the Tokaj name.

appellations.name: Vinohradnícka oblasť Tokaj
appellations.created: 2006 (EU reg.); upheld by EU courts 2012 and 2013
appellations.summary: The Slovak Tokaj PDO covers seven villages and about 908 hectares of classified vineyards on the northern edge of the Zemplén hills. It makes the full range of Tokaj styles: dry Furmint and Lipovina, samorodné from bunches with botrytised berries, Tokajský výber (the Slovak name for aszú) graded from 3 to 6 puttony, výberová esencia and esencia, plus mášláš and fordítáš made by re-fermenting must on aszú lees. The Hungarian state long argued that only Hungarian wine should bear the name, but after the 2004 bilateral agreement and failed EU court actions in 2012 and 2013, both countries use it. Malá Tŕňa and Veľká Tŕňa, with tuff cellars dating back centuries, are the centre.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic tuff, andesite and loess; humid autumns from the Bodrog river favour botrytis.
appellations.nerd_note: Slovak Tokaj producers still nominally follow the Hungarian Tokaj law of 1908 (Law XLVII) for traditional styles.

appellations.name: Karpatská perla
appellations.summary: Karpatská perla ('Carpathian pearl') is a PDO registered in 2011 for 34 municipalities of Bratislava and the Little Carpathian foothills, used as a tasting-controlled quality label for local wines. Not to be confused with the producer Karpatská Perla in Šenkvice.
appellations.terroir: Granite and loess of the Little Carpathian foothills.

appellations.name: Skalický rubín
appellations.summary: Skalický rubín ('Skalica ruby') is a traditional red blend from six municipalities around Skalica in the far west of Slovakia, near the Moravian border, registered as a PDO in 2017. It must blend Frankovka modrá, Modrý Portugal and Svätovavrinecké, revived from a nineteenth-century local tradition.
appellations.terroir: Loess and sand at the foot of the White Carpathians.
appellations.nerd_note: One of the few PDOs defined by a specific red blend of three grapes.

sites.name: Bernkasteler Doctor
sites.text: A steep, south-facing slate slope of only about 3.3 hectares directly above the rooftops of Bernkastel, and Germany's most famous vineyard. Legend says Archbishop Boemund of Trier was cured of a fever by its wine in the fourteenth century. A plan under the 1971 law to enlarge the site triggered years of litigation among the owners before its present boundaries were settled. The wines are rich, smoky Rieslings with a mineral bite; Thanisch, Lauerburg and Kesselstatt are owners.

sites.name: Wehlener Sonnenuhr
sites.text: A sweep of blue slate facing south-west across the Mosel from Wehlen, named for the sundial Jodocus Prüm built among the vines in 1842 so pickers could tell the time. Its Rieslings are the archetype of floral, filigree Mosel Spätlese and Auslese, and J.J. Prüm's bottlings age for decades.

sites.name: Graacher Himmelreich
sites.text: 'Kingdom of heaven' rises above Graach between Bernkastel and Wehlen on deep, stony blue slate. Its Rieslings are a touch rounder and more generous than Wehlen's, and Willi Schaefer's Kabinett and Spätlese from here are cult wines.

sites.name: Graacher Josephshöfer
sites.text: A monopole of Reichsgraf von Kesselstatt between Graach's Domprobst and the Wehlener Sonnenuhr, named after the Josephshof estate that once belonged to St. Martin's abbey in Trier. Dense, slate-rich Riesling that needs time.

sites.name: Zeltinger Sonnenuhr
sites.text: Downstream neighbour of the Wehlener Sonnenuhr, with its own sundial in the vines. Deep, weathered slate gives Riesling with a little more power and spice than Wehlen; Selbach-Oster's single-parcel bottlings from ungrafted old vines are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ürziger Würzgarten
sites.text: The 'spice garden' is a near-vertical cliff of red Rotliegend slate and volcanic rock above Ürzig, where vines grow in pockets between rock outcrops. Its Rieslings smell of exotic spice and red fruit, unlike anything else on the Mosel; many vines are ungrafted because phylloxera cannot thrive in the rocky soil.
producers: Joh. Jos. Christoffel Erben (leased to Mönchhof)

sites.name: Erdener Prälat
sites.text: A tiny strip of red slate between rock walls and the river opposite Erden, the warmest microclimate on the Mosel. The 'prelate' gives opulent, tropical Auslese of great intensity. Dr. Loosen's old vines here are a reference.

sites.name: Erdener Treppchen
sites.text: The 'little staircase' takes its name from the steps cut into the rock so growers could reach the vines. Red and blue slate give Riesling that sits between the spice of Ürzig and the elegance of the Middle Mosel.

sites.name: Brauneberger Juffer-Sonnenuhr
sites.text: The heart of the Juffer slope across the river from Brauneberg, with its own sundial. In the nineteenth century Brauneberg wines were among the most expensive on the Mosel, and Fritz Haag's Juffer-Sonnenuhr Auslese remains one of the great sweet wines of Germany.

sites.name: Brauneberger Juffer
sites.text: A broad, steep, south-facing amphitheatre of grey slate opposite Brauneberg. The name is said to come from the unmarried daughters ('Juffern') of a local official who owned vines here. Its Rieslings are firm and slow-ageing.

sites.name: Piesporter Goldtröpfchen
sites.text: A south-facing amphitheatre of blue slate curving behind the village of Piesport, the 'little gold drop' is one of the Mosel's most perfect sites, making juicy, peachy Riesling. Its fame was abused by the vast Großlage Piesporter Michelsberg, which had nothing to do with it.

sites.name: Trittenheimer Apotheke
sites.text: A steep slate slope in the river bend at Trittenheim, the first great site of the Middle Mosel heading downstream from Trier. It gives racy, citrus Riesling with a herbal edge. Coordinates are approximate (Trittenheim bend).

sites.name: Scharzhofberg
sites.text: A single steep, south-facing slope of grey slate in a side valley of the Saar near Wiltingen, about 28 hectares, and arguably the greatest Riesling vineyard in the world. Egon Müller's Scharzhofberger Kabinett tastes of white flowers and lime and lasts for decades; his TBA routinely sets world auction records. Like Schloss Johannisberg, it is so famous that no village name is required.

sites.name: Ockfener Bockstein
sites.text: A steep grey-slate hillside above Ockfen on the Saar. Bockstein Riesling is famous for its cut and its notes of grapefruit and herbs.

sites.name: Saarburger Rausch
sites.text: A south-facing slope above Saarburg whose grey slate is laced with green diabase, a volcanic rock. Hanno and Dorothee Zilliken's Rausch Rieslings, especially their Auslese and Eiswein, are among the most finely etched wines in Germany.

sites.name: Kanzemer Altenberg
sites.text: A long, very steep slope on the Saar's left bank near Kanzem, owned in part by von Othegraven (since 2010 owned by TV presenter Günther Jauch) and Van Volxem. Its wines are powerful by Saar standards, with yellow fruit and spice.

sites.name: Ayler Kupp
sites.text: A rounded hill of slate at Ayl on the Saar. Peter Lauer bottles historic sub-parcels of the Kupp under 'Fass' numbers, revealing how much one slope can vary.

sites.name: Maximin Grünhaus
sites.class: Historic estate with monopoles Abtsberg, Herrenberg, Bruderberg
sites.text: An estate at Mertesdorf on the Ruwer owned by the Benedictine abbey of St. Maximin in Trier from 966 until secularisation, and by the von Schubert family since 1882. The steep slopes behind the manor were divided by their medieval users: Abtsberg for the abbot, Herrenberg for the monks, Bruderberg for the lay brothers. Abtsberg's blue slate gives one of the most delicate Rieslings in Germany.

sites.name: Karthäuserhof
sites.text: The former Carthusian estate at Eitelsbach (Trier), given to the monks in 1335 and secular since 1811. Its monopole Karthäuserhofberg rises behind the buildings, and its bottles famously wear only a neck label.

sites.name: Bremmer Calmont
sites.text: A cliff of slate on the Mosel's outside bend at Bremm, generally billed as the steepest vineyard in Europe, with a via ferrata climbing path through the vines. Romans had a temple on its summit. Kilian Franzen, who took over after his father Ulrich died in an accident in 2010, and a few others keep its tiny terraces planted with Riesling.

sites.name: Winninger Uhlen
sites.class: Einzellage; three sections are EU PDOs since 2018
sites.text: A curved, terraced cliff on the Lower Mosel between Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf, with three soil zones that became separate EU PDOs in 2018: Blaufüßer Lay, Laubach and Roth Lay. Reinhard Löwenstein's dry Rieslings from here are powerful and long.

sites.name: Weingut Egon Müller (Scharzhof)
sites.text: The manor house at the foot of the Scharzhofberg, in the family since Jean-Jacques Koch bought the secularised church estate in 1797. Egon Müller IV makes wines in a traditional style from ungrafted old vines; the family also owns Le Gallais (Wiltinger Braune Kupp) and a Slovak estate at Château Belá.

sites.name: Weingut Dr. Loosen
sites.text: The St. Johannishof estate at Bernkastel-Kues, run by Ernst Loosen since 1988. Holdings in six Grosse Lagen from Bernkastel to Ürzig and a crusading role abroad helped bring Mosel Riesling back to world wine lists.

sites.name: Weingut Joh. Jos. Prüm
sites.text: Founded in 1911 when the Prüm estate at Wehlen was divided, and run by Dr. Manfred Prüm and now his daughter Katharina. Its Sonnenuhr Spätlese and Auslese, often with a reductive, sulphurous youth, are among the longest-lived white wines in the world.

sites.name: St. Nikolaus-Hospital (Cusanusstift)
