sites.text: A late-Gothic almshouse at Kues founded by the philosopher-cardinal Nicholas of Cusa for 33 poor men. The foundation still owns vineyards and its cellars house a Mosel wine museum and vinothek.

sites.name: Römische Kelteranlage Piesport
sites.text: The largest excavated Roman wine press house north of the Alps, discovered in 1985 at Piesport-Müstert. Its basins show that wine was made in volume on these slopes in the fourth century, when Trier was an imperial capital. A 'Roman harvest' is re-enacted here.

sites.name: Neumagener Weinschiff
sites.class: Roman funerary monument, c. 220 AD (replica on site)
sites.text: A replica of the famous stone wine ship stands in Neumagen, where the original was excavated in 1878. The carving shows oarsmen and a cargo of casks, and a grinning helmsman who seems to have tasted the load.

sites.name: Rheinisches Landesmuseum Trier
sites.text: Home to the original Neumagen wine ship and a large collection of Roman wine vessels, reliefs and tools from the Mosel valley.

sites.name: Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg
sites.text: The steepest part of Rüdesheim's Berg, terraced quartzite and slate around the ruined Ehrenfels castle where the Rhine turns north into the gorge. It gives intense, mineral dry Riesling; Georg Breuer's Schlossberg is a classic.

sites.name: Rüdesheimer Berg Rottland
sites.text: The eastern, slightly gentler part of the Berg, with quartzite and slate under loess, giving fleshier Riesling than the Schlossberg.

sites.name: Schloss Johannisberg
sites.class: Historic estate; Ortsteil site needing no village name
sites.text: A former Benedictine monastery on a hill above the Rhine, acquired by the Prince-Abbots of Fulda, planted entirely with Riesling around 1720 and given to Prince Metternich in 1816. A statue honours the courier whose late return in 1775 created the Spätlese. Its colour-coded capsules (from yellow to gold) mark quality levels.

sites.name: Steinberg
sites.class: Ortsteil site, monopole; VDP Grosse Lage
sites.text: A walled vineyard of about 37 hectares below Kloster Eberbach, laid out by the Cistercians in the twelfth century and enclosed by a wall completed in the eighteenth. Owned by the Hessian State Wine Estates, it gives taut, long-lived Riesling, and needs no village name on the label.

sites.name: Kloster Eberbach
sites.class: Cistercian abbey founded 1136; Hessian State Wine Estates
sites.text: One of the best preserved medieval monasteries in Germany, founded by Bernard of Clairvaux's monks in 1136. Its monks ran a fleet of wine ships and the abbey's 'Cabinet' cellar for reserve wines may have given the word Kabinett. It houses the Hessian State Wine Estates, historic presses, and served as a film set for The Name of the Rose.

sites.name: Erbacher Marcobrunn
sites.text: A low-lying site on deep marl next to the Marcobrunn spring on the border of Erbach and Hattenheim, long the most expensive Rheingau vineyard. Its Rieslings are broad, spicy and long-lived.

sites.name: Hochheimer Hölle
sites.text: A south-facing slope above the Main at Hochheim, the warm eastern outpost of the Rheingau. Heavy marl and limestone give dense, powerful Riesling. Künstler's Hölle GG is a reference.

sites.name: Hochheimer Domdechaney
sites.text: A small vineyard below Hochheim's church, named after the cathedral dean of Mainz who once owned it; deep calcareous soils give rich Riesling.

sites.name: Kiedricher Gräfenberg
sites.text: A steep slope of phyllite slate behind the Gothic village of Kiedrich, high on the Rheingau slope. Robert Weil's Gräfenberg Riesling, dry and sweet, is among Germany's most celebrated, and his TBAs set records.

sites.name: Weingut Robert Weil
sites.text: Founded in 1875 at Kiedrich by Dr. Robert Weil, who had taught German at the Sorbonne until the Franco-Prussian war forced him to leave Paris. Owned by Suntory since 1988 and run by Wilhelm Weil, it is the Rheingau's flagship.

sites.name: Weingut Georg Breuer
sites.text: Rüdesheim estate whose late Bernhard Breuer was a founder of the Charta movement for dry Riesling and left the VDP over classification policy. Now run by his daughter Theresa, it has monopole Rauenthaler Nonnenberg and parcels in Berg Schlossberg.

sites.name: Schloss Vollrads
sites.text: A moated castle near Winkel that documents wine sales back to 1211, among the oldest records of a wine business still operating. Owned for centuries by the Greiffenclau family, it now belongs to a bank foundation.

sites.name: Hochschule Geisenheim
sites.text: The world-famous wine research institute where Hermann Müller bred Müller-Thurgau in 1882, and where generations of German and international winemakers have trained.

sites.name: Rauenthaler Baiken
sites.text: A high site on phyllite and loess at Rauenthal, historically one of the Rheingau's most expensive, giving spicy, firm Riesling.

sites.name: Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle
sites.text: The Nahe's most celebrated vineyard, a steep slope above the river at Niederhausen of grey slate mixed with porphyry and melaphyre. Helmut and Cornelius Dönnhoff's Hermannshöhle Riesling, dry and sweet, ranks with the finest in Germany. Coordinates are near the site's namesake adit.

sites.name: Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube
sites.text: A vineyard cut from the spoil of an old copper mine by the Prussian state domain in the early 1900s, with convict labour. Volcanic soils give taut, smoky Riesling. Coordinates are from a trail sign near the site.

sites.name: Monzinger Halenberg
sites.text: A steep slope of blue slate and quartzite at Monzingen on the upper Nahe. Emrich-Schönleber's Halenberg GG is one of Germany's great dry Rieslings, smoky and mineral.

sites.name: Weingut Emrich-Schönleber
sites.text: The Monzingen estate of Werner and now Frank Schönleber, which raised the upper Nahe from obscurity with precise dry and sweet Riesling from the Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen.

sites.name: Weingut Dönnhoff
sites.text: The Oberhausen estate whose Helmut Dönnhoff made the Nahe internationally famous; his son Cornelius farms the Hermannshöhle, Brücke (a monopole), Kupfergrube and Dellchen.

sites.name: Niersteiner Pettenthal
sites.text: The steepest part of the Roter Hang, a cliff of red Permian slate rising directly from the Rhine north of Nierstein. Its Rieslings are spicy, concentrated and mineral. Kühling-Gillot, Gunderloch and Schätzel are key owners.

sites.name: Niersteiner Hipping
sites.text: A red-slate slope just north of Nierstein on the Roter Hang facing east over the Rhine, known for vibrant, aromatic Riesling. Keller's Hipping helped revive the area's image.

sites.name: Nackenheimer Rothenberg
sites.text: The northern end of the Roter Hang at Nackenheim, steep red slate overlooking the Rhine and protected as a nature reserve. Gunderloch's Rothenberg has been a benchmark since the 1990s.

sites.name: Westhofener Morstein
sites.text: A limestone and clay slope near Westhofen in the Wonnegau, now among Germany's most famous dry Riesling sites thanks to Keller and Wittmann. Morstein GGs combine power with chalky tension. Coordinates are approximate.

sites.name: Dalsheimer Hubacker
sites.text: A gentle limestone slope at Flörsheim-Dalsheim enclosed by an old wall, and the original source of Keller's fame. Keller's Hubacker GG first showed what the Wonnegau could do.

sites.name: Weingut Keller
sites.text: The Flörsheim-Dalsheim estate of Klaus Peter and Julia Keller, whose G-Max, Abtserde, Morstein and Hubacker dry Rieslings are among the most sought-after white wines in the world. They also make a Mosel Riesling from Piesport.

sites.name: Weingut Wittmann
sites.text: Philipp Wittmann's biodynamic estate in Westhofen, known for limestone-driven GG from Morstein, Brunnenhäuschen, Kirchspiel and Aulerde.

sites.name: Liebfrauenkirche Worms (Liebfrauenstift-Kirchenstück)
sites.class: Church and vineyard; origin of the name Liebfraumilch
sites.text: A Gothic church surrounded by the vineyards of the former Liebfrauenstift. Their wine, 'Liebfrauenmilch', was famous by the eighteenth century; the name was later applied to a blend from four regions that became a global export phenomenon. The Liebfrauenstift-Kirchenstück vineyard itself still exists.

sites.name: Deutsches Weinbaumuseum Oppenheim
sites.text: Germany's national wine-growing museum in Oppenheim, with presses, tools and a collection on the history of German viticulture.

sites.name: Forster Kirchenstück
sites.text: A walled vineyard of under 4 hectares behind Forst's church, ranked at the top of the 1828 Bavarian tax survey. Basalt, limestone and sandstone give Riesling of finesse rather than power; Bürklin-Wolf, Bassermann-Jordan and von Buhl share it.

sites.name: Forster Jesuitengarten
sites.text: Neighbour of the Kirchenstück, once owned by the Jesuits, on sandy loam with basalt. It gives elegant, floral Riesling.

sites.name: Forster Pechstein
sites.text: Named after the black basalt ('pitch stone') quarried from the Pechsteinkopf above Forst and scattered through its soil, the most basalt-rich of the Pfalz's great sites. The dark stones store heat and give smoky, mineral Riesling. Coordinates are approximate, west of the village.

sites.name: Forster Ungeheuer
sites.text: The 'monster' is a larger site south of Forst on basalt and sandstone, giving full, spicy Riesling. Bismarck is said to have pronounced its wine 'ungeheuer gut'.

sites.name: Kallstadter Saumagen
sites.text: A former Roman limestone quarry turned vineyard at Kallstadt, named after its shape (a stuffed pig's stomach, the local dish). Its warm, chalky soils give powerful, long-lived dry Riesling; Koehler-Ruprecht's Saumagen was legendary.

sites.name: Birkweiler Kastanienbusch
sites.text: A high, steep slope on the edge of the Palatinate Forest at Birkweiler, with red Rotliegend slate, sandstone and granite. It gives some of the Pfalz's finest, most mineral dry Riesling.

sites.name: Weingut Dr. Bürklin-Wolf
sites.text: The Wachenheim estate of the Bürklin family, one of the 'three Bs' of the Pfalz and Germany's largest biodynamic private estate. It pioneered Burgundy-style G.C. and P.C. labels in the 1990s, based on the 1828 Bavarian classification.

sites.name: Deutsches Weintor
sites.text: The monumental gate at Schweigen on the French border marking the southern end of the German Wine Route, built in 1936 as a Nazi-era promotion of the struggling region.

sites.name: Dürkheimer Riesenfass
sites.text: A 1.7-million-litre barrel built by a cooper in 1934 at Bad Dürkheim, never filled with wine and now a restaurant beside the Wurstmarkt festival grounds.

sites.name: Historisches Museum der Pfalz (Speyer wine bottle)
sites.class: Holds the oldest known bottle of wine
sites.text: The museum in Speyer displays the Roman bottle of the fourth century found in 1867, still containing liquid wine under a seal of olive oil, plus the Wine Museum of the Pfalz.

sites.name: Achkarrer Schlossberg
sites.text: A steep volcanic hill crowned by a ruined castle above Achkarren on the Kaiserstuhl. Weathered tephrite gives Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder of power and smoky minerality.

sites.name: Ihringer Winklerberg
sites.text: Terraced volcanic slopes at Ihringen, the hottest spot in Germany, protected as a nature reserve for its rare plants and lizards. Dr. Heger's Winklerberg Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder are benchmarks.

sites.name: Oberrotweiler Henkenberg
sites.text: A steep volcanic slope at Oberrotweil on the western Kaiserstuhl, where Salwey makes taut Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder.

sites.name: Weingut Dr. Heger
sites.text: Ihringen estate founded in 1935 by a country doctor, Max Heger; under Joachim Heger and now Rebecca Heger it became the Kaiserstuhl's reference for Pinot.

sites.name: Würzburger Stein
sites.class: Einzellage; VDP Grosse Lage; part of PDO Würzburger Stein-Berg
sites.text: Germany's largest famous single vineyard, about 85 hectares of shell limestone rising above the Main north of Würzburg. 'Steinwein' was the wine of Goethe and of princes; a 1540 vintage was still drinkable in 1961. Juliusspital, Bürgerspital and the Hofkeller share it.

sites.name: Randersackerer Pfülben
sites.text: A steep, south-facing bowl of shell limestone at Randersacker just upstream of Würzburg, giving rich, spicy Silvaner and Riesling.

sites.name: Escherndorfer Lump
sites.text: A steep curve of shell limestone on the Volkach Main loop. Horst Sauer's Lump Silvaner and Riesling, including spectacular TBA, put it on the map.

sites.name: Iphöfer Julius-Echter-Berg
sites.text: A Keuper slope below the Schwanberg at Iphofen in the Steigerwald, named after Prince-Bishop Julius Echter. Gypsum-rich marl gives broad, powerful Silvaner.

sites.name: Bürgstadter Centgrafenberg
sites.class: Einzellage; VDP Grosse Lage; within PDO Bürgstadter Berg
sites.text: A red sandstone slope on the lower Main at Bürgstadt, source of Rudolf Fürst's famous Spätburgunder and Riesling.

sites.name: Juliusspital Würzburg
sites.text: Founded in 1576 by Prince-Bishop Julius Echter as a hospital, still running a hospital, care home and one of Germany's largest wine estates, with vineyards in the Stein, Pfülben, Lump and Julius-Echter-Berg. Its cellars stretch under the baroque building.

sites.name: Bürgerspital zum Heiligen Geist
sites.text: Founded in 1316 by a Würzburg patrician to care for the poor and elderly, funded by wine. Its wine tavern and ancient cellars are a city institution.

sites.name: Staatlicher Hofkeller Würzburg
sites.class: Bavarian state estate, cellars beneath the Residenz
sites.text: The former prince-bishops' wine estate, now owned by the Free State of Bavaria, with its vaulted cellars under the UNESCO-listed Würzburg Residenz.

sites.name: Sommeracher Katzenkopf
sites.text: A shell-limestone slope in the Volkach Main loop, home of the Sommerach cooperative's popular Silvaners.

sites.name: Hessigheimer Felsengärten
sites.text: Dramatic cliffs and dry-stone terraces of Muschelkalk on the Neckar between Hessigheim and Mundelsheim, among the most spectacular vineyard landscapes in Württemberg.

sites.name: Ahrweiler Rosenthal
sites.text: A sheltered slope on slate and loess north of Ahrweiler, giving supple, perfumed Spätburgunder.

sites.name: Walporzheimer Kräuterberg
sites.text: A tiny, terraced amphitheatre of slate at Walporzheim, so hot that wild herbs grow between the vines. One of the Ahr's most famous Pinot sites.

sites.name: Weingut Meyer-Näkel
sites.text: Werner Näkel's Dernau estate, now run by his daughters Meike and Dörte, defined modern Ahr Pinot Noir. Destroyed in the July 2021 flood, it was rebuilt and its Pfarrwingert and Kräuterberg wines are again released.

sites.name: Winzergenossenschaft Mayschoß
sites.text: Founded in 1868 by growers seeking a way out of poverty, the Mayschoß cooperative is generally counted as Germany's oldest winegrowers' cooperative; its cellars were badly hit by the 2021 flood.

sites.name: Bopparder Hamm
sites.class: Einzellage group in the Rhine's largest loop
sites.text: A sweeping slate slope in the biggest loop of the Rhine at Boppard, divided into sites such as Feuerlay, Mandelstein and Ohlenberg, giving lively, mineral Riesling.

sites.name: Heppenheimer Steinkopf
sites.text: A granite and loess slope at Heppenheim, one of the Bergstraße's best Riesling and Pinot sites, close to the state domain's monopole Centgericht.

sites.name: Herzoglicher Weinberg Freyburg
sites.class: Historic terraced vineyard and nature reserve
sites.text: Terraced shell-limestone slopes at Freyburg with small vineyard houses, laid out for the Dukes of Saxe-Weissenfels in the eighteenth century and now a protected landscape.

sites.name: Freyburger Edelacker
sites.text: The best-known vineyard of Freyburg, below the Neuenburg castle on shell limestone; Pawis makes acclaimed dry Riesling and Weißburgunder here.

sites.name: Rotkäppchen Sektkellerei
sites.text: Founded in Freyburg in 1856, renamed after its red-capped bottles in 1894, nationalised in East Germany and bought by its managers after reunification. Rotkäppchen-Mumm is now Germany's largest sparkling wine company; its cathedral-like cask cellar holds a giant 120,000-litre barrel.

sites.name: Landesweingut Kloster Pforta
sites.class: State estate on former Cistercian lands
sites.text: The Saxony-Anhalt state estate near Naumburg, heir to the Cistercian abbey of Pforta (1137), which spread viticulture along the Saale.

sites.name: Schloss Wackerbarth
sites.class: Saxon state winery and Sekt house
sites.text: A baroque palace in Radebeul built for Count Wackerbarth around 1730, now the Saxon state wine and Sekt estate, with terraced vineyards and a belvedere above.

sites.name: Schloss Proschwitz
sites.class: Estate of the Prinz zur Lippe
sites.text: A neoclassical castle north of Meißen, recovered by the Lippe family after reunification and now Saxony's largest private estate.

sites.name: Hoflößnitz
sites.class: Former Wettin wine estate, now a museum
sites.text: The seventeenth-century wine estate of the Saxon electors in Radebeul, with a painted banqueting hall and a museum of Saxon wine history.

sites.name: Meißner Kapitelberg
sites.text: A granite vineyard on the Elbe near Meißen, once owned by the cathedral chapter.

sites.name: Radebeuler Goldener Wagen
sites.text: A steep terraced slope below the Spitzhaus in Radebeul, one of Saxony's most famous sites.

sites.name: Pillnitzer Königlicher Weinberg
sites.text: The royal vineyard below the Pillnitz palace on the Elbe, planted for the Saxon kings.

sites.name: Maximin Grünhäuser Abtsberg
sites.text: The steep blue-slate slope rising directly behind the Grünhaus manor at Mertesdorf, once reserved for the abbot of St. Maximin. Its Rieslings are the most refined of the estate's three sites, floral and long-lived. Coordinates are on the slope above the manor (approximate).

sites.name: Eitelsbacher Karthäuserhofberg
sites.text: The Karthäuserhof's monopole, a south-facing slate slope above the estate at Eitelsbach, worked by the Carthusians from 1335. It gives racy, herbal Ruwer Riesling. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Wiltinger Braune Kupp
sites.text: A slate slope at Wiltingen owned as a monopole by the Le Gallais estate, run by Egon Müller since 1954; it gives slightly broader Riesling than the Scharzhofberg. Coordinates mark Wiltingen and are approximate.

sites.name: Trier (Augusta Treverorum)
sites.text: The Porta Nigra and the Roman monuments of Trier, a capital of the late empire, are the reason vines were planted on the Mosel: the court, the army and the city drank its wine. The city's charitable foundations and the Bischöfliche Weingüter still own famous vineyards.

sites.name: Kessler Sekt, Esslingen
sites.text: Georg Christian Kessler, who had worked for Veuve Clicquot in Reims, founded his sparkling-wine house in Esslingen am Neckar in 1826, making it the oldest Sekt producer in Germany. Coordinates mark Esslingen's old town (approximate).

sites.name: Henkell, Wiesbaden
sites.text: Founded in Mainz in 1832 and based in its palatial Biebrich headquarters in Wiesbaden since 1909, Henkell is now part of Henkell Freixenet, the world's largest sparkling-wine group. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Loreley
sites.text: The slate rock above the narrowest bend of the Rhine at St. Goarshausen, the heart of the Upper Middle Rhine Valley World Heritage Site and of German Romantic legend, with steep vineyards on both banks.

sites.name: Kaiserstuhl
sites.text: The volcanic massif rising from the Rhine plain near Freiburg, the warmest place in Germany and the heart of Baden Pinot. Its terraces and loess gullies are a protected landscape.

sites.name: Ried Achleiten
sites.text: A steep slope of terraced gneiss, amphibolite and serpentine above Weißenkirchen, facing south-east over the Danube. Achleiten Riesling and Grüner Veltliner are famous for their smoky, stony intensity; Prager's and Domäne Wachau's bottlings are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ried Klaus
sites.text: A narrow, steep terrace of gneiss next to the Achleiten at Weißenkirchen and Joching, giving taut, saline Riesling. Prager and Josef Jamek make classic examples.

sites.name: Ried Loibenberg
sites.text: The broad, south-facing hillside above Unterloiben and Oberloiben, one of the warmest sites in the Wachau, of gneiss covered in places with loess. It gives opulent Smaragd Riesling and Grüner. Coordinates are on the slope below the Loibenberg summit.

sites.name: Ried Kellerberg
sites.text: Terraces of gneiss between Dürnstein and Oberloiben, cooled by air flowing down a side gully at night. F.X. Pichler's Kellerberg Riesling and Grüner Veltliner Smaragd are among Austria's most celebrated whites.

sites.name: Ried Steinertal
sites.text: A cool, narrow side valley east of the Loibenberg with gneiss and amphibolite, where the temperature drops sharply at night. Alzinger's and F.X. Pichler's Steinertal Rieslings are known for their cut and finesse.

sites.name: Ried Schütt
sites.text: A site at the mouth of a side valley at Unterloiben whose name refers to the scree washed down from the hills; gravelly gneiss gives powerful yet clear Riesling and Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Ried Höhereck
sites.text: A high, steep site between Dürnstein and Loiben on gneiss and mica schist, giving finely structured Riesling and Grüner Veltliner. Alzinger's Höhereck is a reference.

sites.name: Ried Singerriedel
sites.text: A steep, terraced amphitheatre of mica schist and gneiss behind Spitz, facing south-east. Franz Hirtzberger's Singerriedel Riesling Smaragd is one of the great Wachau wines, with floral lift from the cooler western end of the valley.

sites.name: Weingut F.X. Pichler
sites.text: The Oberloiben estate of F.X. and now Lucas Pichler, whose Kellerberg, Loibenberg and Steinertal Smaragds set the standard for powerful, concentrated Wachau wines from the 1980s onward.

sites.name: Weingut Emmerich Knoll
sites.text: A family estate in Unterloiben known for its baroque-style label of St. Urban and for long-lived Riesling and Grüner from the Loibenberg, Kellerberg and Schütt.

sites.name: Weingut Leo Alzinger
sites.text: A small Unterloiben estate whose precise, elegant Rieslings from the Steinertal, Loibenberg and Höhereck rank among the Wachau's finest.

sites.name: Weingut Prager
sites.text: Founded by Franz Prager in Weißenkirchen and run by Toni Bodenstein, a geologist and mayor who mapped the Wachau's soils; famed for Achleiten and Klaus Riesling.

sites.name: Weingut Franz Hirtzberger
sites.text: The Spitz estate of Franz Hirtzberger, long-time president of Vinea Wachau, whose Singerriedel and Honivogl wines are icons of the western Wachau.

sites.name: Nikolaihof
sites.text: An estate in Mautern built on Roman foundations, which claims to be one of the oldest wine estates in Austria. Biodynamic since 1971, it holds Riesling for decades in old casks before release as 'Vinothek'.

sites.name: Domäne Wachau
sites.text: The cooperative of some 250 growers at Dürnstein, farming about a third of the Wachau, with a baroque Kellerschlössel (1715) on the grounds.

sites.name: Dürnstein
sites.text: The blue-towered abbey church and the ruined Kuenringer castle where Richard the Lionheart was held captive in 1192 and 1193 make Dürnstein the Wachau's emblem.

sites.name: Stift Göttweig
sites.text: A baroque Benedictine abbey on a hill south of the Danube opposite Krems, whose vineyards around Furth are now farmed by the Stift Göttweig wine estate.

sites.name: Ried Wachtberg
sites.class: Kremstal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: Loess and gneiss terraces rising directly above the old town of Krems, a warm site that gives rich, spicy Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Ried Pfaffenberg
sites.class: Kremstal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A steep gneiss site at Stein on the Wachau border, first documented in 1230. Salomon Undhof's and Stift Göttweig's Pfaffenberg Rieslings are classics.

sites.name: Zöbinger Heiligenstein
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A ridge of Permian desert sandstone and conglomerate, about 270 million years old, rising south of Zöbing. Its name ('holy stone') replaced the earlier 'Hellenstein' (hell's stone), a nod to the heat on its south face. Heiligenstein Riesling from Bründlmayer, Hirsch, Jurtschitsch or Schloss Gobelsburg is among the greatest in Austria.

sites.name: Ried Gaisberg
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: The eastern neighbour of the Heiligenstein above Zöbing and Strass, on crystalline gneiss and amphibolite rather than sandstone, giving finer-boned, more floral Riesling.

sites.name: Ried Lamm
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A sheltered hollow of deep loess and calcareous soils at the foot of the Heiligenstein in Kammern, a heat trap that gives Austria's most opulent Grüner Veltliners. Bründlmayer's and Hirsch's Lamm are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ried Spiegel
sites.class: Kamptal Riedenwein site; ÖTW Erste Lage
sites.text: A loess slope at Gobelsburg and Langenlois with a cooling breeze, giving elegant, spicy Grüner Veltliner.

sites.name: Weingut Bründlmayer
sites.text: Willi Bründlmayer's Langenlois estate helped define modern Austrian wine, from Heiligenstein Riesling and Lamm Grüner to a celebrated traditional-method Sekt.

sites.name: Schloss Gobelsburg
sites.text: A baroque castle that the Cistercians of Zwettl Abbey owned for centuries; since 1996 run by Michael Moosbrugger with vineyards in Heiligenstein, Gaisberg, Lamm and Grub.

sites.name: Weingut Hiedler
sites.text: Ludwig Hiedler's Langenlois estate, known for slow-fermented, age-worthy Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from Heiligenstein, Gaisberg and Thal.

sites.name: Loisium Langenlois
sites.text: A visitor centre by Steven Holl over a medieval cellar labyrinth beneath Langenlois, telling the story of Kamptal wine.

sites.name: Stift Klosterneuburg
sites.class: Augustinian abbey (1114) and Austria's largest private wine estate
sites.text: The abbey founded by Margrave Leopold III, who became Austria's patron saint, has made wine for about 900 years. Its estate farms vineyards in Vienna, Klosterneuburg, Gumpoldskirchen and Tattendorf, and the nearby school (1860) created the KMW must scale and Zweigelt.

sites.name: Kellergasse Hadres
sites.text: A long lane of small press houses and cellars dug into loess at the edge of Hadres, among the longest Kellergassen in Austria and a classic image of the Weinviertel.

sites.name: Carnuntum Roman city
sites.text: The Roman legionary fortress and provincial capital of Pannonia Superior, where emperors stayed and where the Danube frontier wine trade flowed. The archaeological park at Petronell gives the wine region its name.

sites.name: Freigut Thallern
sites.text: A wine estate at Gumpoldskirchen owned by the abbey of Heiligenkreuz since 1141, known for Zierfandler and Rotgipfler.

sites.name: Rust
sites.text: A small baroque town on Lake Neusiedl with storks on its chimneys, whose sweet Ausbruch made it rich; it paid for its status as a royal free town in 1681 partly with wine.

sites.name: Weingut Feiler-Artinger
sites.text: A family estate in a baroque house in Rust, famous for Ruster Ausbruch and Blaufränkisch-based red blends.

sites.name: Kracher
sites.text: The Illmitz estate of Alois 'Luis' Kracher (died 2007), whose numbered TBAs made Seewinkel botrytis wines world famous; now run by his son Gerhard. Coordinates mark Illmitz.

sites.name: Weingut Gernot und Heike Heinrich
sites.text: A Gols estate that co-founded the Pannobile group of local red blends and moved to biodynamics, with vineyards on the lake's north shore and the Leithaberg.

sites.name: Seewinkel
sites.text: The flat 'lake corner' east of Lake Neusiedl with Illmitz, Apetlon and Podersdorf, dotted with salty ponds; its autumn mists make it one of the world's most reliable sources of noble rot. Part of the Fertő/Neusiedlersee UNESCO landscape (2001) and a national park.

sites.name: Neusiedler See
sites.text: Central Europe's largest steppe lake, 315 square kilometres but at most 1.8 metres deep, shared with Hungary. It warms the region, moderates frost and feeds the autumn mists that bring botrytis.

sites.name: Weingut Prieler
sites.text: The Schützen am Gebirge estate of the Prieler family, whose Goldberg Blaufränkisch from mica schist is a Leithaberg icon.

sites.name: Leithagebirge
sites.text: A low range of Leitha limestone and schist between the Vienna basin and Lake Neusiedl that gives the Leithaberg DAC its mineral character.

sites.name: Rosaliengebirge
sites.text: The forested hills of the Rosalia DAC, crowned by a chapel to St. Rosalia.

sites.name: Weingut Gesellmann
sites.text: A Deutschkreutz estate whose Blaufränkisch from old vines and Opus Eximium blend are Mittelburgenland classics.

sites.name: Moric (Lutzmannsburg)
sites.text: Roland Velich's Moric made its name from century-old Blaufränkisch vines at Lutzmannsburg and Neckenmarkt, fermented and aged without makeup to show soil rather than oak. Coordinates mark Lutzmannsburg village.

sites.name: Eisenberg
sites.text: A greenschist hill near Deutsch-Schützen in southern Burgenland, giving its name to the DAC and to Blaufränkisch of finesse.

sites.name: Ried Zieregg
sites.class: Südsteiermark Riedenwein site; STK Große Lage
sites.text: A steep amphitheatre of coral limestone and marl on the Slovenian border at Ehrenhausen, Tement's flagship. Zieregg Sauvignon Blanc is one of the most complex in the world.

sites.name: Weingut Tement
sites.text: Manfred Tement and his sons Armin and Stefan built the Ehrenhausen estate into Styria's most famous; they also farm across the border as Ciringa.

sites.name: Ried Grassnitzberg
sites.class: Südsteiermark Riedenwein site; STK Große Lage
sites.text: A south-facing slope of opok marl near Spielfeld, giving taut, smoky Sauvignon Blanc. Polz and Tement are key owners.

sites.name: Weingut Polz
sites.text: The Spielfeld estate of Erich and Walter Polz, specialists in Sauvignon Blanc from Grassnitzberg and Hochgrassnitzberg.

sites.name: Weingut Gross
sites.text: A Ratsch family estate known for Sauvignon and Morillon from the Nussberg and for finely tuned, long-lived whites.

sites.name: Weingut Sattlerhof
sites.text: Gamlitz estate of the Sattler family, now organic, known for Sauvignon from the Kranachberg and Pfarrweingarten.

sites.name: Kitzeck im Sausal
sites.text: A hilltop village in the Sausal whose slate vineyards climb to over 600 metres, among the highest in Austria; it has a wine museum and Wohlmuth's estate.

sites.name: Weingut Neumeister
sites.text: The Straden estate of Christoph Neumeister, the Vulkanland's leading producer of Sauvignon Blanc and Weißburgunder on volcanic soils.

sites.name: Weinbaumuseum Klöch
sites.text: The wine museum of Klöch on the slopes of an extinct volcano, the home of Styrian Traminer.

sites.name: Schilcherweinstraße (Stainz)
sites.text: The Schilcher wine route through West Styria starts in Stainz, a market town with a castle, and links Buschenschanken serving the region's pink Blauer Wildbacher wine.

sites.name: Nussberg
sites.text: A limestone hill above Nussdorf and Grinzing with views over the Danube and the city, home of Vienna's finest Gemischter Satz and Riesling and a ring of Heurigen.

sites.name: Bisamberg
sites.class: Vineyard hill north of the Danube
sites.text: Vienna's vineyard hill on the left bank of the Danube above Stammersdorf and Strebersdorf, with loess and gravel soils and a long Heurigen tradition.

sites.name: Weingut Wieninger
sites.text: Fritz Wieninger's Stammersdorf estate led the revival of Vienna wine and the creation of the Gemischter Satz DAC; it farms the Nussberg and Bisamberg biodynamically.

sites.name: Mayer am Pfarrplatz
sites.text: A Heuriger and wine estate in Heiligenstadt in the house where Beethoven lived in 1817, now owned by the Rotes Haus group and known for Nussberg Gemischter Satz.

sites.name: Dézaley
sites.text: The terraces of Dézaley, founded by Cistercian monks in the twelfth century, drop to the lake between Epesses and Rivaz. Chasselas here is the richest and longest-lived in Switzerland.

sites.name: Calamin
sites.text: Sixteen hectares of slowly slipping clay-limestone terraces at Epesses, the smallest AOC in Switzerland; its Chasselas is earthy and full.

sites.name: Clos des Abbayes
sites.text: A walled vineyard owned by the city of Lausanne since the Reformation, when it took over church property from the Cistercians; its annual auction is a Lavaux event.

sites.name: Clos des Moines
sites.text: The neighbouring clos owned by the city of Lausanne, also a former monastic vineyard, at Treytorrens in the Dézaley; like the Clos des Abbayes its wine is sold at an annual city auction.

sites.name: Lavaux Vinorama
sites.text: A wine centre at Rivaz at the foot of the Dézaley that sells and pours wines from all Lavaux producers and tells the region's story.

sites.name: Lavaux terraces (UNESCO)
sites.text: About 830 hectares of terraced vineyards on 30 km of Lake Geneva's north shore, built by monks from the eleventh century and inscribed by UNESCO as 'Lavaux, Vineyard Terraces' in 2007.

sites.name: Fête des Vignerons, Vevey
sites.text: Vevey's market square hosts the Fête des Vignerons, staged by the Confrérie des Vignerons since 1797, about once a generation. The 2019 edition had a 20,000-seat arena and some 6,000 performers.

sites.name: Château de Chillon
sites.text: The famous lakeside castle near Montreux has its own small vineyard, the Clos de Chillon, and wine has been stored in its vaults for centuries.

sites.name: Yvorne
sites.text: A Chablais village whose vineyards lie on the debris of a great landslide in 1584; its Chasselas is famous for its flinty, smoky character.

sites.name: Château d'Aigle (Musée de la Vigne et du Vin)
sites.text: A medieval castle among vineyards above Aigle that houses the Vaud wine museum and a wine-label museum.

sites.name: Féchy
sites.text: A La Côte village known for structured Chasselas, home of Raymond Paccot's biodynamic Domaine de la Colombe.

sites.name: Mont-sur-Rolle
sites.text: One of the largest wine communes of Vaud, on slopes above Rolle facing the lake and Mont Blanc.

sites.name: Visperterminen (Riebe vineyards)
sites.text: Terraced vineyards climbing from about 650 to over 1,100 metres above Visp, often called among the highest in Europe, planted with Heida (Savagnin). The St. Jodern cooperative and the 'Heidadorf' village make it a pilgrimage for Alpine wine. Coordinates mark the village.

sites.name: Salgesch
sites.text: A wine village at the French-German language border in the Valais, known for Pinot Noir and its own Grand Cru rules; it shares the Valais wine museum with Sierre.

sites.name: Château de Villa (Musée valaisan de la Vigne et du Vin)
sites.text: A sixteenth-century manor in Sierre housing the Valais wine museum's oenothèque and a restaurant famous for raclette; the museum's second site is in Salgesch, linked by a vineyard trail.

sites.name: Chamoson
sites.class: Largest wine commune of the Valais
sites.text: A broad alluvial fan below the Haut de Cry, the Valais' largest wine commune and a stronghold of Johannisberg (Sylvaner).

sites.name: Fully
sites.text: A granite slope at the bend of the Rhône below Martigny, famous for Petite Arvine, Gamay and Marie-Thérèse Chappaz's biodynamic sweet wines.

sites.name: Vétroz
sites.text: The village that holds most of the world's tiny plantings of Amigne, labelled with one to three bees for sweetness.

sites.name: Château d'Auvernier
sites.text: A sixteenth-century château and the largest private estate in Neuchâtel, run by the Montmollin family for generations.

sites.name: Château de Boudry
sites.text: A medieval castle housing the Musée de la vigne et du vin of Neuchâtel and the Compagnie des Vignolants wine brotherhood.

sites.name: Ligerz
sites.text: A wine village on the steep north shore of Lake Biel, with a vineyard museum and a hillside church among the vines.

sites.name: Fläsch
sites.text: The northernmost village of the Bündner Herrschaft, home of Gantenbein, whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are among Switzerland's most coveted.

sites.name: Maienfeld
sites.text: The 'Heidi' town of the Bündner Herrschaft, centre of Pinot Noir in Graubünden, home of Schloss Salenegg, one of the oldest wine estates in Switzerland.

sites.name: Malans
sites.class: Bündner Herrschaft village, home of Completer
sites.text: The village where the ancient Completer grape survived, now made by Donatsch and others; also fine Pinot Noir from Georg Fromm and Thomas Studach.

sites.name: Agroscope Wädenswil
sites.text: The federal research station on Lake Zurich, on Müller-Thurgau-Strasse, heir to the 1890 Wädenswil fruit and wine institute where Hermann Müller worked.

sites.name: Weinbaumuseum am Zürichsee
sites.text: A wine museum in Au near Wädenswil with historic presses, on a peninsula of vineyards above Lake Zurich.

sites.name: Hallau
sites.text: The largest wine commune of German-speaking Switzerland, a sea of Pinot Noir around a hilltop church.

sites.name: Gudo
sites.text: A village on the sunny right bank of the Ticino plain near Bellinzona whose granite terraces give fine Merlot.

sites.name: Mendrisio
sites.text: The wine capital of the southern Ticino, centre of the Mendrisiotto vineyards on limestone and clay, hit by Japanese beetle in 2025.

sites.name: Wormeldinger Koeppchen
sites.text: A steep shell-limestone slope above Wormeldange crowned by a chapel, Luxembourg's most famous Riesling vineyard.

sites.name: Musée du Vin, Ehnen
sites.text: A wine-growers' house in the village of Ehnen, now a museum of Moselle viticulture with old presses and a vineyard.

sites.name: Caves Bernard-Massard
sites.text: Grevenmacher's leading sparkling-wine house, with cellars tunnelled into the hillside and one of the largest Crémant productions in Luxembourg.

sites.name: Institut viti-vinicole, Remich
sites.text: The state institute in Remich that analyses every Luxembourg wine, runs the Marque Nationale and does vine research.

sites.name: Schengen
sites.class: Southern gateway of the wine route
sites.text: The wine village at the meeting point of Luxembourg, Germany and France where the Schengen Agreement was signed on a Moselle riverboat in 1985; its castle estate is home to Domaine Thill.

sites.name: Nyetimber
sites.text: The estate at West Chiltington where Stuart and Sandy Moss planted Champagne grapes in 1988; owned since 2006 by Eric Heerema and made by Cherie Spriggs, it now farms about 425 ha across Sussex, Hampshire and Kent and won the IWC Champion Sparkling Wine trophy in 2025.

sites.name: Ridgeview
sites.text: Founded by Mike and Christine Roberts at Ditchling Common in 1995, Ridgeview made only sparkling wine from the start and led the campaign for the Sussex PDO.

sites.name: Rathfinny Wine Estate
sites.text: A large chalk-downland estate near Alfriston, planted from 2012 by Mark and Sarah Driver, three miles from the sea.

sites.name: Wiston Estate
sites.text: The Goring family's estate below Chanctonbury Ring on the South Downs chalk, planted in 2006; its early vintages were made by Dermot Sugrue. Coordinates mark Wiston parish.

sites.name: Bolney Wine Estate
sites.text: One of the oldest Sussex vineyards, planted in 1972 at Bolney in the Weald, known for still Pinot Noir as well as sparkling.

sites.name: Breaky Bottom
sites.text: Peter Hall's tiny vineyard in a fold of the South Downs near Rodmell, planted in 1974 and famous for sparkling Seyval Blanc.

sites.name: Gusbourne
sites.text: An estate at Appledore in Kent, on the edge of Romney Marsh, planted in 2004, known for vintage sparkling and still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Chapel Down
sites.text: England's largest wine brand, at Small Hythe near Tenterden, famous for Bacchus and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Hambledon Vineyard
sites.text: Planted by Sir Guy Salisbury-Jones in 1952 on Hampshire chalk and revived from 1999 by Ian Kellett, who made it a traditional-method sparkling estate.

sites.name: Hattingley Valley
sites.text: A Hampshire chalk estate near Medstead and Lower Wield, founded in 2008 and known for a winery that makes wine for many smaller growers.

sites.name: Camel Valley
sites.text: Bob and Annie Lindo's Cornish vineyard, founded in 1989 and now run by their son Sam, with award-winning sparkling wine and the Darnibole Bacchus PDO.

sites.name: Denbies Wine Estate
sites.text: One of the largest single vineyards in England, on the North Downs chalk near Dorking, planted in 1986.

sites.name: Painshill Park vineyard
sites.text: Charles Hamilton's 1740s landscape garden in Surrey included a vineyard whose sparkling wine was said to be sold as Champagne; it has been replanted.

sites.name: Wollaston Roman vineyard
sites.text: Excavations in the Nene valley near Wollaston found trenches for a Roman vineyard covering several hectares, the best evidence of Roman wine-growing in Britain.

sites.name: Ancre Hill
sites.text: A biodynamic estate near Monmouth, Wales' best-known vineyard, making sparkling and still wines.

sites.name: Domaine du Chant d'Eole
sites.text: An estate at Quévy near Mons planted from 2010 on chalk among wind turbines, now Belgium's most famous sparkling-wine producer.

sites.name: Ruffus (Domaine des Agaises)
sites.text: Raymond Leroy's estate at Haulchin near Binche, planted from 2002 on chalk with Champagne grapes, a pioneer of Belgian sparkling wine.

sites.name: Château de Bioul
sites.class: Côtes de Sambre et Meuse / Crémant de Wallonie
sites.text: A castle estate near Anhée in the Meuse valley whose owners replanted vines and built a modern winery.

sites.name: Wijnkasteel Genoels-Elderen
sites.text: A castle estate at Riemst near Tongeren, Belgium's best-known and long its largest wine estate, with oak-aged Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Wijndomein Aldeneyck
sites.text: An estate at Aldeneik near Maaseik on the Maas gravel terraces, one of the leading Flemish producers.

sites.name: Wijngoed Monteberg
sites.text: A vineyard on the slopes of the Monteberg at Dranouter in the Heuvelland hills, close to the French border and the First World War front.

sites.name: Apostelhoeve
sites.class: PDO Mergelland; oldest modern Dutch vineyard (1970)
sites.text: A farm estate on the Louwberg south of Maastricht where the Hulst family planted vines in 1970, beginning the modern Dutch wine revival.

sites.name: Wijngaard St. Martinus
sites.text: A vineyard on the slopes near Vijlen in the Limburg hills, the sole producer of the Vijlen PDO.

sites.name: Wijngoed Thorn
sites.text: A vineyard and tasting room in the white-washed village of Thorn on the Maas, one of the leading Dutch estates.

sites.name: Hof te Oolde
sites.text: A large estate near Laren in Gelderland, farmed with fungus-resistant grapes and holder of the Oolde PDO.

sites.name: Wijngaard Hof van Twente
sites.text: A Twente estate near Bentelo, sole producer of the Ambt Delden PDO.

sites.name: Wijngaard Hesselink
sites.text: A family vineyard at Winterswijk-Henxel, the main producer of the Achterhoek-Winterswijk PDO.

sites.name: Wageningse Berg vineyard
sites.text: A vineyard on the moraine slope of the Wageningse Berg above the Rhine, linked to the town's agricultural tradition.

sites.name: Skærsøgaard
sites.text: Sven Moesgaard's estate at Dons near Kolding, planted in 1998, whose sparkling wines led to Denmark's first PDO.

sites.name: Dyrehøj Vingaard
sites.text: A vineyard on the Røsnæs peninsula near Kalundborg, one of Denmark's largest and best known.

sites.name: Lille Gadegård
sites.text: A Bornholm farm estate near Pedersker that makes wine, cider and spirits in the island's sunny climate.

sites.name: Kullabergs Vingård
sites.text: A vineyard near Arild on the Kullaberg peninsula, on sea-warmed slopes facing the Kattegat.

sites.name: Arilds Vingård
sites.text: One of Sweden's best-known estates, at Brunnby near Arild on the Kullaberg, with sparkling and still wines.

sites.name: Valtice Château and Salon vín
sites.class: National Wine Salon in the Liechtenstein château cellars
sites.text: The baroque château of the Liechtensteins at Valtice, part of the Lednice-Valtice Cultural Landscape (UNESCO, 1996), houses in its cellars the Salon vín České republiky, which each year presents the 100 best Czech wines chosen in a national competition. Valtice also had a wine school from 1873.

sites.name: Mikulov Castle
sites.text: The Dietrichstein château towering over Mikulov houses the regional museum and a giant wine barrel built in 1643, one of the largest in central Europe.

sites.name: Svatý kopeček, Mikulov
sites.text: A limestone hill with a Way of the Cross and chapel above Mikulov's vineyards, with views over the Pálava and the Austrian border.

sites.name: Děvín (Pálava hills)
sites.class: Highest point of the Pálava, UNESCO biosphere reserve
sites.text: The 549-metre summit of the Pálava hills, a Jurassic limestone ridge whose southern slopes are planted with vines among protected steppe grassland.

sites.name: Vinařství Sonberk
sites.text: A modern winery on the Sonberk hill at Popice, overlooking the Nové Mlýny reservoirs and the Pálava, known for Riesling and Pálava.

sites.name: Kraví hora, Bořetice
sites.class: VOC Kraví hora cellar village and lookout
sites.text: A sunny hill above Bořetice with rows of wine cellars, a lookout tower and vineyards on loess and sandstone, now its own VOC.

sites.name: Šobes vineyard
sites.text: A sun-trap slope in a meander of the Dyje in the Podyjí National Park, one of the oldest vineyards in central Europe and its own PDO.

sites.name: Znojmo
sites.text: A historic town on a cliff above the Dyje, with an underground labyrinth once used for wine, an annual historic harvest festival and the first Czech VOC.

sites.name: Novosedly
sites.text: A large wine village west of Mikulov, the only village with its own straw-wine PDO.

sites.name: Mělník Château (Lobkowicz)
sites.class: Historic château winery at the Elbe-Vltava confluence
sites.text: The Lobkowicz château on a cliff above the meeting of the Vltava and the Elbe, with terraced vineyards below and cellars that are the symbol of Bohemian wine.

sites.name: Grébovka (Prague Vinohrady)
sites.text: A restored vineyard and pavilion in the Havlíčkovy sady park in the Prague district of Vinohrady, named after the vineyards Charles IV encouraged around the city.

sites.name: Svätý Jur
sites.class: Royal free town of the Little Carpathians
sites.text: A small Little Carpathian town that became a royal free town in the seventeenth century thanks to its wine trade, with burgher houses, courtyard cellars and vineyards climbing to the forest.

sites.name: Pezinok Castle (Zámok Pezinok)
sites.text: A castle in Pezinok, a royal free town since the seventeenth century, whose cellars are used by a winery; the town hosts Little Carpathian wine festivals.

sites.name: Modra
sites.class: Royal free town and seat of Slovak grape research
sites.text: A royal free town since the seventeenth century, famous for its majolica pottery and its vine research station, where Slovak grape crossings were developed.

sites.name: Château Topoľčianky
sites.text: A large winery in Topoľčianky, the Habsburg estate town with its castle and national stud, in the Nitra region.

sites.name: Malá Tŕňa tuff cellars
sites.text: A Slovak Tokaj village whose hillside is riddled with cellars cut into volcanic tuff, including those of Tokaj Macik and other producers.

sites.name: Tokaj Macik Winery
sites.text: One of the leading Slovak Tokaj producers, based in Malá Tŕňa with historic tuff cellars.

sites.name: Viničky
sites.text: The easternmost Slovak Tokaj village, whose name means 'little vineyards', on the edge of the Bodrog plain.

sites.name: Veľká Tŕňa
sites.text: A Tokaj village with long rows of tuff cellars and producers such as J&J Ostrožovič.

sites.name: Palm House on Wine Hill, Zielona Góra
sites.text: A glass palm house on Zielona Góra's Wine Hill, surrounded by a small vineyard, symbol of the city's wine tradition and centre of the Winobranie festival held since 1852.

sites.name: Winnica Srebrna Góra
sites.text: A vineyard on limestone slopes below the Camaldolese monastery at Bielany in Kraków, one of Poland's largest.

sites.name: Winnica Turnau
sites.text: A large vineyard at Baniewice in West Pomerania, near the German border, one of Poland's most successful modern wineries.

sites.name: Winnica Płochockich
sites.text: A family vineyard and guest house at Przyłogi near Sandomierz in the Vistula valley.

sites.name: Winnica Jasło
sites.text: A vineyard at Ulaszowice near Jasło, the centre of Podkarpacie's wine revival.
